Literature R eview
Luxury Brands on the Social M edia Landscape
T he communication st rategies of luxury brands on soci al media remain a topi c of debate
(Irshaid et al., 2020). This tension may stem from the reluctance of luxury brands to fully
embrace digital platforms, as some fear that increased visibility can undermine uniqueness
(Oliveira & Fernandes, 2022). On one hand, a new generation of luxury consumers, who are
more comfortable with digital commu nication, has prompted a shift in how luxury products are
consumed and discussed (Irshaid et al., 2020). This evolution has sparked significant academic
interest in the intersection of luxury branding and social media marketing (Creevey et al., 2022).
On the other hand, the potential risk of brand dilution (Park et al., 2020) reinforces the urgent
need for luxury brands to maintain control over their narratives (Pentina et al., 2018).
At its core, luxury is linked to attributes such as durability, exceptional performance, and
distinctive design (Brun & Castelli, 2013), while also acting as a status symbol tha t carries
psychological value (Nelissen & Meijers, 2011). Luxury brands are distinguished by their
uniqueness, premium pricing, and emotional resonance they evoke in consumers (Heine & Phan,
2011). This symbolic dimension of luxury evokes complex consumer experiences (Ko et al.,
that go beyond product ownership, centring on identity expression, social distinction, and
the pursuit of aspirational lifestyle s (Neuhofer et al., 2021). O n social media, these as pirational
qualities are amplifi ed as consumers eng age with entertainm ent-driven, visually impactful, and
socially interactive content that fosters emotional connections and shapes attitudes toward luxury
brands (Aldhamiri et al., 2024).
As inconsistencies in brand communication can lead to mixed impressions among
consumers (Lee & Cho, 2025), it is crucial for luxury brands to enhance community engagement
through storytelling and deeper connections with their audience (Üçok Hughes et al., 2016).
Research indicates that the more consumers engage in discussions about a brand on social media,
the higher their purchase intentions tend to be (Park et al., 2021). Furthermore, brand-consumer
dialogue on social media is essential not only for enhancing brand visibility but for conveying
brand vision and identity (Heine & Berghaus, 2014). Engaging potential consumers goes beyond
mere ly informational content and taps into emotional connections (Creevey et al., 2022). Since
the aesthetic appeal o f products is a v ital aspect of fost ering engagement, luxury brands need to
provide optimal digital experiences i n an era where social media is satur ated with visual i magery
(Aldhamiri et al., 2024).
V isual A esthetics in L uxury Br anding
Understanding visual aesthetics involves two primary paradigms: subjective and
objective (Keshtkaran et al., 2017). The subjective paradigm relies on individual perception and
experiences, whereas the objective paradigm focuses on the inherent qualities of an object
(Kerebel et al., 2019), such as symmetry, balance, and harmonious proportions. While the
objective approach offers a more standardised framework for evaluating aesthetics, it remains
underutilised in aes thetic preferenc e analysis (Gülçin & Yalçınkaya, 2024), potentially due to the
complexity of quantifying inherent qualities. Building on the objective paradigm, scholars in
digital marketing have identified classical an d expressive aesth etics as two key framework s for
understanding design effectiveness (Bhandari et al., 2019; Lavie & Tractinsky, 2004). C lassical
aesthetics emphasise o rder, symmetry, and clarity in design (Lee et al., 2018). Ex pressive
aesthetics highlight creativity an d originality (Kusumasondjaja, 2019), incorporating complexity,
vibrant colours, and asymmetrical arrangements (Lee et al., 2018).
For luxury brands, visual elements (e.g., style, design, colour, logo, and shape) shape
perceptions of product quality and social status, influencing the emotional value of the luxury
consumption experience (Butcher et al., 2016). Thoughtfully designed visuals are not mere
aesthetic s but strategic tools to enhance interaction on visually centred plat forms such as
Instagram (Kusumasondjaja, 2019). A visually appealing design can stimulate customers to
engage with their preferred luxury brands on social media (Bazi et al., 2020). Expressive
aesthetics, like asymmetry, evoke arousal and hedonic motivation, thereby enhancing user
engagement on social media (Kusumasondjaja, 2019). Within expressive aesthetics, visual
complexity plays a nuanced role. For users unfamiliar with the brand, higher visual complexity
boosts luxury perceptions, while simpler imagery is perceived as more luxurious by those
familiar with the brand (Lee et al., 2018).
Despite the growing recognition, visual aesthetics in luxury branding faces significant
challenges. The hum an affective system continually generates spontaneous visual preferences
(Graf & Landwehr, 2015), making it essential to balance individual design elements with
overarching concepts to craft cohesive visu al narratives. Howev er, much research rem ains
fragmented, often focusing on isolated element s such as colo u r (Kanuri et al., 2024; Yu & Egger,
2021). Effective design requires an integrat ed approach that quant ifies visual aesth etics into a
single unified framework (Mayer & Landwehr, 2018), aligning aest hetic appeal with branding
goals. Another challenge is the reliance on manual data coding methods (Kusumasondjaja,
2019), which can be subjective and time-consuming. Consequently, inter disciplinary research is
encouraged (Keshtkaran et al., 2017) to advance understanding of visual aesthetics in luxury
branding (Kusumasondjaja, 2019) to better explore the interplay between v isual materials and
consumer engagement in the digital landscape (Kanuri et al., 2024).
Quantifying V isual A esthetic T hrough Image F luency
The greater the perceptual fluency, the more favou rable the aesthetic j udgment (Reber et
al., 2004). One way to quantify visual aesthetic pr eferences is by examining the concept of image
fluency (Gülçin & Yalçınkaya, 2024). Rooted in the theory of processing fluency, this notion
concerns to the ease o f mental processin g (Mayer & Landwehr, 2018; Yu et al., 2024). While
processing fluency influences brand evaluations (Hur et al., 2020) and user engagement on social
media marketing (Yu et al., 2024) mainly via textual and person- centric content, its application
to the visual structural elements of luxury branding remains empirically underdeveloped. To
employ processing fluency to visuals, image fluency is defined by four core low- lev el visual
characteristics: symmetry, self- similarity, simplicity, and contrast (Mayer & Landwehr, 2018).
Scholars have explored these effects in logos (Séraphin et al., 2016), website design (Lavie &
Tractinsky, 2004), and advertisements (Hur et al., 2020). However, their implications for luxury
branding are especially distinct due to the unique consumer expectations and symbolic values
associated with luxury goods (Ko et al., 2019).
Visual simplicity, contrast ing with complexity, is the amount of infor mation processed
with minimal cognitive effort (Gülç in & Yalçınkaya, 2024). Although simpler features are
generally easier to process than complex ones (Lee et al., 2018), extremely low complexity may
reduce engagement, whereas moderate complexity can enhance aesthetic a rousal in line with
classical arousal t heory (Silvia, 2005). Interestingly, in luxury contexts, younger generations'
emotional connection drives a preference for minimalism, fostering deeper appreciation and
reducing excessive consumption (Polisetty & Pahari, 2025). The rise of minimalism has made
strategic use of white space, unoccupied areas free from other design elements, a key tool to
enhance luxury perception and signal superior product quality (Iseki et al., 2025). On social
media branding platforms, low visual complexity reinforces scarcity and exclusivity, serving as
essential attributes of luxury consumption (Lee et al., 2018).
S elf- similarity, another facet of image flu ency, refers to repeating patterns within objects
and is often observed in natural phenomena such as clouds (Peng et al., 2024). Research shows
that both complex natural environments and artworks such as cartoons and photographs (Koch et
al., 2010) exhibit higher self- similarity across multiple resolution sc ales than other image types.
S elf- similarity parallels image similarity in brand extension literatur e, where shared attributes
between a brand and its extensions influence consumer evaluation s (Kim et al., 2020). Ju st as
image similarity facilitates a ssociation and perception transfer ( Punj & Moon, 2022), self-
similarity in luxury design, manifested in consistent motifs like Louis Vuitton's monogram or
Gucci's GG pattern, reinf orces brand identity. In luxury branding, a differentiated brand identity
and value proposition are critical to meeti ng both practical n eeds and emotional desires (Fionda
& Moore, 2009). Thus, self- similarity not only enhance s visual appeal by creating coheren ce
(Deng et al., 2010) but also accentuates luxury brand value.
Furthermore, v isual symmetry involves mirror ed similarity of image parts arou nd a
central axis (Mayer & Landwehr, 2018), easily recognised and linked to simplicity, timelessness,
and continuity (Treder, 2010). It influences marketing outcomes in package design (Bigoin-
Gagnan & Lacoste-Badie, 2018) and brand logo (Luffarelli et al., 2019; Mayer & Landwehr,
2018), especially with celebrity endorsers (Jin & Ryu, 2019). Visual asymmetry, on the other
hand, may enhance consumer ev aluations and in crease brand value for brands with an exciting
personality, though not for other traits (Luffarelli et al., 2019). For luxury displays, symmetry
became a defining aes thetic since the lat e 17 th century, tied to natural history collections,
decorative cabinets, and the fusion of architectural beauty, curiosity, and elite consumption
(Spary, 2004). In luxury branding, symmetrical designs convey balance (Venkatesh et al., 2010)
and appeal to harmony-seeking consumers (Luffarelli et al., 2019). Bajaj and Bond (2018)
highlighted a strong link between symmetry and perceived brand sophistication, aligning with
Messaris (1997) on luxury's classical, tranquil, and structure d a esthetic where symmetry is
fundamental.
Moreover, visual contrast, the perceptual distinction between figure and ground,
enhances image fluency by directing attention and improving visual discrimination (Gülçin &
Yalçınkaya, 2024). It is not merely stylistic but a ke y determinant of how much informa tion is
retained and how quickly it is processed after distortion or transformation (Reber et al., 2004).
Drawing from image quality research, improvements in contrast can enhance perceived visual
quality, even if they alter to the original image (Sheikh & Bovik, 2006). While much litera ture
focuses on figure-ground contrast, overall design contrast is crucial for standing out in a market
(Mayer & Landwehr, 2018). In luxury contexts, however, moderate colo u r contrast more
strong ly influence s stay- attraction than excessively high or low contrast, which can damp en
perceived luxury (Cho & Suh, 2020). This aligns with flagship retail observations, where luxury
brands prioritise visual harmony over stark contrast to cultivat e immersive experiences (Moo re
& Doherty, 2007). Thus, contrast aids legibility and salience but is context-dependent, a nd its
application in digital luxury contexts remains understudied.
Methodology
Luxur y Brands S election and Data E xtraction
To derive insights from exemplary practices, this study draws on the Gartner Digital IQ
Index (Marzano et al., 2021), which quantifies the digital competence of leading luxury brands.
This index evaluates a brand's digital performance across key dimensions, including search
engine optimisation (e.g., traffic and keyword effectiveness), brand translation (e.g., aesthetics
and messaging), leveraging the medium (e.g., user interface and interactivity), social media
presence, and user- gener ated mentions.
Within the luxury category, a total of 73 brands is classified into five le vels: Genius
(n=3), Gifted (n=10), Average (n=48), Challenged (n=7), and Feeble (n=4). Brands designated as
“Genius” brands demonstrate superior search visibility, aesthet ic coherence, functionality, and
interactivity, giving them a strong competitive edge on social media. “Gifted” brands are also
digitally advanced, typically offering e- commerce integration and enhanced web applications. In
this research, the top three Genius and Gifted brands serve as the primary data s ources for further
analysis.
Given the emphasis of luxury brands on visually driven platforms to enhan ce image and
engagement (Kusumasondjaja, 2019; Yoo, 2023), Instagram was selected for data extraction.
Table 2 lists the selected brands and their associated account information. Data extraction was
conducted in January 2025. All available posts from the six brands were scraped. After excluding
video-based posts, the dataset contain ed a total of 31,387 posts. The extracted data included the
number of likes and comments, post URLs, image URLs, captions, and timestamps.
Specifically, the number of likes and comments was transformed into user engagement
rates by dividing the total by the number of followers of the corresponding account. This
adjustment controls differences in brand audience size and allows for fairer comparisons of
engagement across accounts with varying follower counts. To account for temporal variation in
engagement, the datas et was re-extracted based on post URLs two weeks later (Yu & Egger,
2021). This allowed time for engagement to stabilise. The updated figures were used to calculate
final engagement rate s, ensuring consistency across posts with post timing. Yet, some posts have
been archived or removed from the account, resulting in a final dataset of 30,770 posts. Notably,
although captions were also retrieved, these non- numerical text data were excluded from th e
visual-analytic model described in subsequent sections.

Image Annotation and C lustering
Due to the focus on visual content, all images were bulk downloaded based on their
URLs. Next, acknowledging that luxury brands may share a variety of products and categories,
the initial step involved annotating the extracted images. Specifically, the Google Cloud Vision
API was employed using an R package. A maximum of seven labels was returned for each
image, which represented the key features and objects identified within the visual content. These
labels provided valuable insights into the types of products being showcased and their
associations within the luxury market. Subsequently, BERTopic (Grootendorst, 2020) with a
silhouette- optimi s ed k-means clustering algorithm was employed to extract topics from detected
image labels (Groot et al., 2022). The datas et of textual l abels was first proces sed using
lemmati sation to standardise word forms, ensuring semantic consistency before embedding
generation and topic extraction. Next, BERTopic was used to generate topics with all- MiniLM-
L6- v2 embedding model (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019) and UMAP (Uniform Manifold
Approximation and Projection) for dimensionality reduction (McInnes et al., 2018).
The topic embeddings were then clustered using k- means with silhouette analysis to
optimise the number of clusters. For each k-value, the silhouette score, an internal validation
metric that measures clustering qua lity, was computed using cosine similarity. The k-value with
the highest silhouette score, 0.492 in this study, was selected as the optimal number of clusters,
which was 13. Keywords were generated through BERTopic's class- based term frequency-
inverse document frequency (c- TF- IDF) algorithm, which weights ter ms by their inter- cluster
distinctiveness while preserving contextual relationships through transformer-derived
embeddings. Gensim's CoherenceModel ( c_v score) (Röder et al., 2015) was used to assess the
semantic consistency of top words per topic, leveraging a dictionary-filtered representation of
tokenised labels. The resulting coherence value was 0.574, demonstrating a moderate to high
level of topic coheren ce and clustering effectiveness.
Analysis of Image F luency
T he R package imagefluency is used to detect image fluency scores for each picture to
measure the fluent cog nitive processin g of images. The aesth etics metrics incl ude image
simplicity, contrast, self- similar ity, and symmetry (Gülçin, 2021). Image simplicity r efers to the
ease with which an image can be understood and is calculated as one minus its complexity.
Image contrast indi cates the difference b etween the light and dark areas of an image, where high
contrast can make an im age more visu ally striking. Self- similarity m easures the presence of
repeated patterns wit hin an image. Symmetry assesses the balance and proportion within an
image, with this study focusing on horizontal symmetry. Notably, rather than treating individual
visual features as sep arate antecedents of aesthetic appeal, this study conce ptuali s es the metrics
as four operational dimensions that together define image fluency. Meanwhile, ins tead of
estimating causal ef fects at the aggregate l evel, the focus on visual- level predictors allows the
exploration of the explanatory power of image fluency for each visually co herent cluster. Visual
examples and concret e illustrations b ased on the current dat asets are demon strated in Figure 1.

Robustness Check with Control Variables
To further ensure that the effects of image fluency on engagement were not driven by
omitted low- level visual factors, a suppl ementary robust ness test was condu cted at the aggregat e
level. While the main an alyses were perfo rmed within vis ually coherent clusters, where each
cluster already repr esents a semanticall y and aesthetical ly homogeneous set of images, the
robustness test examined whether the four image-fluency dimensions remained significant after
introducing additional controls. Four widely used image- level variables were ad ded as controls:
brightness, colourfulness, saturation mean, and hue variance. Thes e factors are frequen tly
considered in prior image- analytics research to c apture colour properties that could influence
engagement ( Li & Xie, 2020; Wilms & Oberfeld, 2018). Two models were compar ed: a baseline
model including only the four fluency metrics (contrast, symmetry, complexity, and self-
similarity) and a full model including both the fluency metrics and the four control variables.
Model comparison was performed using the change in explained variance ( Δ R²) and the
F-change test to determine whether the inclusion of controls significantly improved fit. Variance-
inflation factors (VIFs) were also e xamined to assess potential multicollin earity among
predictors. This robustness analysis provided an additional check on the validity of the within-
cluster models.

Model Evaluation and Justification
To enhance robustness and transparency, this study evaluated three different modelling
approaches using Altair RapidMiner Studio, a data analytics platfor m that facilitates artificial
intelligence-driven automation for data predictions and model optimisation. The selected models
include random forest, support vector machine, and generalised linear models due to their
widespread use in marketing analytics, open-source availability, and ability to capture non- linear
patterns (Cui & Curry, 2005; Ellickson et al., 2023; Tsai et al., 2011). Random forest is an
ensemble learning method that builds multiple decision trees and averages their outputs to reduce
overfitting (Halabaku & Bytyçi, 2024). Support vector machines construct hyperplanes in high-
dimensional space to predict continuous outcomes (Cui & Curry, 2005). Generalised linear
models extend ordinary least squares regression to support non-normality and are particularly
suitable for modelling non-standard distributions (Kesleman et al., 2016).
To evaluate model perf ormance, two comm only accepted erro r metrics were used: Mean
Squared Error (MSE) and Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) (Willmott, 1982; Yu & Egger,
2021). MSE calculates th e average of the squar ed differences bet ween predicted and a ctual
values; RMSE represents the square root of MSE and is in the same unit as the dependent
variable. Lower valu es indicate better p redictive performan ce. As shown in Tabl e 4, generalised
linear models outperformed the other models in most cluster-specific applications, yielding the
lowest MSE and RMSE scores overall. Hence, for the sake of interpretability and consistent
predictive accuracy, generalised lin ear models were pref erred for subsequent analysis.

Essentially, Auto Model automatic ally generates optimi s ed cross-validated models and
highlights the model's most influential variables based on weight vectors, calculated based on a
local interpretable model explanations (LIME) method (Ribeiro et al., 2016). To uncover the
relationship between image fluency metrics and engagement rate, a combination of generalised
linear models (Duffett, 2017; Kesleman et al., 2016) and LIME (Yu & Egger, 2021; Zhang &
Srinivasan, 2023) was proceeded. The outco me variable was th e engagement rat e (as explained
in methodology), whereas the predictor variable included the four imag e fluency metrics.
Notably, LIME offer s a high degree of interpretability to machine learning by providing
local weights that indicate the most r elevant metrics influencing the model's predictions (Zhang
& Srinivasan, 2023), with values ranging from 0 to 1. Specifically, LIME approximates complex
machine learning models with simpler and interpretable models locally around individual
predictions. Generally, higher weights indicate a stronger influence of the corresponding metric
on the prediction. Yet, it is important to note that a weight of 0 does not necessarily suggests that
a specific metric is i rrelevant overall; rather, it may indicate that a particular variable does not
contribute significantly to predictions within th e study context (Yu & Egger, 2021).
D espite some might argue LIME as a black-box explanation tool, its inclusion in this
study was deliberate and driven by the complexity and high dimensionality of the dataset. The
goal was not merely to test linear or curvilinear associations, but to capture local and context-
specific patterns across heterogeneous clusters. Traditional regression models, while easier to
interpret, often assume linearity or quadratic relationships, which may not fully account for
visual features in image data. LIME, in contrast, approxi mates local decisio n b oundaries and
provides interpretable weights that reveal the dominant predictors for each segment (Ribeiro et
al., 2016). Though interpretability is a trade- off, LIME allows the extraction of key influencing
variables from a predictive model without assuming the nature of the functional form. This level
of granularity is essential in visual analysis, where aesthetic preferences may vary significantly
by cluster. Furthermore, as marketing decisions often require context- specific actionable outputs,
the use of AI- based predictive models prioritise s practical utility over theoretic al parsimony.
This approach aligns with recent calls for integrating AI-based model explanation techniques in
business and marketing to improve real-world predictive performance and strategy simulation
(Zhang & Srinivasan, 2023).
Interplay Between Image Fluency and User Engagement
Prior to performing the generalised linear models, feature selection was conducted to
ensure the inclusion of high-quality variables. This assessment was based on criteria including
the degree of correlation with the engagement rate, the proportion of constant non- missing
values, and the fraction of unique values. Thus, variables with high multicollinea rity or minimal
variation were excluded to improve model performance. This selection was implemented through
RapidMiner's Auto Model feature, which automatically evaluates input variables based on data
quality, relevance, and their contribution to predictive accuracy before finalising the most
effective variable s et for mode l training. Image fe atures identified as u nsuitable were t hen
excluded from the model to enhance overall performance and ensure robustness and reliability.
As part of the automated process handled internally by the system, manual addition of further
control variables was not feasible within the workflow. Yet, to improve methodological rigour,
likes count, comment count, and follower count were added to the input dataset for feature
evaluation; howeve r, as these variabl es are mathematical ly embedded in the en gagement- ra te
outcome, the Auto Model did not retain them as significant predictors.
Before delving into the effects across different clusters, the analysis initially began by
examining each specific brand to identify overarching trends. Overall, the findings suggest that
simplicity emerged as a significant pred ictor of engagemen t rate acr oss most brands, showing a
positive correlation when included in the model, ( p Chanel<0.001; p KateSpad e <0.001; p LouisVuitto n
=0.004; p RalphLaure n <0.001). Similarly, self- similarity w as identified as a critical fac tor for Coach
( p<0.001), Kate Spade ( p<0.001), and Ralph Lauren ( p<0.001). Yet, other metrics did not show
significant results at the brand level. While these general findings provide valuable insights, the
subsequent analysis focuses more deeply on the identified clusters, which group products based
on their shared visual characteristics. This focus on product- level clusters is particularly
important because social media alg orithms often recommend a mix of products to users, rather
than consistently showcasing a single brand. Consequently, consumers are more likely to
encounter multiple products simultaneously, making product- specific attributes more influen tial
in shaping engagement. Moreover, the identified clusters, which span across brands, offer
practical insights for brands with similar product categories to optimi s e their visual strategies.

Results of Robustness Check
The aggregate-level robustness analysis showed that adding four standard image- level
controls led to a small but statistica lly significant increase in e xplained variance ( Δ R² = 0.009, F-
change = 69.6, p < 0.001). All variance- inflation factors (VIF = 1.09–3.70) were below 5,
indicating low multicollinear ity. Importantly, the core image-fluency dimensions, particula rly
s elf-s imilarity ( β = 0.072, p < 0.001), complexity ( β = –.046, p < .001) and s ymmetry ( β =
−0.0 48, p < 0.001), remained significant and directionally stable. This finding suggests that
colo u r properties account for only limited additional variance beyond the theoretically grounded
fluency metrics, thereby suggesting the robustness and validity of the within- cluster models.
Discussion
The findings provide a nuanced understanding of the interplay between processing
fluency and user engagement (Gülçin & Yalçınkaya, 2024; Yu et al., 2024) with luxury brands
on social media (Aldhamiri et al., 2024; Lee & Cho, 2025). Central to this discussion is the role
of visual aesthetics (Gül çin & Yalçınkaya, 2024; Mayer & Landwehr, 2018), specifically
simplicity, self- similarity, symme try, and contrast, which operate not merely as decorative
elements but as subliminal factors shaping consumer perception and interaction in competitive
digital environments (Gülçin, 2021; Hur et al., 2020).
Overall, simplicity and self- simila rity emerge d as influential metrics of engagement
across luxury brand posts. Self- similarity, defined as the repetition of visual pattern s, proved
particularly influential. This aligns with the notion that luxury brands utilise self- simila rity to add
depth and richness to their campaigns to create more engaging narratives (Gurzki et al., 2019). In
fact, this design approach resonates with perceptua l priming in visual search tasks, which
suggests that exposure to certain stimuli facilitates the processing of similar subsequent stimuli
(Kristjánsson & Campana, 2010). In luxury contexts, consumers are naturally drawn to familiar
patterns (Kristjánsson & Campana, 2010), especial ly for high- value items such as bags,
jewellery, footwear, and clothing. Given the financial investment involved (Oliveira &
Fernandes, 2022), consumers often seek re assurance of quality and reliability (Brun & Castelli,
2013). Hence, repetition of messages can height en perceived credibility (Ernst et al., 2017) and
reinforc e the aesthetic co nsistency achieved through self- similar imagery (Gülçin & Yalçınkaya,
2024).
Moreover, simplicity plays a vital role in luxury branding by conveying exclusivity (Lee
et al., 2018) and enabling quick comprehension in digital communication (Yu et al., 2024). F or
wearable items (e.g., “formal attire” and “model edition”), higher levels of simplicity appear to
resonate more strongly with consumers, fostering emotional connections that reflect self- identity
and aspiration al lifestyle (Duong et al., 2023; Yoo, 2023). On a broader level, this supports
processing fluency theory, which posits that ease of cognitive processing leads to more positive
evaluations (Mayer & Landwehr, 2018). Hence, the principles of fluency extend beyond textual
content (Yu et al., 2024) to include image- based materials (Hur et al., 2020).
Conversely, the minimal impact of contrast presents an intriguing divergence from prior
findings, which typically associate high er contrast with great er visual appeal and attention
capture (Mayer & Landwehr, 2018; Reynolds-McIlnay et al., 2017). Although contrast generally
enhances visual hierarchy and emphasis es focal points (Gülçin & Yalçınkaya, 2024), this
research indicates t hat in luxury contexts, it may not impactfully contribute to engagement. On
social media, consumers may be shifting away from striking contrasts, which can elicit stronger
or even negative emotions such as anger and disgust (Voodla et al., 2020). Such responses are
misaligned with the exclusiv e vibe mentioned pr eviously (Lee et al., 2018). The reduced
importance of contrast, especially when considered alongside other metrics, suggests that brands
may need to re- evaluate their vis ual strategies to al ign with evolving consumer preferences
(Gurzki et al., 2019; Kusumasondjaja, 2019; Yoo, 2023).
Meanwhile, symmetry also did not uniformly enhance engagement across different
luxury topics. This inconsistency invites further inquiry into the psychological underpinnings
(Bajaj & Bond, 2018) in luxury branding. Prior research links symmetry with beauty, health, and
attractiveness (Fink et al., 2006) and associates it with aesthetic harmon y (Friedenberg, 2018).
The findings of this study indicate that topics related to symmetry (e.g., such as “jewellery and
fine materials”, “ lifestyle”, and “retail displ ay”) may resonate more with consum ers who
prioritise beauty and elegance in their consumption and self- expression. Particularly in jewellery
imagery, where symmet ry is associated wi th facial appearan ce (Bertamini et al., 2019), this is
thought-provoking given that accessory items often feature human faces to showcase personal
products. The results are consistent with existing knowledge that underscores the positive
associations between s ymmetry and attract iveness (Fink et al., 2006). However, the effect o f
symmetry appears con text-dependent, vary ing by product type and consumer expectations (Bajaj
& Bond, 2018; Bertamini et al., 2019).
Finally, it is important to note tha t the models in this study intentionally focused on four
key image fluency metrics (Ryu, 2024) derived from processing fluency (Hur et al., 2020) and
visual aesthetics (Mayer & Landwehr, 2018). This theoretical fo cus aimed to isolate and quantify
the influence of foundational low- level image characte ristics known to shape perceptual fluency
and consumer behaviour (Mayer & Landwehr, 2018). Although other visual attributes, such as
colour saturation or brightness, may also affect engagement, th eir exclusion was a del iberate
methodological choice to avoid multicollinearity, reduce model complexity, and preserve
conceptual clarity. Including multiple overlapping variables would have diluted the explanatory
power of the theoretical constructs and compromised model interpretability. Consequently, the
novelty of this study lies in its integration of theory- driven visual fluency metrics w ith
explainable AI techniques, offering a scalable and interpretable framework for understanding
how specific image features drive consumer engagement in the luxury context.
Conclusion
Theoretical C ontribution
By bridging the fields of visual aesthetics, processing fluency (Gülçin & Yalçınkaya,
and digital marketing communication (Kanuri et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2018), this research
offers a novel persp ective on the role of image fl uency in driving consumer engagement within
the luxury market. Specifically, it employs image fluency, a higher- order concept that synergis es
four low- level features (i.e., simplicity, symmetry, self- similarity, and contrast) into cohesive
perceptual experiences. This approach advances the understanding of how cognitive ease of
processing visual representations shapes consumer interactions with luxury brands on social
media.
While previous resear ch has acknowled ged the importance o f visual aestheti cs
(Kusumasondjaja, 2019; Yang et al., 2021), this paper focus es on the visual configuration of
images, particularly as it rela tes to low- level characteristi cs associated with i mage fluency
(Mayer & Landwehr, 2018). These low- level characterist ics are unique in t hat they reflect
fundamental visual elements that (un)consciously influence consumer perceptions and
preferences (Gülçin & Yalçınkaya, 2024). For luxury businesses, the alignment between fluent
visual designs and the aspirational identity of the consumer further amplifies engagement. The
present study focuses on these primary visual factors as its main theoretical contribution, while
recognising that additional contextual variables may further enrich future research in this area.
By moving beyond traditional notions of processing fluency, which have primarily
focused on textual data (Yu et al., 2024), this research situates itse lf within a broader conceptual
framework that unders cores the signi ficance of fluent visual aesthetics in brand communication
(Farace et al., 2025). It not only elucidates the relationship between visual fluency metrics and
user engagement, but extends the theoretical contributions related to visual presentations in
luxury branding (Lee et al., 2018). S ince luxury consumers often seek a seamless blend of
aesthetic appeal and b rand storytell ing (Üçok Hughes et al., 2016), the findings open new
avenues for scholars to continue exploring the evolving dynamics of consumer engagement in
the digital landscape (Kanuri et al., 2024; Oliveira & Fernandes, 2022; Ryu, 2024).
Moreover, this research moves beyond commonly explored topics in landscape imagery
(Gülçin, 2021; Kerebel et al., 2019) to specifically address social media user engagement within
the marketing discipline. For luxury branding, these characteristics reinforce brand identity and
value, playing a pivotal role in crafting compelling narratives that resonate with high- value
consumers. Finally, this research introduces methodological advancement by integrating
advanced artificial i ntelligence and data analytics t ools to operational ise image fluency and
predict user engagement. This study demonstrates how existing AI-based techniques (e.g.,
LIME) can be effecti vely applied to large- s cale visual data i n marketing. This interdisciplinary
approach enhances the precision of marketing strategy optimisation (Zhang & Srinivasan, 2023),
and paves the way for future research on the intersections of visual aesthetics, brand
communication, and consumer behaviour.
Practical I mplications
The findings of this research offer actionable and data-driven recommendations for
marketers and content creators in the luxury branding space, particularly those responsible for
visual marketing strategy on social media. Given the competitive nature of the digital landscape,
brands must adopt st rategies that effe ctively resonate wit h consumers' prefer ences and
expectations. Overall, marketers should spotlight simplicity and self- similarity in their visual
content. First, self-similarity can be operationalised through consistent use of motifs, shapes, or
layouts across posts. By doing so, luxurious brands can reinforce brand identity and facilitate
faster recognition, which in turn enhances engagement. For instance, increasing self- similarity
within product categories (e.g., leather accessories, footwear, formal at tire, and retail di splay)
can elevate user engag ement rates. For example, a luxury leather brand can improve engagement
by repeating signature stitching patterns, consistent framing of bags, or using recurring props
such as branded dust bags. Meanwhile, simplicity should be emphasised by reducing excessive
visual clutter, avoiding overly complex backgrounds, and using clear focal points. For instance, a
brand promoting eyewear should isolate the product against neutral or blurred backgrounds,
avoiding busy patterns that distract from frame design. In the case of formal wear, high-
performing images typically showed sharply dressed models photographed with minimalist
lighting and monochrome palettes.
Importantly, contrast, commonly used in mainstream advertising to provoke attention,
proved non-significant in nearly all clusters, with some even a slight negative association. This
implies that luxury consumers may find high-contrast images too harsh or jarring. For example, a
high-contrast image of a luxury watch with a stark black background and spotlight might seem
overly commercial, while a sof tly lit ambient shot with consi stent tones could b e more ideal.
Moreover, the strategic use of symmetry shoul d be selectively applied. While symmetry
positively influenced engagement in luxurious products related to jewellery and fine materials, it
showed little to no effect in others. For jewellery, symmetrical visuals (e.g., centred product
placement or balanced face framing) help communicate premium quality and precision. In
contrast, for fashion clusters, asymmetric styling may enhance perceived creativity, aligning
better with trend-conscious consumers.
Overall, these insights go beyond general aesthetic advice by demonstrating how specific
combinations of image fluency metrics can be simulated to yield optimal results. In practical
terms, managers can fi ne-tune image design guidelines by cluster or campaign type, rather than
adopting a single-brand-wide approach. By emphasising the interplay between image fluency
metrics and consumer engagement, the implication of this work enables marketers to move from
intuitive design choices to evidence-based visual planning.
Limitations and Recommendations
This research is not without its limitations. While it focuses on luxury brands, a
comparative analysis with fast fashion brands (e.g., H&M) or other sectors that heavily rely on
visual marketing would provide valuable insights for further exploration. Within the luxury
context, while this study positions itself by learning from best practices, as indicated by the
Digital IQ Index (Marzano et al., 2021), it is crucial to acknowle dge that slightly lower- tier
brands may not necessarily fit into the same scenario. Similarly, while this study focuses on
image fluency, it does not explore potential moderators that could influence this dynamic (e.g.,
brand personality, saturation, and brightness). For instance, a minimalist luxury brand may
benefit more from simplicity and symme try, while a brand emphasising bold cr eativity might see
greater effects from contrast and complexity. Investigating these moderating influences could
further refine the theoretical model proposed in this study and enhance its predictive power
across diverse brand i dentities. While this st udy focused specifically on image fluency variables,
the potential risk of omitted variable bias was acknowledged. Given the use of AI- based
predictive models and the inherent trade-offs between performance and interpretability, future
research could address this limitation by employing parametric models (e.g., polynomial
regression or mixed- effects modelling) to examine potential non- linearitie s or moderating
variables more explicitly.
Moreover, despite the significance of the user engagement metrics identified in this
study, it is essential to recognise that higher engagement does not guarantee actual purchases;
rather, it is merely one indicator of a more favourable attitude toward the showcased products.
This distinction underscores the need for research that exam ines the conversi on rates and actual
buying decisions of consumers. Another notable limitation lies in the scope of visual features
included in the modelling framework. This s tudy specifically operationalis ed image fluen cy
through four foundational low- level visual dimensions (i.e., simplicity, self- similarity, symmetry,
and visual contrast). However, other image- level characteristics ( e.g., colour saturation, lightness
(Hagtvedt & Brasel, 2017)), or the prototypicality of product design (Landwehr et al., 2011)
were not incorporated. Future research is encouraged to expand the current framework by
integrating such variables, thereby enhancing the explanatory capacity of predictive models and
contributing to a more comprehensive understanding of visually driven branding dynamics.
Additionally, while embracing the potential of big data research in the marketing context
(Dekimpe, 2020), it is important to recognise that the interpretation of the findings relies heavily
on existing knowledge and literature. This strengthens the need for further experimental resea rch
to deepen the current understanding. Such studies could help establish clearer links between
image fluency metri cs and consumer behaviours in the luxury sector. Meanwhile, i t is also
important to consider demographic factors, such as gender and cultural background, which may
play a subtle role in influencing how consumers interpret visual content. Future research should
incorporate these variables to provide a more comprehensive understanding of how diverse
audiences respond to luxury branding and marketing communication.

Peggy J Liu Peggy J Liu
Cary L. Anderson
Brands and retailers often offer different aesthetic versions of the same base product, which vary from visually simple to visually complex. How should managers price these different aesthetic versions of the same base product? This research provides insights for such decisions through uncovering a novel consumer lay belief about the relationship between visual complexity and production costs. Consumers associate simple (vs. complex) visual aesthetics with lower production costs when evaluating different aesthetic versions of a product. This lay belief occurs in joint evaluation mode but is mitigated in separate evaluation mode. An important downstream implication of this lay belief is that consumers' willingness to pay is lower for visually simple (vs. complex) versions. This gap in willingness to pay occurs even when consumers like both product versions or aesthetics equally, and it is only eliminated when consumers like the visually simple version substantially more than the complex version. Finally, reducing the diagnosticity of the lay belief by disclosing information that the two versions took similar amounts of production time and effort reduces the gap in willingness to pay between visually simple (vs. complex) versions.

In order to retain the characteristics and style of traditional settlements and respect their layout and structure, it is necessary to carry out original planning and expansion of traditional settlements. This model of planning and expansion aims to protect the unique character of the settlement, maintain its original historical and cultural value, and integrate with the surrounding environment. Early research on the space complexity of settlements was dominated by qualitative analysis, and the depth of quantitative research on the spatial form of traditional settlements was insufficient. This article takes Xiaoliangjiang Village in Jingxing County, Shijiazhuang City, Hebei Province, which entered the fifth batch of the list of Chinese traditional villages list, as the research object. The spatial relationship of the settlement was obtained through field surveys and drone oblique photography, and the spatial morphological elements of Xiaoliangjiang Village were analyzed and extracted. Based on three quantitative theories of spatial form, namely topology theory, fractal theory, and space syntax, the self-similarity of settlements is analyzed from the perspectives of buildings, streets, and spaces. The research uses Matlab and DepthMap software to quantitatively analyze the spatial form of Xiaoliangjiang Village and obtains data. Through the analysis of data, it was found that Xiaoliangjiang Village has self-similarity at three levels: buildings, roads and settlement spaces. The buildings iteratively generate various forms of architectural courtyards through the basic “L”-shaped pattern. The spatial structures at all levels of roads and settlement space in Xiaoliangjiang Village are relatively similar, in line with the bottom-up traditional settlement evolutionary law. By studying settlement self-similarity, people can better understand the formation mechanism of traditional settlement space structure and its evolution law. At the same time, it enriches the research perspective of traditional settlements and provides technical support for analyzing the self-similarity of traditional settlements and settlement protection planning.

Purpose This study investigates the minimalist approach of Gen Z, which diverges from traditional minimalist ideals that emphasize curated and meaningful consumption. Gen Z's minimalism is deeply rooted in sustainability, self-expression and social identity, promoting intentional living by focusing on what truly matters and eliminating unnecessary excess. Design/methodology/approach Grounded in self-determination theory, this research employs a mixed-method approach combining netnography with a quantitative survey involving 316 respondents. This comprehensive analysis aims to uncover the factors influencing Gen Z's distinct minimalist behaviors. Findings The study presents three key insights. First, the concept of voluntary simplicity, representing older minimalist notions, is found to be irrelevant in the fashion context, highlighting a shift in minimalist values. Second, contrary to common beliefs, minimalism does not significantly impact emotional well-being, suggesting that its psychological benefits may be overstated. Lastly, social crowding negatively moderates the relationship between minimalism and social connectedness, indicating that higher levels of social connections can diminish the sense of community often associated with minimalist lifestyles. Research limitations/implications The study is limited by its focus on a specific demographic and geographic area, which may affect the generalizability of the findings. Future research could explore minimalist behaviors in other contexts and among different age groups to provide a broader understanding. Originality/value This research provides fresh insights into Gen Z's minimalist practices, emphasizing their motivations around sustainability, self-expression and social identity. It explores how their approach to minimalism intersects with fashion, contributing to a deeper understanding of contemporary consumption trends and intentional living among younger generations.

Purpose This study addresses the lack of exploration of whether posting luxury products purchased on social media contributes to a favorable impression of oneself. It uncovers the underlying mechanisms shaping observers' attitudes toward account holders sharing luxury posts. Design/methodology/approach To test the hypotheses, a one-factor between-subjects experimental design involving 400 South Korean participants with social media accounts was employed. Participants in each condition recalled their experiences of encountering either luxury or non-luxury posts on social media and completed several measures, including attitudes toward the account holder. Purpose This study aims to examine the visual effects of cause-related marketing (CM) posts on Instagram, with a focus on image resolution and consumer engagement. Design/methodology/approach Three studies were conducted through an experimental design. Study 1 (N = 155) uncovered the mediation underlying the effects of image quality (low and high image resolution). Study 2 (N = 160) replicated the findings of the first study and extended the investigation by examining the mediator (fluency) and moderator (visual sensitivity). Study 3 (N = 291) further extended the effects of image resolution by demonstrating its interactive effects with the visual complexity of an Instagram post design in a 2 × 2 factorial experiment. Findings The serial mediation analysis demonstrated that high image resolution CM posts yielded more favorable evaluations in terms of brand credibility and information costs saved, subsequently leading to positive brand attitudes, purchase intentions and increased Instagram engagement. Processing fluency mediated image effects on brand credibility, while individual differences in visual sensitivity moderated the image effects. The image resolution effects were greater for visually complex CM posts compared to simple ones. Originality/value To one's best knowledge, little to no research has examined the image quality of Instagram posts in the context of CM and the extent to which such visual cues can affect consumers' brand evaluations and engagement on the platform. The current research findings aim to bridge the research gap.

Abstract
Typography is the art of visually arranging and presenting text in design. Its accurate use significantly enhances a design's appeal and communicative effectiveness. The impact of typography spans from conveying meaning to ensuring text readability. It serves as a tool to strengthen the meaning of text, with different fonts, colors, and layouts emphasizing emotions and messages. The right typography choice establishes a more effective connection with the target audience. Noteworthy is its impact on readability through factors like font sizes, line spacing, and letter spacing, ensuring a clear understanding of the message. Creating a visual hierarchy is a significant function of typography, providing a sense of prioritization between headings, subheadings, and main text. From a brand identity perspective, unique typography contributes to brand recognition and loyalty. Aesthetically, color coordination, font selection, and layout determine a design's overall appeal. Typography's compatibility with the intended media type is crucial for effectiveness, requiring different strategies for web design, print, or digital platforms. In summary, typography is vital in the design process, enhancing text, increasing communicative power, and fostering deeper audience interaction.

INTRODUCTION
Graphic design an d typography are fundamental elements of design that have a significant impact on
aesthetics, communication, and functionality. The message can be effectively conveyed to the audience
through graphic design, as designers can create visually appealing and understandable communication to ols
using colour, shape, layout, and typography.
Typography enhances the readability of texts and helps to emphas ize messages. Graphic design creates and
strengthens a b rand's identity. The brand logo, color palette, typography, and other visual e lements increase
brand recognition. Graphic de sign can enhance the aesthetic value of a product or service. Well-designed
packaging, website or ad vertising material enhances the appeal of a product or service and attracts potential
customers.
Graphic design is crucial for improving user experience. Well-designed graphics and layouts make websites,
applications and other user interfaces more user-f riendly. Typography improv es the readability and
comprehensibility of texts, making it easier for users to ob tain information.
Graphic design and typography also have a significant impact on people's emotional responses. Colour, shape,
and typography choices can evoke specific emotions. For instance, warm colours a nd elegant typography can
convey that a prod uct or service is luxurious and sophis ticated. By prioritizing hierar chy an d focus, designers
can guide users' attention and create a clear visual hierarch y.
Graphic design plays a crucial role in determining the hierarchy and visual focal points of a design. Typography,
on the other hand, effectively emphas izes importan t information by setting priorities for headings,
subheadings, and text. It is important to note that graphic design creates the first imp ression of a design, and
people quickly evaluate a design when they s ee it. Good graphic design not only encourages users to show
more interest but also creates a positive first impression.
Typography plays a crucial role in enhancing th e visual appeal of a design, making it more attractive,
sophisticated, and professional. Additionally, typo graphy can significantly improve the readability of a design.
Good typography enhances the readability of text, making it easier and faster for readers to understand.
Properly used typography can be employed to more effectively convey a d esign's message. Graphic design and
typography are po werful tools that help designers communicate their messages, market products and services,
and improve user experience. The impact of typography on design depends on the font, size, and alignment
used.
TYPOGRAPHY AND THE BASIC ELEMENTS OF TYPOGRAP HY
Typography is an art and science that deals with the arran gement, d esign, an d p rinting of texts and writing.
This term encompasses th e use of typefaces and letter layou ts, aiming to present texts in the b est possible way
IJOESS
International Journal of Eurasia Social Sciences Vol: 15, Issue: 57, 2024
1448
in terms of aesthetics, readability, and communication. Typography includes variou s design elements such as
typefaces, font sizes, spacing, line lengths, text formatting, and color selection. (Metin, 2008, p.21).
Typography's Key Elements:
The text characters are: Typography involves the selection of different typefaces. T hese characters include
letters, numbers, special symbols, and p unctuation marks. Typography requires choosing appropriate typefaces
to represent the text or convey a specific purpose.
Letter Size and Weight: The size and thickness of letters affect the readability and emphasis of the text.
Headings typically use larger and bolder font sizes, wh ile body text uses smaller and lighter font sizes.
Ranges and Kerning: Typography includes spacing elements such as letter spac ing and kerning (special
adjustments between letters). These elements ensure that texts flow and are read smoothly.
Line Length: Typography involves adjusting the line length of texts. An ideal line length enhances readability,
while excessively long or short lines can negatively impact t he reading experience.
Text Layout: Typography deals with the organization of texts and page layout. Determining how headings,
subheadings, and texts are arranged makes the text more effective and u nderstandable.
Color and Contrast: Font color contributes to the contrast between the text and the background, affecting the
text's purpose and readability.
Typography is a crucial design element that ensures the proper presentation of texts in terms of aesthetics and
communication. Good typography enhances the readability and eff ective communication of the text while
elevating its aesthetic and emotion al impact (Özp olat, 2023).
TYPOGRAPHY'S DEVELOPMENT
Stone lithography is a printing art that involves drawing shapes and text with oily ink onto lim estone. This
technique, also known as hand lith ography, is commonly used in the fields of visual arts and graphic design.
The drawn design is tra nsferred onto the stone, ink is applied, and then the print is made. Stone printing had a
significant impact on the beginning of modern art du ring the 19th century (Keskin, 2017).
Woodcut (8th century BC): In China, woodblock printing was utilized. Letters and symbols were carved into
wooden blocks, and ink was applied for the printing process.
Movable lithograph (10th century): Once again in China, movable clay printing was invented. This method
allowed the use of separate blocks for printing texts.
IJOESS
International Journal of Eurasia Social Sciences Vol: 15, Issue: 57, 2024
1449
Moving Woodcut (11th century): Movable woodblock printing was developed in China, enabling the ra pid and
easy printing of texts using individual wooden blocks.
Printing (15th century): In vented by Johannes Gutenberg, the p rinting press represents one of typography's
most crucial periods. It allowed for the fast and efficient printing of texts using movable metal letter blocks.
This invention greatly accelerated book production and t he dissemination of knowledge.
Handwriting and Printing: From the 15th to the 19th century, texts were still printed using handwriting or
traditional printing methods. Different typefaces a nd writing styles were developed during this period.
Artistic Typography (20th century): From the mid-20th century onward, typography gain ed an artistic
dimension. Designers aimed to create visually impressive texts using different typefaces and layouts (Yazar,
2020).
Digital Typography (late 20th century): With the advancement of computer technology, digital typograph y
emerged. Computers w ere used to design, edit, and print typefaces, making typography more accessible and
customizable.
Typography has continuously changed and progressed alongside the evolution of typefaces and printing
techniques. Today, typography is still considered a significant element in design, with a rich field encompas sing
various typefaces and design styles ( Aslıer, 1983).
Factors Influencing Typography's Development:
Technology: Technological advancements have significantly contributed to the development of typography.
Printing pres ses, computers, and other technologies have allowed typography to be used mor e rapidly, easily,
and creatively.
Social and cultural changes: Social and cultural changes have also influenced the development of typography.
For example, during the Renaissance period, typography progressed parallel to advancements in art and
sc ience (Meyrick, 2016).
Creative Designers: Creative designers have played a crucial role in the development of typography. These
designers have contributed to the evolution of typography by developing new typefaces and printing
techniques.
TYPOGRAPHY IN TURKEY
Typography has a long history in Turkey and has evolved an d developed during different historical periods.
Here are some important points about the development of t ypography in Turkey:
IJOESS
International Journal of Eurasia Social Sciences Vol: 15, Issue: 57, 2024
1450
Turkish typography has a rich history. The first Turkish writing characters were used in the Orkhon inscriptions,
which were written in the Göktürk alphabet.
During the Seljuk period in the 12th century, n ew script characters were developed, ins pired by the Kufic and
Naskh script styles. In the 13th century, during the Ottoman Empire, new script characters were deve loped,
inspired by Diwani and Thuluth script s tyles (Özkal, 2018).
In the 14th century, with the arrival of printing presses from Europe, significant developments occurred in
typography in Turkey. Many new script characters w ere designed during this period (Başaran, 2023).
In the 15th century, typography developments accele rated in Turkey. With the advancement of computer
technology, creative and innovative use of ty pography became possible (Mercin, and Şahin,2010).
Ottoman Empire Period: Manuscripts and documents were w idely used in the Ottoman Empire. Ottoman
Turkish texts were typically written using the pros e and Naskh script characters. Some manuscripts from this
period carried artistic value and were enriched with d ecorations (Demir,2023).
Introduction of the Printing Press (18th Century): Turkey adopted printing press technology during the era
when it became widespread in Europe. The first Ottoman printing press was established in 172 7 by İbrahim
Müteferrika. The printing press expedited book production and contributed to the sprea d of written culture in
the Ottoma n Empire (Sarıkavak, 2022).
Republican Era: Following the establis hment of the Republic of Turkey, the acceptance and use of the Latin
alphabet led to changes in typography design. The Turkish alp habet required the creation of new script
characters suitable for the Turkish language. Designers, such as İsmail Hakkı Baltacıoğlu, developed new Turkish
letter script characters dur ing this period (Özka l, 2018).
Development of the Press and Publishing Sector: As the press and publishing sector grew in Turkey, typ ography
design also advanced. Different script characters and design styles were used for newspapers, magazines,
books, and posters. The publishing sector contrib uted to the progress of typography design in Turkey.
Digital Revolution and Web Design: The rise of digital technology also influenced typography design in Turkey.
Web design and digital media brought new design requirements and the use of script characters. Turkish
websites, mobile applications, and digital content are among t he factors affecting typography.
Education an d Design Schools: Schools and design cours es providing education in ty pography design in Turkey
teach young designers typography skills. These educational institutions have contributed to the development
of typography design.
IJOESS
International Journal of Eurasia Social Sciences Vol: 15, Issue: 57, 2024
1451
Typography design in Turkey has und ergone significant cha nges and developments throughout history. Today,
typography design plays a crucial role in various fields in Turkey, including media, advertising, book publishing,
and digital design. Designers use various script characters and design techniques, both tradition al and modern,
to effectively convey their messages (Sarı kavak, 2022).
Web technology has influenced the field of typography in many ways. Usability: Web technology has increas ed
the usability of ty pography. Thanks to responsive web design and the use of fonts com patible with different
devices, texts can be displayed clearly and legibly o n any screen size.
Variety: Web fonts have enriched typography. Now web d esigners can create original and remarkable texts by
choosing from a wide range of fonts.
Experimentation: Web technology has encouraged the experimental use of typogr aphy. Thanks to animations,
transition effects and interactive text elements, typography has become more impressive on websites.
Readability: Web technology has increased the readab ility of typography. Well-designed websites can presen t
texts in a way that readers can easily read them and strengthen the visual hierarchy of typography (Yazar,
2020).
Accessibility: Web techn ology has made typ ography more accessible. For example, web browsers offer options
such as adjusting the size, colour and style of text. This makes it easier for people who are blind or have poor
eyesight to read the text.
More options: Web technology offers more op tions for typography. These options include different fonts, s izes,
styles and colours. This allows designers to create more cr eative and effective typograp hy. "Typography on the
Web" (Richard, 2013).
New design trends: Web technology has led to the emergence of new typography design trends. These trends
include dynamic typography, moving typography a nd abstract typography.
It Has Had A Significant İmpact On Typography, Especial ly İn The Following Areas:
Mobile devices: The proliferation of mobile devices has led to new design approaches that allow typography to
be readable on smaller screens. "Web Typography in a Digita l World", Lucy Carney
Digital games: Digital games have required the development of new design approaches that make typography
more interactive and fun. "The Impact of Technology on Typograp hy" by Jessica Farris.
IJOESS
International Journal of Eurasia Social Sciences Vol: 15, Issue: 57, 2024
1452
Image1: http://www.gozmedya.com/blog/yaz
TYPOGRAPHY AROUND THE WORLD
Typography design worldwide has evolved and changed over time due to technology, cultural influences, and
design trends. Here are some significant periods in the development and transformation of typography des ig n
throughout history:
Invention of Printing (15th Century): The printing press, invented by Johannes Gutenberg, marked a crucial
turning point in typography. It allowed for the rapid and efficient printing of texts using movable metal letter
blocks, greatly accelerating book production a nd the spread of knowledge (Gates, 1998).
Renaissance Period (15-16th Century): The Renaissance era was a period of signifi cant progress in typography
design. Italian designers worked to enhance letter forms and design aesth etics. During this time, sans-serif
(serifless) typefaces were invented.
Industrial Revolution (18-19th Century): With the Industrial Revolution, printing press technology and
typography design became more accessible. More typefaces an d styles of writing were developed.
Bauhaus Movement (20th Century): The Bauhaus school aimed to simplify and modernize typography design.
The minimalist design p hilosophy of Bauhaus influenced typography, contributing to the popularity of sans-
serif typefaces.
Digital Revolution (20 th Century): The development of co mputer technology gave rise to digital typography.
Computers began to be u sed for designing, editing, and printing typefaces, speeding up design processes and
allowing for greater personalization.
Web Design (2000s and Beyond): The widespread use of the internet brought typography design to the web.
Web designers focused on responsive design and web typography to ensure texts looked good on various
devices and screen sizes.
IJOESS
International Journal of Eurasia Social Sciences Vol: 15, Issue: 57, 2024
1453
Multimedia Design (2000s and Beyond): Typography design became important not only for print and web
design but also for various multimedia formats such as video, animation, mobile applications, and games.
Retina Displays and High Re solution (2010s and Beyond): High-resolution displays made typography design
sharper and more detailed. Achieving smooth and sharp a ppearance for typefaces required more attention.
Personalized Typography (2020s and Beyond): Des igners began adopting personalized typo graphy by creating
unique typefaces for brands. This is us ed to establish and define brand identity.
Typography is used across various cultures and periods worldwide, each developin g its own unique typography
styles (Bilgin, and Ketenci, 2006).
TYPOGRAPHY AND CHARACTERS
Typography characters are various elements expressing different forms of typefaces used in the design of texts.
These characters significantly impact the r eadability and aesthetics of texts. Here are some fun damental
examples of typography characters:
Serif Characters: Serifs are small projections at the ends of letter strokes. Serif characters help texts achieve a
more traditional and formal appearance. Typeface examples with serif characteristics include Times New
Roman, Garamond, and Georgia.
Sans-serif Characters: Sans-serif characters have straighter lines w ithout serifs at the ends of letter strokes.
These characters offer a modern and clean loo k and are commonly used in digital texts. E xamples of sans-serif
typefaces include Arial, Helvetica, and Calibri.
Monospace Characters: Monospace characters refer to a type of typeface where each letter has the same
width. These characters are commonly used in texts re quiring regular arrangements, such as coding or table
creation. Examples of monospace typefaces include Courier, Consolas, and Monaco.
Decorative (Display) Characte rs: Decorative typefaces are o ften used for highlighting purposes, such as titles or
logos. While these characters provide an aesthetic and at tention-grabbing appearance, they are not suitable
for long texts. Examples include Brush Script, L obster, and Blackletter.
Script Characters: Script characters mimic handwriting and are often used for person al notes, cards, or designs.
Examples include Comic Sans, Bradley Hand, and Segoe Scrip t.
Digital Characters: Digital typ efaces are designed to appear well on computer monitors or other digital screens.
These characters are typically pixel or vector-bas ed, ensuring high readability.
IJOESS
International Journal of Eurasia Social Sciences Vol: 15, Issue: 57, 2024
1454
Symbol Characters: Symbol characters include various symb ols enriching the text, such as arrows, boxes, s tars,
and other special symbols.
Usage Of Characters İn Typography
In typography, characters can be used for various purp oses. Characters used in a logo can reflect the brand's
identity and personality. Characters used on a webs ite can influence the user experience, and those used in an
advertising campaign can effectively convey the message.
Impact of Characters in Typography
Characters in typography can affect the visual app eal, readability, and comprehensibility of a design. Properly
chosen characters can make a design more attractive, readab le, and understandable.
Selection of Characters İn Typography

TYPOGRAPHY IN LETTER STRUCTURE
Typography is crucial for understanding the structure of letters and typefaces. Each letter possesses a unique
structure, and comprehending and controlling this structure in typography d esign s ignificantly influences the
appearance and impact of texts. Here are the fundamental components of typography letter structure:
Baseline: The baseline represents an invisible line where the lower edges of letters sit. Ensuring letters align
with this line maintains the text's layout and readability.
Cap Height: Cap height signifies the height of uppercase letters, representing the upper edge of uppercase
letters and is vital for adjusting letter heights.
X-Height: X-height represents the height of lowercas e letters, determining the height of lowercase letters in the
text and is crucial for readability.
Ascender: Ascender refers to the parts of a letter that extend above the normal height. For example, letters lik e
"b," "d," and "h" have ascenders.
Descender: Descender refers to the parts of a letter that extend below the normal height. For example, letters
like "g," "p," and "y" have descenders.
Stems: Stems denote the vertical or upright lines of a letter, forming th e letter's main structure.
Terminals: Terminals define the sh ape of letter terminals or ends. For instance, the turn at the end of the tail of
the "a" is a terminal.
Serifs: Serifs are small projections added to the ends or corners of letterforms. Serifs are characteristic of s erif
typefaces and lend a more traditional and formal appearan ce to the text.
Sans-serif: Sans-serif typefaces typically lack s erifs, presenting a straighter appearance.
Character Width: Each letter has a unique width, which is combined with letter spacing and text layout.
Optical Adjustment: In typ ography design, it's crucial to optically adjust letters to compensate for differences in
space and attention-grabbing characteristics among letters.
These letter structure components form the foundation of typography design. Designers arrange and stylize
texts by paying attention to these components, maximizing the readability and aesthetics of the text. Precise
adjustment of letters is a key element in typography design and aids in the effective communication of texts
(Başaran, 2023).

While previous research has largely focused on the direct effects of visual elements on brand recognition, this paper delves deeper into the psychological mechanisms that translate design into purchasing decisions. Employing a quantitative research design, data were collected from a diverse sample of consumers and analyzed using structural equation modeling (SEM). Findings revealed that the Maguindanaon-based worktext was rated highly acceptable across all dimensions. Both groups showed improvement in their posttest scores; however, the experimental group demonstrated significantly higher gains compared to the control group. Statistical results also indicated significant differences in selected lessons, including Aralin 4 (t (82) = 2.53, p = 0.013) and Aralin 5 (t (82) = 3.54, p < .001). The results suggest that culturally contextualized instructional materials enhance learner performance, with cultural manifestation more evident among learners exposed to the worktext. The study concludes that culturally responsive materials positively influence learner achievement.

The traditional literature on the Ottoman printing enterprise has for long placed the traditional actors of the written word including the ulema and the calligraphers at a counter position to new technology and its connotations. The printed medium, however, has incorporated many of these actors, who continued to fulfill some of the most important tasks. From editorial work to the techno-material aspects of printing, these actors did not remain isolated, but garnered new opportunities for themselves in a rapidly changing cultural environment. By focusing exclusively on the Imperial Press to reveal the editorial workload largely owned up by the ulema, this paper reveals how the know-how of these scholars was critical for the transition to a new cultural medium. It also illuminates the central role played by the scribes and the calligraphers, who had allegedly 'revolted' against İbrahim Müteferrika in the eighteenth century, in providing the aesthetic continuity from the manuscript to the printed book in the Ottoman Empire. Overall, this paper argues that the new technology did not necessarily eliminate old professions, but allowed professionals to adapt and carry their skills to the new environment.

It is questioned how original the designs produced with AI are and whether these designs have artistic value. Literature Review/Background: The impact of artificial intelligence (AI) technology in the field of design and the reconsideration of the concept of originality are mentioned. Methodology: The research design of the study was qualitative, document scanning method was used as the data collection method, and content analysis method was used to analyse the data. Findings: The impact of artificial intelligence (AI) technology in the field of design necessitates a reconsideration of the concept of originality. While AI offers speed and efficiency in design processes, it produces creative solutions through learning from data and algorithms. However, originality in this process can often be derived from existing data or based on style transfers. While the innovations and efficiency advantages offered by AI expand the creative capacities of designers, it may cause you to question the concepts of originality and personal expression. Abstract and Figures
Typographic elements have a huge impact on how designed mediums affect visual literacy. This paper reviews the principles, perspectives and approaches in the production and function of typographic design visual media (print and digital), with the aim to understand the relationship between typographic design on digital mediums, with the aim of examining its influence on people's ability to communicate ideas, meaning and messages effectively, while reflecting on its commercial implications for brands and marketers. Research via survey and a focus group implied there is a positive association between literacy and the application of graphic design and typography on digital communication mediums. Findings revealed that type design complements textual word elements to enhance cognition and understanding of messages. The integration of visual and texts facilitates reading, and for digital mediums, both legible layout and engaging typefaces are equally crucial. Graphic typeface for digital media, from smartphones to e-texts for learning, should apply visual hierarchy arrangement to achieve these objectives. Findings show typographic design is an essential aspect of social communication today, and digital designers play a fundamental role to enable audiences to improve their economic and social participation and gain its full advantages.

Introduction
The era of web technologies has created unprecedented responses to digital media and visual communication. This is
apparent in the design and innovation for an endless array of digital tools and resources. Technology, as an extension of
post- industrial societies, has been observed and praised for its ability to construct new knowledge, new realities and
social experiences and to develop various aspects of modern culture (Burnett, 2005).
It is evident that engaging visual design acts to ensure message efficiency, such as reading, consuming and exchanging
information on screens and making connections with others using digital texts, images, emojis, multimedia content a nd
diverse audio- visual artefacts (Reyna et al, 2008).
While some concerns are raised that th e true potential behind digital and new media forms maybe buried under
complex digital systems, others are more optimistic in their outlook. For example, the French sociologist Bruno Latour
in 1996 (Burnett, 2005, p.125) predicted that man and machines would in future exchange relational positions: the
virtual and real collide in and through participatory pursuits and activities.
In the 21 st- century, evolving digital literacy skills are crucial for researchers considering how te chnology, media
communication and design sectors boost participatory culture in society. With digital literacy and participation comes
education: the knowledge disadvantaged are in hindered in their desire for socioeconomic improvements and
transformation, e.g. access to government a nd pu blic services, technological innovation, healthcare, education, civic
involvement, social networking, and growth opportunities (Lankshear and Kno bel, 2008).
Visual media and design communication involving visual intertextuality and literacy are thus important to clarify and
examine to understand their transformative capabilities. Howe ver, some recent human- computer interaction studies
show many web designers more inclined towards homogeneity in visual communication a daptation and commercial
works, rather than demonstrating originality and skills in personalisation, due mainly to the two indicators of interface
usability i.e. efficiency and effecti veness of web layouts (Alshaali, 2011).
Typically, contemporary digital media designers surmount challenges that are attributed to a poor grasp of aesthetic

principles including weak or undistinguishable visual properties of clear type, colour, sizing, position and placement of
