stroke-width Accessibility forced-color-adjust Core concepts Adding custom styles Best practices for adding your own custom styles in Tailwind projects. Often the biggest challenge when working with a framework is figuring out what you're supposed to do when there's something you need that the framework doesn't handle for you. Tailwind has been designed from the ground up to be extensible and customizable, so that no matter what you're building you never feel like you're fighting the framework. This guide covers topics like customizing your design tokens, how to break out of those constraints when necessary, adding your own custom CSS, and extending the framework with plugins. Customizing your theme If you want to change things like your color palette, spacing scale, typography scale, or breakpoints, add your customizations using the @theme directive in your CSS: CSS ``` @theme { --font-display: "Satoshi", "sans-serif"; --breakpoint-3xl: 120rem; --color-avocado-100: oklch(0.99 0 0); --color-avocado-200: oklch(0.98 0.04 113.22); --color-avocado-300: oklch(0.94 0.11 115.03); --color-avocado-400: oklch(0.92 0.19 114.08); --color-avocado-500: oklch(0.84 0.18 117.33); --color-avocado-600: oklch(0.53 0.12 118.34); --ease-fluid: cubic-bezier(0.3, 0, 0, 1); --ease-snappy: cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1); /* ... */} ``` Learn more about customizing your theme in the theme variables documentation. Using arbitrary values While you can usually build the bulk of a well-crafted design using a constrained set of design tokens, once in a while you need to break out of those constraints to get things pixel-perfect. When you find yourself really needing something like top: 117px to get a background image in just the right spot, use Tailwind's square bracket notation to generate a class on the fly with any arbitrary value: HTML ```
``` This is basically like inline styles, with the major benefit that you can combine it with interactive modifiers like hover and responsive modifiers like lg : HTML ```
``` This works for everything in the framework, including things like background colors, font sizes, pseudo-element content, and more: HTML ```
``` If you're referencing a CSS variable as an arbitrary value, you can use the custom property syntax: HTML ```
``` This is just a shorthand for fill-[var(--my-brand-color)] that adds the var() function for you automatically. Arbitrary properties If you ever need to use a CSS property that Tailwind doesn't include a utility for out of the box, you can also use square bracket notation to write completely arbitrary CSS: HTML ```
``` This is really like inline styles, but again with the benefit that you can use modifiers: HTML ```
``` This can be useful for things like CSS variables as well, especially when they need to change under different conditions: HTML ```
``` Arbitrary variants Arbitrary variants are like arbitrary values but for doing on-the-fly selector modification, like you can with built-in pseudo-class variants like hover:{utility} or responsive variants like md:{utility} but using square bracket notation directly in your HTML. HTML ```
    {#each items as item}
  • {item}
    • {/each}
``` Learn more in the arbitrary variants documentation. Handling whitespace When an arbitrary value needs to contain a space, use an underscore ( _ ) instead and Tailwind will automatically convert it to a space at build-time: HTML ```
``` In situations where underscores are common but spaces are invalid, Tailwind will preserve the underscore instead of converting it to a space, for example in URLs: HTML ```
``` In the rare case that you actually need to use an underscore but it's ambiguous because a space is valid as well, escape the underscore with a backslash and Tailwind won't convert it to a space: HTML ```
``` If you're using something like JSX where the backslash is stripped from the rendered HTML, use String.raw() so the backslash isn't treated as a JavaScript escape character: ```
``` Resolving ambiguities Many utilities in Tailwind share a common namespace but map to different CSS properties. For example text-lg and text-black both share the text- namespace, but one is for font-size and the other is for color . When using arbitrary values, Tailwind can generally handle this ambiguity automatically based on the value you pass in: HTML ```
...
...
``` Sometimes it really is ambiguous though, for example when using CSS variables: HTML ```
...
``` In these situations, you can "hint" the underlying type to Tailwind by adding a CSS data type before the value: HTML ```
...
...
``` Using custom CSS While Tailwind is designed to handle the bulk of your styling needs, there is nothing stopping you from just writing plain CSS when you need to: CSS ``` @import "tailwindcss";.my-custom-style { /* ... */} ``` Adding base styles If you just want to set some defaults for the page (like the text color, background color, or font family), the easiest option is just adding some classes to the html or body elements: HTML ``` ``` This keeps your base styling decisions in your markup alongside all of your other styles, instead of hiding them in a separate file. If you want to add your own default base styles for specific HTML elements, use the @layer directive to add those styles to Tailwind's base layer: CSS ``` @layer base { h1 { font-size: var(--text-2xl); } h2 { font-size: var(--text-xl); }} ``` Adding component classes Use the components layer for any more complicated classes you want to add to your project that you'd still like to be able to override with utility classes. Traditionally these would be classes like card , btn , badge — that kind of thing. CSS ``` @layer components { .card { background-color: var(--color-white); border-radius: var(--radius-lg); padding: --spacing(6); box-shadow: var(--shadow-xl); }} ``` By defining component classes in the components layer, you can still use utility classes to override them when necessary: HTML ```
``` Using Tailwind you probably don't need these types of classes as often as you think. Read our guide on managing duplication for our recommendations. The components layer is also a good place to put custom styles for any third-party components you're using: CSS ``` @layer components { .select2-dropdown { /* ... */ }} ``` Using variants Use the @variant directive to apply a Tailwind variant within custom CSS: app.css ``` .my-element { background: white; @variant dark { background: black; }} ``` Compiled CSS ``` .my-element { background: white; @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { background: black; }} ``` If you need to apply multiple variants at the same time, stack them using the same syntax you would in HTML: app.css ``` .my-element { background: white; @variant hover:focus { background: black; }} ``` Compiled CSS ``` .my-element { background: white; &:hover { @media (hover: hover) { &:focus { background: black; } } }} ``` To apply the same styles for multiple variants, separate each variant with a comma: app.css ``` .my-element { background: white; @variant hover, focus { background: black; }} ``` Compiled CSS ``` .my-element { background: white; &:hover { @media (hover: hover) { background: black; } } &:focus { background: black; }} ``` Adding custom utilities Simple utilities In addition to using the utilities that ship with Tailwind, you can also add your own custom utilities. This can be useful when there's a CSS feature you'd like to use in your project that Tailwind doesn't include utilities for out of the box. Use the @utility directive to add a custom utility to your project: CSS ``` @utility content-auto { content-visibility: auto;} ``` You can now use this utility in your HTML: HTML ```
``` It will also work with variants like hover , focus and lg : HTML ```
``` Custom utilities are automatically inserted into the utilities layer along with all of the built-in utilities in the framework. Complex utilities If your custom utility is more complex than a single class name, use nesting to define the utility: CSS ``` @utility scrollbar-hidden { &::-webkit-scrollbar { display: none; }} ``` Functional utilities In addition to registering simple utilities with the @utility directive, you can also register functional utilities that accept an argument: CSS ``` @utility tab-* { tab-size: --value(--tab-size-*);} ``` The special --value() function is used to resolve the utility value. Matching theme values Use the --value(--theme-key-*) syntax to resolve the utility value against a set of theme keys: CSS ``` @theme { --tab-size-2: 2; --tab-size-4: 4; --tab-size-github: 8;}@utility tab-* { tab-size: --value(--tab-size-*);} ``` This will match utilities like tab-2 , tab-4 , and tab-github . Bare values To resolve the value as a bare value, use the --value({type}) syntax, where {type} is the data type you want to validate the bare value as: CSS ``` @utility tab-* { tab-size: --value(integer);} ``` This will match utilities like tab-1 and tab-76 . Available bare value data types are: number , integer , ratio , and percentage . Literal values To support literal values, use the --value('literal') syntax (notice the quotes): CSS ``` @utility tab-* { tab-size: --value("inherit", "initial", "unset");} ``` This will match utilities like tab-inherit , tab-initial , and tab-unset . Arbitrary values To support arbitrary values, use the --value([{type}]) syntax (notice the square brackets) to tell Tailwind which types are supported as an arbitrary value: CSS ``` @utility tab-* { tab-size: --value([integer]);} ``` This will match utilities like tab-[1] and tab-[76] . Available arbitrary value data types are: absolute-size , angle , bg-size , color , family-name , generic-name , image , integer , length , line-width , number , percentage , position , ratio , relative-size , url , vector , and * . Supporting theme, bare, and arbitrary values together All three forms of the --value() function can be used within a rule as multiple declarations, and any declarations that fail to resolve will be omitted in the output: CSS ``` @theme { --tab-size-github: 8;}@utility tab-* { tab-size: --value([integer]); tab-size: --value(integer); tab-size: --value(--tab-size-*);} ``` This makes it possible to treat the value differently in each case if necessary, for example translating a bare integer to a percentage: CSS ``` @utility opacity-* { opacity: --value([percentage]); opacity: calc(--value(integer) * 1%); opacity: --value(--opacity-*);} ``` The --value() function can also take multiple arguments and resolve them left to right if you don't need to treat the return value differently in different cases: CSS ``` @theme { --tab-size-github: 8;}@utility tab-* { tab-size: --value(--tab-size-*, integer, [integer]);}@utility opacity-* { opacity: calc(--value(integer) * 1%); opacity: --value(--opacity-*, [percentage]);} ``` Default values Use --default() inside --value() to support a default value when the utility is used without an explicit value: CSS ``` @utility tab-* { tab-size: --value(integer, --default(4));} ``` This matches both tab-2 and tab-4 , as well as just tab which uses the default value of 4 : Compiled CSS ``` .tab { tab-size: 4;}.tab-2 { tab-size: 2;} ``` The --default() function can also be used inside --modifier() to provide a default value when no modifier is present: CSS ``` @utility tab-* { tab-size: --value(integer); line-height: --modifier(integer, --default(1));} ``` This matches tab-2/3 with a line-height of 3 , and tab-2 with a line-height of 1 . Negative values To support negative values, register separate positive and negative utilities into separate declarations: CSS ``` @utility inset-* { inset: --spacing(--value(integer)); inset: --value([percentage], [length]);}@utility -inset-* { inset: --spacing(--value(integer) * -1); inset: calc(--value([percentage], [length]) * -1);} ``` Modifiers Modifiers are handled using the --modifier() function which works exactly like the --value() function but operates on a modifier if present: CSS ``` @utility text-* { font-size: --value(--text-*, [length]); line-height: --modifier(--leading-*, [length], [*]);} ``` If a modifier isn't present, any declaration depending on a modifier is just not included in the output. Fractions To handle fractions, we rely on the CSS ratio data type. If this is used with --value() , it's a signal to Tailwind to treat the value and modifier as a single value: CSS ``` @utility aspect-* { aspect-ratio: --value(--aspect-ratio-*, ratio, [ratio]);} ``` This will match utilities like aspect-square , aspect-3/4 , and aspect-[7/9] . Adding custom variants In addition to using the variants that ship with Tailwind, you can also add your own custom variants using the @custom-variant directive: ``` @custom-variant theme-midnight { &:where([data-theme="midnight"] *) { @slot; }} ``` Now you can use the theme-midnight: `` variant in your HTML: ``` ``` You can create variants using the shorthand syntax when nesting isn't required: ``` @custom-variant theme-midnight (&:where([data-theme="midnight"] *)); ``` When a custom variant has multiple rules, they can be nested within each other: ``` @custom-variant any-hover { @media (any-hover: hover) { &:hover { @slot; } }} ``` Colors Detecting classes in source files On this page Customizing your theme Using arbitrary values Arbitrary properties Arbitrary variants Handling whitespace Resolving ambiguities Using custom CSS Adding base styles Adding component classes Using variants Adding custom utilities Simple utilities Complex utilities Functional utilities Adding custom variants Refactoring UI From the creators of Tailwind CSS Make your ideas look awesome, without relying on a designer. “This is the survival kit I wish I had when I started building apps.” Derrick Reimer, SavvyCal Tailwind CSS Documentation Playground Blog Showcase Resources Refactoring UI Headless UI Heroicons Hero Patterns Community GitHub X Tailwind CSS Documentation Playground Blog Showcase Resources Refactoring UI Headless UI Heroicons Hero Patterns Community GitHub X Copyright © 2026 Tailwind Labs Inc. · Trademark Policy

An Interactive Guide to Web Animation Performance • Siwalik Mukherjee
A description of my image. Siwalik Mukherjee
home
posts
projects
uses
An Interactive Guide to Web Animation Performance
Why does your animation jank on Android but not your MacBook? An interactive guide to how browsers render frames, and the techniques to fix it — FLIP, GPU layers, scroll-driven CSS, and more.
10 min read
Mar 29, 2026
technical
Flip Book
The Pixel Rendering Pipeline
Shadow Boxing
Layer Cake
FLIP It
Scroll-Driven Animations
120Hz Problems
prefers-reduced-motion
Jank Hunting
Closing the Loop
Relevant Reads 
Animation performance advice can start to feel like superstition: use transform not width , never animate height , avoid layout triggers. The rules are real – but without knowing why, you're just hoping they cover your situation. Eventually, they won't.
Tools like (Framer) Motion and GSAP help a lot. But they can't fix a misunderstood rendering pipeline. This is an interactive guide to how browsers actually handle animations, where the real costs hide, and how to outmaneuver them. Let's get into it!
note
This post is heavy on animations and interactive demos. For the best experience, view this post on a wider screen like tablet or desktop.
Flip Book
Every silky smooth motion is just a rapid sequence of still images, like a digital flipbook. The faster you flip, the smoother it looks.
Speed Up
video credits: GIPHY
On screen, each of those images is a frame drawn by the browser. At 60 FPS, you have 16.7 ms to render each one, in 120 FPS, you have 8.3 ms. Miss that budget and you drop a frame. Drop enough frames and the animation feels janky.
Pause Frame: 17/60
Framerate:
60 FPS
30 FPS
15 FPS
5 FPS 16
0ms 500ms 1000ms
rendered frames skipped frames
The Pixel Rendering Pipeline
Every frame goes through a series of stages inside the browser. Triggering an earlier stage cascades into everything that follows, so the stage you hit determines the cost you pay.
JavaScript
Style
Layout
Paint
Composite
You can hover on the pixel rendering pipeline stages above to learn more about them
Width Animation
Scale Transform
JS-based Animation
Position Transform
Opacity Fade
Color Transition
Clip Path
Code
Width animations trigger all pipeline stages because changing width affects element geometry/Layout. Watch how it pushes sibling elements. This is computationally expensive as it forces the browser
to recalculate layout for affected elements and their dependents
paint affected areas of the screen
and composite the layers back together for final display
A better alternative would be using a scale (transform) - try it from the dropdown!
note
Worth burning into your brain: if you trigger Layout, you also pay for Paint and Composite. But if you only trigger Composite - via transform or opacity , you skip the expensive stuff entirely. This one rule explains most of the advice in this post.
Shadow Boxing
Some animations look simple but are quietly expensive. Can we use the pipeline to outsmart them?
Consider box-shadow animations. Each frame of a box-shadow transition triggers Paint → Composite. Shadow calculations and Gaussian blur get re-executed on every single frame.
```
1
/* Usual solution */
2
/* triggers Paint → Composite every frame */
3

4
.card {
5
  transition: box-shadow 0.3s ease;
6
}
7

8
.card:hover {
9
  box-shadow: 0 10px 20px rgba(0,0,0,0.2);
10
}
```
Here's a more efficient approach: pre-render the shadow on a pseudo-element and animate its opacity from 0 to 1. This skips the Paint stage entirely and goes straight to Composite.
```
1
/* GPU-accelerated solution */
2
/* triggers only Composite */
3

4
.card {
5
  position: relative;
6
}
7

8
.card::after {
9
  content: '';
10
  position: absolute;
11
  inset: 0;
12
  opacity: 0;
13
  border-radius: 8px;
14
  box-shadow: 0 0 30px rgba(251, 191, 36, 0.6);
15
  transition: opacity 0.3s ease-in-out;
16
}
17

18
.card:hover::after {
19
  opacity: 1;
20
}
```
Let's see them in action.
Box-shadow animation:
Emulated Render Pipeline (continuous repaints during transition)
scroll to code
Pseudo-element animation:
Emulated Render Pipeline (minimal repaints, only during state change)
scroll to code
info
Open DevTools and hover over the boxes above. The Performance panel will reveal green paint timing bars similar to the emulation. Fewer bars, better performance.
This trick isn't just for shadows. The same pattern applies to any expensive-to-paint effect: gradients, glows, complex borders. Pre-render it on a pseudo-element, then animate opacity .
Layer Cake
When transform and opacity skip paint, where does the work actually happen? The GPU. The browser breaks your DOM into composite layers, stored as textures in GPU memory, and lets the GPU composite them together. These layers are managed in a 3D space, allowing properties like transforms, opacity, and filters to be processed directly by the GPU.
To see this in action, check out the interactive inspector below, which demonstrates how browsers handle layer compositing.
Layer Names: ON Toggle description
Browser Layout

Glass Panel
Card
Floating Circle
GPU Layers

Glass Panel

Floating Circle

Glass Panel
Card
Floating Circle
Layer Controls
Rotate X (0°) 0
Rotate Y (0°) 0
Rotate Z (0°) 0
Layer Spacing (20px) 20
Click on different elements above or increase transform complexities to see element-specific details and how they affect the GPU usage.
Emulated GPU usage - based on selected element
38%
Clicked element
Floating Circle
Compositing Reason
Transform + solid color
Performance Impact
Low memory usage
Think of it like a Photoshop document. The browser separates your page into layers, hands them to the GPU as flat textures, and the GPU stamps them together every frame. Three stages:
Browser Stage: Identifies elements that need their own compositing layers: things with blur effects, transforms, opacity, and so on.
GPU Stage: Each element becomes a texture uploaded to GPU memory. Simpler shapes cost less; glass effects and large blurred surfaces cost more.
Final Output: The GPU composites all layers in the correct order, applying transformations and effects.
note
This demo is an emulation. Actual GPU impact varies by browser, device, and implementation.
Each promoted layer holds a texture in GPU memory. Promote too many and you hit memory pressure, especially on mobile, where this causes stutters that are invisible on your dev machine.
Use will-change strategically: apply it just before the animation starts and remove it as soon as it ends.
```
1
// Apply just before the animation starts
2
element.addEventListener('mouseenter', () => {
3
  element.style.willChange = 'transform, opacity';
4
});
5

6
// Remove once the animation is complete
7
element.addEventListener('transitionend', () => {
8
  element.style.willChange = 'auto';
9
}, { once: true });
```
FLIP It
What about animating things that change layout, like expanding a card or reordering a list? Animating width , height , or top / left directly triggers Layout on every frame.
FLIP (First Last Invert Play) solves this. Measure where an element is and where it's going, then use transform to fake the starting position and animate back to the final one. The layout calculation happens exactly once; the rest is compositor-only.
How FLIP works
‹
›
Press › to walk through each step
First Record current position with getBoundingClientRect().
Last Apply the layout change. Record the new position — layout runs once.
Invert Apply a transform to snap the element back visually to where it was.
Play Animate transform to identity. Compositor-only — no layout per frame.
Element
First position
Live comparison
Click Move to animate
Without FLIP top / left
Move
Layout + Paint + Composite every frame
FLIP transform
Move
Layout measured once; Composite per frame
Layout
Paint
Composite
```
1
const ref = useRef(null);
2
const firstRect = useRef(null);
3
const [trigger, setTrigger] = useState(0);
4

5
function onMove() {
6
  // First: record position before the change
7
  firstRect.current = ref.current.getBoundingClientRect();
8

9
  // Last: commit the layout change via state, then bump trigger
10
  setPosition(p => p === 'A' ? 'B' : 'A');
11
  setTrigger(t => t + 1);
12
}
13

14
// Invert + Play: runs after React commits new position to the DOM, before paint
15
useLayoutEffect(() => {
16
  if (!firstRect.current || !ref.current) return;
17
  const first = firstRect.current;
18
  const last = ref.current.getBoundingClientRect();
19
  firstRect.current = null;
20

21
  const dx = first.left - last.left;
22
  const dy = first.top - last.top;
23

24
  ref.current.animate([
25
    { transform: `translate(${dx}px, ${dy}px)` },
26
    { transform: 'translate(0, 0)' }
27
  ], { duration: 500, easing: 'ease-out' });
28
}, [trigger]);
```
The layout change happens instantly (so we can measure the final position), then the entire visible animation runs purely via transform with no repeated Layout calls.
info
In practice, (Framer) Motion's layout prop handles all of this for you! But now you know exactly why it's fast.
Scroll-Driven Animations
A super common pattern: animate something as the user scrolls, like a progress bar, an element fading in, or a parallax effect or the new Apple launch page. Instinctively most engineers reach for a scroll event listener and update styles in JS. The problem is this runs on the main thread, and if anything else is happening, frames get dropped.
CSS Scroll-Driven Animations let you tie an animation directly to scroll position in CSS. No JS needed, no event listeners. When the animated properties are transform or opacity , the browser can run the whole thing on the compositor thread, without main thread involvement.
```
1
/* A scroll-progress bar, no JavaScript required */
2
@supports (animation-timeline: scroll()) {
3
  .progress-bar {
4
    position: fixed;
5
    top: 0;
6
    left: 0;
7
    height: 4px;
8
    background: #6366f1;
9
    transform-origin: left;
10
    animation: grow-bar auto linear;
11
    animation-timeline: scroll();
12
  }
13

14
  @keyframes grow-bar {
15
    from { transform: scaleX(0); }
16
    to   { transform: scaleX(1); }
17
  }
18
}
```
Compare that to the JS equivalent, which fires on every scroll event on the main thread:
```
1
window.addEventListener('scroll', () => {
2
  const scrolled = window.scrollY / (document.body.scrollHeight - window.innerHeight);
3
  progressBar.style.transform = `scaleX(${scrolled})`;
4
});
```
trivia
The scroll animation you see on this page's Navbar is implemented using this css-only pattern.
Same visual result, very different performance profile under load. animation-timeline is well-supported in Chrome, Safari and other major browsers but still experimental in Firefox at the time of writing; use the @supports wrapper as a progressive enhancement safety net for such cases.
120Hz Problems
Modern devices increasingly ship at 90 Hz, 120 Hz, 144 Hz, or higher. The math matters:
At 60 Hz: 16.7 ms per frame
At 120 Hz: ~8.3 ms per frame
Platforms like iOS (ProMotion) and Android (VRR) adapt refresh rates dynamically. If your animation can't keep up, frames drop and motion feels uneven. JS that sailed through at 60 Hz can suddenly jank at 120 Hz.
You can measure the effective refresh rate using requestAnimationFrame timestamps:
```
1
let lastTime = performance.now();
2

3
requestAnimationFrame(function measure(time) {
4
  const delta = time - lastTime;
5
  console.log(`Frame delta: ${delta.toFixed(1)}ms (~${Math.round(1000 / delta)} Hz)`);
6
  lastTime = time;
7
  requestAnimationFrame(measure);
8
});
```
Test on high-refresh devices when possible. Even with CPU throttling, watching frame deltas will reveal timing sensitivity that your average dev machine hides.
prefers-reduced-motion
Not every user wants motion. Some have vestibular disorders where animations cause real physical discomfort. prefers-reduced-motion is both good UX and, increasingly, a legal accessibility requirement.
```
1
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
2
  *, *::before, *::after {
3
    animation-duration: 0.01ms !important;
4
    transition-duration: 0.01ms !important;
5
  }
6
}
```
For JS-driven animations:
```
1
const prefersReduced = window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches;
2

3
if (!prefersReduced) {
4
  element.animate([/* ... */], { duration: 300 });
5
}
```
Josh Comeau has a reusable useReducedMotion hook worth bookmarking.
One nuance worth knowing: reduce doesn't always mean remove. Some users rely on motion cues to understand UI state changes: a sidebar sliding in, a dialog appearing. The goal is to reduce intensity and duration, not strip all motion away.
note @starting-style (Baseline 2024) lets you define entry animations that work without JS or class-toggling hacks, and they naturally respect prefers-reduced-motion when combined with the pattern above.
Jank Hunting
When I can feel something's wrong but can't explain why, I open DevTools and check three things:
1. Paint Flashing(More Tools → Rendering → Paint flashing):
Highlights regions being repainted every frame. If a large area flashes green during a hover animation, you're likely hitting the box-shadow/gradient trap from earlier. 
2. Layers Panel (More Tools → Layers):
Shows every compositing layer as a 3D visualization with memory cost. If you see dozens of layers on a simple page, something is over-promoting. 
3. Performance Recorder:
Hit record, trigger your animation, stop. In the flame chart, look for long purple (Rendering) or green (Painting) bars; those are your frame-budget killers. A 6x CPU throttle simulates a mid-range Android device. 
Closing the Loop
If you're only taking a few things away from this, make it these:
Prefer transform + opacity for continuous motion.
Avoid layout-triggering properties ( width , top/left ) while animating, use transforms or a library like Motion which use FLIP technique and skip per-frame Layout entirely.
Promote layers intentionally; clean up will-change after animation.
For scroll effects, try animation-timeline before reaching for a JS scroll listener.
Test on high-refresh and mid-range mobile; they surface problems desktops hide.
Respect prefers-reduced-motion .
The rendering pipeline isn't just animation trivia, it's a map. Once you know what Layout, Paint, and Composite actually cost, you stop guessing and start reasoning. That changes how you write CSS, how you review PRs, and what you reach for first when something feels off.
Pick one interaction this week. Profile it, trace it through the pipeline, and swap one property. The gap between a janky and a fluid experience is usually smaller than you think.
If this was useful, share it with someone shipping animations. And if you have a favourite technique I missed, let me know on BlueSky or Twitter.
Relevant Reads
If you want to go deeper, here are some reads that expand on the topics I barely touched.
Rendering Performance (web.dev) - excellent primer on pipeline stages and frame budgets. The authors also have a free course on Udemy which you'll have a lot of fun learning.
Scroll-Driven Animations (Chrome for Developers)
FLIP Your Animations (Aerotwist) - the original FLIP writeup by Paul Lewis
120fps and no jank (Surma) - why high-refresh fundamentally tightens budgets
GPU Accelerated Compositing in Chrome from chromium.org
CSS JS Animation Performance Guide by mozilla.org

Module 00 : Android Introduction & Architecture
This module provides a foundational understanding of the Android operating system, its history, architectural layers, development environment setup, and project structure. Whether you're a beginner or an experienced developer, mastering these fundamentals is essential for building secure and efficient Android applications.
0.1 Introduction to Android OS
Android is an open-source, Linux-based operating system designed primarily for touchscreen mobile devices. It is developed by Google and the Open Handset Alliance (OHA), a consortium of technology companies.
📱 What is Android?
Open Source: Android Open Source Project (AOSP) allows anyone to view, modify, and contribute to the source code
Linux Kernel Based: Built on a modified Linux kernel for security, memory management, and process handling
Touchscreen Optimized: Designed for intuitive finger-based interaction
Multi-Platform Support: Runs on smartphones, tablets, smartwatches (Wear OS), TVs (Android TV), cars (Android Auto), and IoT devices
Application Ecosystem: Supports over 3 million apps on Google Play Store
Global Reach: Powers over 3 billion active devices worldwide (70%+ mobile OS market share)
🏢 Open Handset Alliance (OHA)
Founded: November 5, 2007
Founding Members:
Technology: Google, HTC, Samsung, LG, Sony, Motorola, Dell, Intel, Qualcomm, Texas Instruments, NVIDIA
Telecom: T-Mobile, Sprint, China Mobile, Telefónica, NTT DoCoMo
Purpose: Develop open standards for mobile devices
🎯 Core Objectives of Android
Security
Sandboxing, permissions, encryption
Efficiency
Power management, resource optimization
Compatibility
Multiple devices, form factors
Open Source
Customizable, community-driven
0.2 History & Evolution of Android
Android's journey from a startup acquisition to the world's most popular mobile operating system is remarkable. Understanding its evolution helps appreciate the security improvements and feature additions over time.

0.4 Android Version Architecture
Android follows a layered architecture where each layer provides services to the layer above while abstracting implementation details. Understanding this architecture is crucial for developing efficient apps and troubleshooting issues.
📱 Layered Architecture (Detailed)
Applications Layer – System apps (Phone, Contacts, Settings, Camera) and user‑installed apps (WhatsApp, Chrome, Instagram, Games).
Application Framework – Provides high‑level services to apps including Activity Manager, Window Manager, Content Providers, View System, Package Manager, Resource Manager, Notification Manager, and Location Manager.
Libraries & Android Runtime (ART) – Native C/C++ libraries (WebKit, OpenGL, SQLite, Media Framework, libc, SSL, Skia, ICU) and ART for executing DEX bytecode.
Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL) – Standard interfaces for hardware components (camera, Bluetooth, GPS, sensors, audio, Wi-Fi).
Linux Kernel – Core system services (process management, memory management, power management, network stack, device drivers).
🧠 Key Components & Processes
Dalvik / ART – Virtual machine for running Android applications.
Binder IPC – Inter‑process communication mechanism.
Zygote – Process that preloads core libraries and forks new app processes.
System Server – Hosts core system services (Activity Manager, Window Manager, Package Manager, Power Manager).
init – First userspace process (PID 1), starts Zygote and other daemons.
Service Manager – Manages Binder services and provides naming.
💡 Android applications run in isolated sandboxes – each app has its own Linux user ID (UID) and runs in its own process.
🔄 How Android Works – Complete App Launch Flow
When a user launches an Android application, the following sequence occurs:
```
User Launches App (Taps Icon)
         │
         ▼
Launcher Activity sends Intent to Activity Manager (via Binder)
         │
         ▼
Activity Manager checks manifest and permissions
         │
         ▼
Activity Manager requests Zygote to fork new process
         │
         ▼
Zygote forks (copy-on-write) → New App Process Created
         │
         ▼
App Process loads DEX code and resources
         │
         ▼
System Server provides required services via Binder
         │
         ▼
App runs in its own process with unique UID (sandboxed)
         │
         ▼
Linux Kernel manages resources, memory, and hardware
         │
         ▼
App Lifecycle Begins (onCreate → onStart → onResume)
```

Layer 5: Applications

Layer 4: Framework
Provides high-level services: Activity Manager, Window Manager, Content Providers, Package Manager, Resource Manager.
Layer 3: Libraries & ART
Native C/C++ libraries (SQLite, OpenGL, WebKit) and ART runtime for executing DEX bytecode.

Layer 1: Linux Kernel
Core foundation: Process Management, Memory Management, Power Management, Device Drivers, SELinux Security.
Binder IPC
Primary inter-process communication mechanism. Kernel driver handles transactions with caller UID/PID tracking.
Zygote Process
Preloads core libraries and forks new app processes (copy-on-write). Improves app launch speed.
System Server
Hosts core system services: Activity Manager, Window Manager, Package Manager, Power Manager.
📚 Detailed Layer Descriptions
Layer 1: Linux Kernel
The foundation of Android architecture. Provides core system services and hardware abstraction.
Process Management: Scheduling, creation, termination, IPC via Binder
Memory Management: Virtual memory, paging, Low Memory Killer (LMK)
Power Management: Wake locks, suspend/resume, Doze mode integration
Device Drivers: Display, touch, camera, audio, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, USB, sensors
Security: SELinux (Enforcing mode), KASLR, cgroups, namespaces, seccomp-bpf
```
# Check kernel version on device
adb shell cat /proc/version
# Example output: Linux version 5.10.43-android12-9-g1234567

# View kernel security settings
adb shell getenforce  # Enforcing (SELinux status)
```
Layer 2: Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL)
Standard interfaces for hardware components, hiding vendor-specific implementations.
Camera HAL: Controls image sensors, autofocus, HDR+, night mode, multi-camera
Audio HAL: Manages audio input/output, codecs, amplifiers, spatial audio
Sensors HAL: Reads accelerometer, gyroscope, proximity, light, compass, barometer
Display HAL: Hardware Composer (HWC) for smooth display composition
Connectivity HALs: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, NFC, GPS, Cellular radio
💡 Project Treble (Android 8.0+): HALs run in isolated binderized processes for faster OS updates and better security.
Layer 3: Native Libraries & ART
📚 Key Native Libraries:
Bionic libc: Custom C library (BSD-licensed, smaller footprint)
WebKit: Browser engine for WebView (HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript)
OpenGL ES / Vulkan: 3D graphics rendering for games and UI
SQLite: Embedded relational database (ACID compliant)
Media Framework: Audio/video playback (Codecs: H.264, H.265, VP9, AAC, MP3)
Skia: 2D graphics engine (canvas drawing, text rendering)
BoringSSL: Cryptography (TLS/SSL, encryption, certificate validation)
🚀 Android Runtime (ART):
Executes DEX bytecode (converted from Java/Kotlin)
Hybrid compilation: AOT (Ahead-Of-Time) + JIT (Just-In-Time) + PGO (Profile-Guided Optimization)
Replaced Dalvik VM in Android 5.0 (5x performance improvement)
Concurrent Copying Garbage Collection (minimal pause times <1ms)
Layer 4: Application Framework
The Application Framework provides high-level services for app development.
Activity Manager: Manages app lifecycle and activity stack
Window Manager: Handles windowing, input dispatching, orientation
Content Providers: Enables data sharing between apps
Package Manager: Installs, updates, and removes apps

Notification Manager: Displays system/app notifications
Location Manager: Provides GPS and network location
Telephony Manager: Cellular calls, SMS, network info
Sensor Manager: Accesses hardware sensors
Power Manager: Wake locks, battery optimization
Job Scheduler: Background task scheduling

The topmost layer containing all user-facing applications.

Android uses a 5-layer architecture from Linux Kernel to Applications Layer
Each layer has specific responsibilities and interacts only with adjacent layers

0.8 Emulator & Physical Device Testing
Testing Android apps on emulators and physical devices is crucial for ensuring compatibility, performance, and security. Both approaches have their advantages and use cases.
🤖 Android Emulator
Virtual Device Testing
✅ Advantages:
Test multiple Android versions (API 24 to 34) easily
No physical device needed - cost effective
Simulate sensors (GPS, accelerometer, rotation)
Test different screen sizes/resolutions (phone, tablet, foldable)
Save/load device snapshots (quick state restore)
Simulate network conditions (2G, 3G, 4G, 5G, Wi-Fi, airplane mode)
Test low battery/memory/low storage conditions
Simulate incoming calls, SMS, battery level changes
Google Play Store available on some images
❌ Disadvantages:
Slower than physical device (even with HAXM/WHPX acceleration)
Limited hardware sensor simulation accuracy
Requires virtualization enabled in BIOS
Not all device features simulated (bluetooth, camera quality, etc.)
Higher resource usage (CPU/RAM)
📱 Physical Device Testing
Real Hardware Testing
✅ Advantages:
Real hardware performance (actual CPU/GPU speeds)
Actual battery consumption measurement
Real camera quality, GPS accuracy, sensor precision
Actual network connectivity (cellular, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth)
Authentic user experience testing (touch response, haptics)
Install/run from Play Store (beta testing)
USB debugging for real-time monitoring and log capture
Test device-specific features (fingerprint sensor, face unlock, notch)
❌ Disadvantages:
Limited device models (can't test all)
Cost of purchasing multiple devices
Android version fragmentation (users on different OS versions)
Manual testing required for many scenarios
Device availability for multiple team members

Module 01 : Complete Android Architecture
This module provides an in-depth exploration of Android's layered architecture, from the top-level applications down to the Linux kernel. Understanding each layer's responsibilities, interactions, and design patterns is crucial for building secure, efficient, and performant Android applications.
📱 Application Layer
1.1.1 Overview of Application Layer
The Application Layer is the topmost layer of Android architecture, containing all applications that users interact with directly. This layer includes both pre-installed system applications and third-party applications installed by users. Each application runs in its own secure sandbox with a unique Linux user ID (UID), ensuring isolation and security. This layer is where all user-facing functionality resides, from basic phone calls to complex gaming and productivity applications.
The Applications Layer is the topmost layer of the Android architecture, containing all the applications that users interact with directly. This layer includes both system applications (pre-installed by the manufacturer) and user-installed applications (downloaded from Google Play Store or side-loaded). All apps run in their own sandboxed environment and communicate with the underlying framework through well-defined APIs.

The Applications Layer contains all user-facing apps, both system and third-party.
📌 Key Characteristics of Application Layer:
✓ Contains all user-facing applications (system + third-party)
✓ Each app runs in isolated process with unique UID
✓ Apps communicate via Intents and Binder IPC
✓ Permissions control access to sensitive data/features
✓ Apps can be updated independently of the OS
✓ Apps are distributed as APK (Android Package Kit) files
✓ Each app has its own Linux user ID (UID) and SELinux context
✓ Apps run in Dalvik/ART virtual machine instances
⚠ Security Implications of Application Layer:
✓ Malicious apps can steal sensitive data (contacts, SMS, location)
✓ Permission abuse by third-party apps seeking excessive access
✓ Repackaged apps with embedded malware trojans
✓ Side-loaded apps bypass Google Play Protect scanning
✓ Overlay attacks (tapjacking) can steal user credentials
✓ Exported components can lead to privilege escalation
✓ Intent hijacking can redirect sensitive data to malicious apps

1.1.2 System Applications
System applications are pre-installed applications that come with the Android operating system. They provide essential functionality like calling, messaging, contacts, camera, settings, and more. These apps have special privileges and are signed with the platform certificate. System apps are located in read-only partitions and cannot be uninstalled by users without root access.
📌 Key Characteristics of System Applications:
✓ Pre-installed during factory flashing, cannot be uninstalled (only disabled)
✓ Signed with platform certificate (same signature as the OS)
✓ Located in read-only partitions: /system/app/ , /system/priv-app/ , /product/app/
✓ Have special privileges and can access protected APIs

1.1.3 User Applications (Third-Party Apps)
User applications are installed by users from Google Play Store, Amazon Appstore, or side-loaded from APK files. They run in isolated sandboxes and must request permissions to access sensitive data or device features. These apps form the vast Android ecosystem, with over 3 million apps available on Google Play Store.
📌 Key Characteristics of User Applications:
✓ Installed by users from Play Store or side-loaded from APK files
✓ Run in isolated sandboxes with unique Linux UID (10000-99999)
✓ Must request dangerous permissions at runtime (Android 6.0+)
✓ Can be uninstalled by users at any time
✓ Located in /data/app/ with private data in /data/data/<package>/
✓ Updated via Play Store or manual APK installation
✓ Subject to Google Play Protect scanning (if installed from Play Store)
⚠ Security Considerations for User Apps:
Apps can request dangerous permissions (CAMERA, LOCATION, MICROPHONE)
Malicious apps may steal sensitive data or display intrusive ads
Side-loaded apps bypass Google Play Protect scanning
Apps from unknown sources pose higher security risk
Repackaged popular apps may contain malware trojans
Apps can request accessibility service permission for screen reading
Overlay permission (SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW) enables tapjacking attacks
📊 Common App Categories & Security Risks:
Social Media: Data collection, location tracking
Messaging: Message interception, metadata collection
Banking: Financial fraud, credential theft
E-commerce: Purchase history tracking, payment info risk
Health/Fitness: Health data leakage, location tracking

2⃣ Dangerous Permissions Commonly Abused
🚨 Most Abused Dangerous Permissions:
READ_CONTACTS – Contact data theft, social engineering
ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION – Precise location tracking, stalking
ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION – Continuous background tracking
RECORD_AUDIO – Eavesdropping, voice recording, ambient listening
CAMERA – Unauthorized photos/videos, spying
READ_SMS – SMS interception, 2FA code theft
READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE – File theft, photo access, document exfiltration
WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE – Malware injection, file modification
SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW – Overlay attacks, tapjacking
BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE – Screen reading, input injection, keylogging
GET_ACCOUNTS – Account enumeration, email address theft
READ_PHONE_STATE – IMEI/phone number theft, device tracking
PROCESS_OUTGOING_CALLS – Call interception, call recording
BODY_SENSORS – Health data theft (heart rate, steps)
ACTIVITY_RECOGNITION – Movement tracking (walking, driving, cycling)
✅ Permission Best Practices for Developers:
Request only minimum required permissions (principle of least privilege)
Explain why each permission is needed (with rationale dialog)
Handle permission denial gracefully (don't crash or force exit)
Request permissions in context (not at app startup)
Allow users to revoke permissions (check with checkSelfPermission() )
Use shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale() for denied permissions
Request permission only when feature is actually used
Consider using intent-based alternatives instead of permissions
Document all permissions in Play Store listing
📊 Permission Usage Statistics:
80% of apps request INTERNET permission

35% of apps request STORAGE permission
25% of apps request CAMERA permission
20% of apps request CONTACTS permission

3⃣ Malicious App Behavior Patterns
🚨 Common Malware Behaviors & Indicators
Spyware – Steal contacts, SMS, location, photos, keystrokes

Fake Apps – Impersonate legitimate apps to steal credentials
Dialer Fraud – Make premium rate calls without user knowledge
SMS Fraud – Send premium rate SMS messages
Keyloggers – Record keystrokes to steal passwords

5⃣ Repackaged Apps & Malware Distribution Techniques
🔧 Common Repackaging Techniques:
Decompile → Inject Malware → Recompile – Add malicious code to legitimate APK
Remove Security Protections – Disable ProGuard, remove signature verification
Add Permissions – Insert dangerous permissions into manifest
Replace Ad IDs – Redirect ad revenue to attacker
Modify Payment Logic – Bypass purchases, steal payment info
Add Backdoors – Remote access, command & control (C2)
Modify URL Endpoints – Redirect traffic to attacker servers
🛡 Detection & Prevention:
```
# Compare APK signatures
apksigner verify --verbose original.apk
apksigner verify --verbose suspicious.apk

# Check certificate fingerprints
keytool -printcert -jarfile original.apk
keytool -printcert -jarfile suspicious.apk

# Decompile and compare
jadx -d original/ original.apk
jadx -d suspicious/ suspicious.apk
diff -r original/ suspicious/

# Check for unexpected permissions
aapt dump badging suspicious.apk | grep "uses-permission"

# Check for modified resources
apktool d original.apk
apktool d suspicious.apk
diff -r original/ suspicious/
```

1.1.4 APK Structure (Android Package Kit)
APK (Android Package Kit) is the file format used to distribute and install Android applications. It's essentially a ZIP archive containing all necessary components for an app to run on an Android device. Understanding APK structure is crucial for security analysis, reverse engineering, and malware detection.
📁 Complete APK Structure
```
MyApp.apk
├── AndroidManifest.xml          # App metadata, permissions, components (binary XML)
├── classes.dex                  # Dalvik Executable bytecode (primary)
├── classes2.dex                 # Additional DEX files (multidex support)
├── classes3.dex                 # More DEX files (if needed)
├── resources.arsc               # Compiled resources (strings, layouts, IDs)
├── res/                         # Resources directory
│   ├── drawable/                # Images (PNG, JPG, XML vectors)
│   ├── drawable-hdpi/           # High DPI images
│   ├── drawable-xhdpi/          # Extra high DPI
│   ├── drawable-xxhdpi/         # Extra extra high DPI
│   ├── drawable-xxxhdpi/        # Extra extra extra high DPI
│   ├── layout/                  # XML layout files
│   ├── layout-land/             # Landscape layouts
│   ├── mipmap-hdpi/             # App icons (high DPI)
│   ├── mipmap-mdpi/             # App icons (medium DPI)
│   ├── mipmap-xhdpi/            # App icons (extra high)
│   ├── mipmap-xxhdpi/           # App icons (extra extra high)
│   ├── mipmap-xxxhdpi/          # App icons (extra extra extra high)
│   ├── values/                  # Strings, colors, dimensions, styles
│   ├── values-night/            # Dark theme resources
│   ├── values-v23/              # API 23+ resources
│   ├── anim/                    # Property animations
│   ├── animator/                # View animations
│   ├── raw/                     # Raw resources (audio, video)
│   ├── xml/                     # XML configuration files
│   └── font/                    # Custom font files
├── lib/                         # Native libraries (.so files)
│   ├── armeabi-v7a/             # 32-bit ARM (most common)
│   ├── arm64-v8a/               # 64-bit ARM (modern devices)
│   ├── x86/                     # 32-bit Intel x86
│   ├── x86_64/                  # 64-bit Intel x86_64
│   └── mips/                    # MIPS architecture (rare)
├── META-INF/                    # Signatures and certificates
│   ├── MANIFEST.MF              # Manifest file (SHA-1 hashes of all files)
│   ├── CERT.SF                  # Signature file (signature of MANIFEST.MF)
│   └── CERT.RSA                 # RSA certificate (public key + signature)
├── assets/                      # Raw asset files (accessed via AssetManager)
├── kotlin/                      # Kotlin metadata (if using Kotlin)
├── okhttp3/                     # Network library files (if used)
├── Firebase/                    # Firebase configuration (if used)
└── lib/                         # Additional native libraries
```
APK is a ZIP archive containing compiled code, resources, and manifest.
📋 Detailed APK Components
| Component | Description | Security Relevance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AndroidManifest.xml | App configuration, permissions, components | Critical – Defines exported components |
| classes.dex | Dalvik bytecode (Java/Kotlin compiled code) | High – Can be decompiled to Java |
| resources.arsc | Compiled resources index | Medium – May contain sensitive strings |
| lib/*.so | Native C/C++ libraries | Critical – Buffer overflow vulnerabilities |
| META-INF/ | Digital signatures and certificates | High – Verifies app integrity |

1.1.5 Android App Lifecycle
Android applications have a lifecycle managed by the Activity Manager Service (AMS). Apps can be in different states: foreground, visible, background, or empty. The system may kill apps to free resources based on priority using the Low Memory Killer (LMK). Understanding app lifecycle is crucial for memory management and battery optimization.
📊 Android App Process Importance Levels
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    ANDROID APP PROCESS IMPORTANCE LEVELS                    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                             │
│  LEVEL 1: FOREGROUND PROCESS (Killed last)                                  │
│  • Activity in onResume() (user interacting with the app)                   │
│  • Service bound to foreground activity                                     │
│  • Service running startForeground() (with visible notification)            │
│  • Service executing onCreate()/onStart()/onDestroy() callbacks             │
│  • BroadcastReceiver executing onReceive() method                           │
│                                                                             │
│  LEVEL 2: VISIBLE PROCESS                                                   │
│  • Activity in onStart() but not onResume() (partially visible)             │
│  • Service bound to visible activity                                        │
│  • Visible activity showing a dialog (e.g., permission request)             │
│                                                                             │
│  LEVEL 3: SERVICE PROCESS                                                   │
│  • Started service (non-foreground, running in background)                  │
│  • Uploading/downloading files, playing music (without notification)        │
│                                                                             │
│  LEVEL 4: BACKGROUND PROCESS (Cached)                                       │
│  • Activity in onStop() (not visible to user)                               │
│  • Process contains no active components                                    │
│  • Kept in LRU cache for faster restart                                     │
│  • Can be killed at any time when memory is needed                          │
│                                                                             │
│  LEVEL 5: EMPTY PROCESS (Killed first)                                      │
│  • No active application components                                         │
│  • Kept only for caching purposes                                           │
│  • First to be killed when memory pressure increases                        │
│                                                                             │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Memory Thresholds (typical values):
• LOW_MEMORY_THRESHOLD: 32MB (varies by device)
• FOREGROUND_APP_ADJ: 0
• VISIBLE_APP_ADJ: 1
• SERVICE_ADJ: 3
• CACHED_APP_MIN_ADJ: 9
• CACHED_APP_MAX_ADJ: 15
```
📋 Process States and Transitions
| State | Description | Memory Priority |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Running | App is in foreground, user actively interacting | Highest |
| Paused | App is partially visible but not in focus | High |
| Stopped | App is completely hidden | Medium |
| Cached | App is in background, kept in memory | Low |
| Killed | App process terminated by LMK | Lowest |
📊 OOM Score Ranges (Android)
0-300: Foreground/Visible apps (protected)
300-600: Service processes
600-900: Backup/Home apps
900-1200: Hidden apps
1200-2100: Cached/Empty apps (kill first)
💡 Apps with higher OOM scores are killed first. Foreground apps have score 0 and are killed last.

✅ Key Takeaways - Android App Lifecycle
Apps have 5 priority levels: Foreground → Visible → Service → Background → Empty
Foreground apps have OOM score 0 and are killed last

📋 Activity Lifecycle Methods Explained
| Method | Purpose | Key Actions | Next Method |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| onCreate() | Initialize activity | setContentView(), findViewById(), init ViewModel | onStart() |
| onStart() | Activity becoming visible | Register receivers, start services | onResume() |
| onResume() | Activity in foreground | Start animations, camera preview, location updates | onPause() |
| onPause() | Partially obscured | Stop animations, release camera, save unsaved data | onStop() or onResume() |
| onStop() | No longer visible | Unregister receivers, stop services, save state | onRestart() or onDestroy() |
| onRestart() | Restart after stop | Prepare for restart (rarely overridden) | onStart() |
| onDestroy() | Activity finishing | Clean up resources, remove callbacks, dismiss dialogs | - |
💾 Saved Instance State (State Preservation)
```
// Saving state (called before onStop)
override fun onSaveInstanceState(outState: Bundle) {
    super.onSaveInstanceState(outState)
    outState.putString("user_input", editText.text.toString())
    outState.putInt("counter", counter)
    outState.putParcelable("user", user)
}

// Restoring state (in onCreate or onRestoreInstanceState)
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
    setContentView(R.layout.activity_main)
    
    if (savedInstanceState != null) {
        val savedText = savedInstanceState.getString("user_input")
        counter = savedInstanceState.getInt("counter")
        user = savedInstanceState.getParcelable("user")
    }
}

// Alternative restoration method
override fun onRestoreInstanceState(savedInstanceState: Bundle) {
    super.onRestoreInstanceState(savedInstanceState)
    val savedText = savedInstanceState.getString("user_input")
}
```
⚠ Note: onSaveInstanceState() is NOT called when user explicitly finishes activity (back button) or when finish() is called.
🚀 Activity Launch Modes
| Launch Mode | Description | Use Case | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| standard | Default mode, new instance every time | Normal activities | Multiple instances allowed in same task |
| singleTop | Reuse top instance if same | Notification taps, search | If activity is on top, onNewIntent() called |
| singleTask | Single instance in its own task | Main/Home activities | Only one instance, clears activities above |
| singleInstance | Single instance, exclusive task | Launcher, system activities | No other activities allowed in same task |

1.1.7 Fragment Lifecycle
A Fragment represents a reusable portion of an Activity's UI. Fragments have their own lifecycle that is closely tied to the Activity's lifecycle. Fragments were introduced in Android 3.0 (Honeycomb) to support dynamic and flexible UI designs, especially for tablets and large screens. Fragments allow modular UI design and better resource management.

📋 Fragment Lifecycle Methods Explained
| Method | Purpose | Key Actions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| onAttach() | Fragment attached to Activity | Get Activity reference, initialize parameters |
| onCreate() | Initialize fragment | Retain instance, parse arguments |
| onCreateView() | Inflate fragment layout | Return View for fragment UI (can be null for headless) |
| onViewCreated() | View creation complete | Setup views, set listeners, find View references |
| onStart() | Fragment visible | Register receivers, start animations |
| onResume() | Fragment interactive | Start camera preview, location updates |
| onPause() | Leaving fragment | Stop animations, release camera, save unsaved data |
| onStop() | Fragment not visible | Unregister receivers, stop services, release resources |
| onDestroyView() | Clean up view references | Set view references to null (prevent memory leaks) |
| onDestroy() | Final cleanup | Clean up resources, cancel tasks, remove callbacks |
| onDetach() | Detach from Activity | Release Activity reference |

| Static Fragment | Declared in XML layout | Fixed UI components (header, footer) |

| DialogFragment | Displays as dialog | Alert dialogs, DatePicker, TimePicker |
| PreferenceFragment | Settings UI | App preferences, user settings |

💻 Fragment Implementation Example
```
class MyFragment : Fragment() {
    
    override fun onAttach(context: Context) {
        super.onAttach(context)
        Log.d("Fragment", "onAttach - Fragment attached to Activity")
    }
    
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        // Retain fragment instance across configuration changes
        retainInstance = true
        Log.d("Fragment", "onCreate - Fragment created")
    }
    
    override fun onCreateView(inflater: LayoutInflater, container: ViewGroup?, savedInstanceState: Bundle?): View? {
        Log.d("Fragment", "onCreateView - Inflating layout")
        return inflater.inflate(R.layout.fragment_my, container, false)
    }
    
    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onViewCreated(view, savedInstanceState)
        // Initialize views
        val button = view.findViewById<Button>(R.id.button)
        button.setOnClickListener { /* handle click */ }
        Log.d("Fragment", "onViewCreated - View created")
    }
    
    override fun onStart() {
        super.onStart()
        Log.d("Fragment", "onStart - Fragment visible")
    }
    
    override fun onResume() {
        super.onResume()
        Log.d("Fragment", "onResume - Fragment interactive")
    }
    
    override fun onPause() {
        super.onPause()
        Log.d("Fragment", "onPause - Leaving fragment")
    }
    
    override fun onStop() {
        super.onStop()
        Log.d("Fragment", "onStop - Fragment not visible")
    }
    
    override fun onDestroyView() {
        super.onDestroyView()
        // Clear view references to prevent memory leaks
        _binding = null
        Log.d("Fragment", "onDestroyView - Cleaning up views")
    }
    
    override fun onDestroy() {
        super.onDestroy()
        Log.d("Fragment", "onDestroy - Fragment destroyed")
    }
    
    override fun onDetach() {
        super.onDetach()
        Log.d("Fragment", "onDetach - Detached from Activity")
    }
}
                             
```

| Feature | Activity | Fragment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lifecycle Methods | 7 methods (onCreate to onDestroy) | 11 methods (onAttach to onDetach) |

| Reusability | Low (specific screens) | High (modular components) |
| Navigation | Intents for navigation | FragmentTransaction (add/replace/remove) |
| Back Stack | Task-based (system manages) | FragmentManager-based (developer manages) |

Fragments have 11 lifecycle methods (vs 7 for Activities)

1.1.8 Android Manifest File (AndroidManifest.xml)

It provides essential information about the app to the Android system, including package name, components (activities, services, receivers, providers), permissions, hardware features, and API level requirements. The manifest is a critical file for security analysis as it defines all exported components and requested permissions.

🚨 Common Manifest Security Mistakes
Exported components without permission checks – Allows any app to access component
debuggable="true" in release builds – Allows debugging and data extraction
usesCleartextTraffic="true" – Allows unencrypted HTTP traffic
allowBackup="true" for sensitive apps – Allows data extraction via ADB backup
Missing android:usesCleartextTraffic – Defaults to true for SDK < 23
Intent filters with broad data schemes – Can be hijacked by malicious apps
1.1.9 Application Permissions
Permissions are the primary mechanism for controlling access to sensitive data and device features in Android. Starting from Android 6.0 (Marshmallow), dangerous permissions are requested at runtime rather than install time. Permissions are categorized into protection levels: normal, dangerous, signature, and signatureOrSystem.
📊 Permission Protection Levels
| Level | Description | Example | Auto-granted |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Normal | Low risk, auto-granted | INTERNET, ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE | ✅ Yes |
| Dangerous | High risk, runtime request | CAMERA, LOCATION, MICROPHONE | ❌ No (user must approve) |
| Signature | Same certificate required | Custom app permissions | ✅ Yes (if signature matches) |
| SignatureOrSystem | System or same signature | System app permissions | ✅ Yes (system apps only) |
🚨 Most Abused Dangerous Permissions
READ_CONTACTS – Contact data theft, social engineering
ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION – Precise location tracking, stalking
ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION – Continuous background tracking
RECORD_AUDIO – Eavesdropping, ambient listening
CAMERA – Unauthorized photos/videos, spying
READ_SMS – SMS interception, 2FA code theft
READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE – File theft, photo access
SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW – Overlay attacks, tapjacking
BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE – Screen reading, keylogging
POST_NOTIFICATIONS – Notification spam (Android 13+)
🔄 Runtime Permission Flow (Android 6.0+)
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    RUNTIME PERMISSION REQUEST FLOW                          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                             │
│  1. App needs dangerous permission (e.g., CAMERA)                           │
│         │                                                                   │
│         ▼                                                                   │
│  2. Check if permission already granted                                     │
│     checkSelfPermission(Manifest.permission.CAMERA)                         │
│         │                                                                   │
│         ├─── GRANTED ──► Proceed with operation                             │
│         │                                                                   │
│         ▼                                                                   │
│  3. Permission NOT GRANTED                                                  │
│         │                                                                   │
│         ▼                                                                   │

1.1.10 Intent & Intent Filters
Intents are messaging objects that request an action from another app component. Intents facilitate communication between components (Activities, Services, Broadcast Receivers) within the same app or across different apps. Intent Filters declare what intents a component can respond to, defined in the AndroidManifest.xml.
📌 Explicit Intents
Specify exact component to launch (by package and class name).
```
// Launch specific activity
Intent intent = new Intent(this, TargetActivity.class);
startActivity(intent);

// Start specific service
Intent intent = new Intent(this, MyService.class);
startService(intent);

// Send explicit broadcast
Intent intent = new Intent("com.example.CUSTOM_ACTION");
intent.setComponent(new ComponentName("com.example.app", ".MyReceiver"));
sendBroadcast(intent);
                                             
```
🎯 Implicit Intents
Declare action to perform, system resolves to appropriate component.
```
// Open URL
Intent intent = new Intent(Intent.ACTION_VIEW);
intent.setData(Uri.parse("https://google.com"));
startActivity(intent);

// Share text
Intent intent = new Intent(Intent.ACTION_SEND);
intent.setType("text/plain");
intent.putExtra(Intent.EXTRA_TEXT, "Hello");
startActivity(Intent.createChooser(intent, "Share"));

// Open dialer
Intent intent = new Intent(Intent.ACTION_DIAL);
intent.setData(Uri.parse("tel:1234567890"));
startActivity(intent);
                                             
```
📡 Broadcast Intents
Send messages to multiple receivers simultaneously.
```
// Send normal broadcast
Intent intent = new Intent("com.example.CUSTOM_ACTION");
intent.putExtra("data", "test");
sendBroadcast(intent);

// Send ordered broadcast (receivers receive in priority order)
sendOrderedBroadcast(intent, null);

// Send sticky broadcast (deprecated, last value retained)
sendStickyBroadcast(intent);
                                             
```
📋 Intent Filter Declaration (AndroidManifest.xml)
```
<activity android:name=".ShareActivity" android:exported="true">
    <intent-filter>
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.SEND" />
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.DEFAULT" />
        <data android:mimeType="text/plain" />
    </intent-filter>
    
    <intent-filter>
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.VIEW" />
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.DEFAULT" />
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.BROWSABLE" />
        <data android:scheme="https" android:host="example.com" android:pathPattern="/.*" />
    </intent-filter>
    
    <intent-filter>
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.VIEW" />
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.DEFAULT" />
        <data android:scheme="content" />
    </intent-filter>
</activity>
                                 
```

| host | Host name | example.com, google.com |
| port | Port number | 8080, 443 |
| path | Exact path | /path/to/resource |

🎯 Common Intent Actions
| Action | Purpose | Example Data |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ACTION_VIEW | View content | Uri.parse("https://google.com") |
| ACTION_SEND | Share data | EXTRA_TEXT, EXTRA_STREAM |
| ACTION_DIAL | Open dialer | Uri.parse("tel:1234567890") |
| ACTION_CALL | Make call | Uri.parse("tel:1234567890") (needs permission) |

⚠ Intent Security Risks
Intent Hijacking: Malicious app intercepts implicit intents
Intent Spoofing: Forged intents to launch protected components
Data Leakage: Sensitive data in intent extras (logs, broadcasts)
Intent Injection: Malicious data passed via intents (SQL injection, XSS)
Activity Launch Attacks: Launching unauthorized activities
Broadcast Injection: Sending forged broadcasts to manipulate app state
Pending Intent Hijacking: Malicious app modifies pending intent
🔒 Intent Security Best Practices
Use explicit intents for internal app components
Set android:exported="false" for components not needed by other apps
Validate incoming intent data before processing
Use permissions on intent receivers (sendBroadcast(intent, permission))
Use LocalBroadcastManager for internal app broadcasts
Avoid putting sensitive data in intent extras
Use PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE for pending intents (Android 12+)
Validate caller UID/PID for sensitive components (Binder.getCallingUid())

⚠ Content Provider Security Risks
🚨 Common Vulnerabilities:
SQL Injection: Malicious projection/selection parameters
Data Leakage: Over-permissive read/write permissions
Path Traversal: Accessing unauthorized files via file:// URIs
Content Provider Injection: Malicious apps providing fake data
Permission Bypass: Accessing provider without proper permissions
Cursor Window Exploitation: Exhausting memory via large cursors
🔐 Content Provider Permission Types
| Permission Type | Purpose | Security Level |
| --- | --- | --- |
| readPermission | Required to read provider data | Protects sensitive data |
| writePermission | Required to modify provider data | Prevents unauthorized modifications |
| grantUriPermissions | Temporary URI permissions | Fine-grained temporary access |
| android:exported | Whether provider is accessible | Should be false for internal providers |

✓ Set android:exported="false" for internal providers
✓ Use readPermission and writePermission for sensitive data
✓ Validate all input parameters to prevent SQL injection
✓ Use parameterized queries instead of raw string concatenation
✓ Avoid using file:// URIs for file sharing (use FileProvider)
✓ Implement grantUriPermissions for temporary access instead of permanent

📢 Notification Channels (Android 8.0+)
📌 Importance Levels:
IMPORTANCE_HIGH – Makes sound, appears as heads-up
IMPORTANCE_DEFAULT – Makes sound, no heads-up
IMPORTANCE_LOW – No sound, appears in shade
IMPORTANCE_MIN – No sound, no visual interruption
IMPORTANCE_NONE – Completely blocked
✅ Channel Types (Examples):
Messages – High importance, sound, popup
Social Interactions – Default importance
Promotions – Low importance, no sound
Download Progress – Low importance, show progress
Ongoing – Min importance, cannot be dismissed
Alarms – High importance, bypass DND
📱 Notification Styles
| Style | Description | Best For |
| --- | --- | --- |
| BigTextStyle | Large text content | Messages, emails, articles |
| BigPictureStyle | Large image preview | Photos, screenshots, memes |

| MessagingStyle | Conversation thread | Chat apps, SMS |
| MediaStyle | Media controls | Music, video players |
| ProgressStyle | Progress indicator | Downloads, uploads |
⚠ Notification Security Risks
🚨 Common Notification Vulnerabilities:
Notification Spam: Flooding user with notifications (DoS)
Data Leakage: Sensitive data displayed on lock screen
Notification Hijacking: Malicious app intercepts notifications
Clickjacking: Fake notification buttons tricking user
Persistent Notifications: Prevents app from being killed (battery drain)
Accessibility Abuse: Notification listeners spy on user activity

1.2.11 Broadcast Receiver
Broadcast Receivers listen for system-wide broadcast announcements (battery low, boot completed, SMS received) and custom app broadcasts. They can be registered statically (manifest) or dynamically (code). Broadcasts are a key mechanism for inter-app and inter-component communication.
📡 Normal Broadcasts
Asynchronous, unordered, all receivers receive simultaneously
```
sendBroadcast(intent)
```
📡 Ordered Broadcasts
Synchronous, one receiver at a time, can propagate results
```
sendOrderedBroadcast(intent, permission)
```
📡 Sticky Broadcasts
Deprecated, last value retained for future receivers
```
sendStickyBroadcast(intent)
```
📋 Common System Broadcast Actions

| --- | --- | --- |
| BOOT_COMPLETED擦了Device finished booting擦了RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED |  |  |
| BATTERY_LOW擦了Battery level low擦了None (system broadcast) |  |  |
| BATTERY_OKAY擦了Battery level okay | None (system broadcast) |  |
| SCREEN_ON / SCREEN_OFF擦了Screen state changed擦了None (system broadcast) |  |  |
| CONNECTIVITY_CHANGE擦了Network connection changed擦了ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE |  |  |

Broadcast Injection: Malicious app sending forged broadcasts

📌 What are Native Libraries? (Simple Explanation)
✓ Pre-compiled C/C++ code (.so files - Shared Objects)
✓ Accessed via JNI (Java Native Interface) - like a translator
✓ High-performance - faster than Java for certain tasks
✓ Located in /system/lib/ (32-bit) or /system/lib64/ (64-bit)
✓ Reusable - same library can be used by multiple apps
⚠ Why Native Libraries Matter for Security:
✓ Buffer Overflows - C/C++ doesn't have memory safety
✓ Use-After-Free - Accessing freed memory
✓ JNI Boundary Bypass - Can bypass Java security checks
✓ Hardcoded Secrets - API keys embedded in .so files
✓ Library Hijacking - Malicious libraries loaded instead
📋 Complete Native Libraries Reference
| Library | Purpose | Simple Explanation | Security Relevance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| libc (Bionic) | Standard C library | Basic functions like memory, strings, math | Buffer overflows, format string bugs |
| libc++ | C++ Standard Library | C++ containers, algorithms, iterators | Memory corruption in complex C++ code |
| libsqlite.so | SQLite database engine | Local database storage for apps | SQL injection, database exposure on rooted devices |
| libssl.so / libcrypto.so | BoringSSL (cryptography) | HTTPS, encryption, certificates | Vulnerabilities can break all secure communication |
| libmedia.so | Media framework | Audio/video playback and recording | Stagefright vulnerabilities, media file parsing |
| libEGL.so / libGLESv2.so | OpenGL ES graphics | 2D/3D graphics for games and UI | Graphics driver exploits, GPU memory access |
| libskia.so | Skia graphics engine | Drawing text, images, shapes on screen | Image parsing vulnerabilities |

1.3.7 SSL & Security Libraries (BoringSSL)
BoringSSL is Google's fork of OpenSSL, used for all cryptographic operations in Android. It handles secure communication (HTTPS), certificate verification, encryption, and digital signatures. Every time you visit a secure website (https://) or make a secure API call, BoringSSL is working behind the scenes.

🔒 Certificate Pinning (Advanced Security)
Certificate pinning prevents man-in-the-middle attacks by hardcoding expected certificates:
```
// OkHttp Certificate Pinning
OkHttpClient client = new OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .certificatePinner(
        new CertificatePinner.Builder()
            .add("example.com", "sha256/AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA=")
            .build())
    .build();
```
⚠ Warning: If the certificate changes, your app will break. Update with app updates!

1.3.8 Android Runtime (ART)
Android Runtime (ART) is the managed runtime environment that executes app code on Android devices. It converts DEX bytecode (from your Kotlin/Java code) into native machine code that the device's processor can understand. ART replaced Dalvik in Android 5.0 and has become faster and more efficient with each release.

1.3.9 Dalvik Virtual Machine (Legacy)
Dalvik was the original virtual machine for Android (Android 1.0 to 4.4 KitKat). It used JIT (Just-In-Time) compilation, meaning it translated DEX bytecode to machine code on the fly as the app ran. While innovative for its time, Dalvik was slower and consumed more battery than modern ART. Understanding Dalvik helps appreciate why ART is better.

📋 Dalvik Characteristics
JIT Compilation: Code compiled during execution
DEX Format: Dalvik Executable (optimized for mobile)
Register-based VM: More efficient than stack-based
Low Memory: Designed for 64-128MB RAM devices
Multi-process: Each app runs in its own Dalvik instance
📋 Why Google Replaced Dalvik
❌ Slow app startup (JIT warm-up time)
❌ Higher battery consumption (CPU constantly compiling)
❌ Poor performance on modern devices
❌ Limited optimization opportunities
❌ Couldn't leverage multi-core CPUs effectively
✅ ART delivers 2-3x better performance
📜 Historical Significance:
Dalvik was groundbreaking when introduced in 2007. Most smartphones had single-core 528MHz CPUs with 128MB RAM. Dalvik's register-based architecture and JIT compilation made Android run smoothly on these limited devices. As phones became more powerful (quad-core, 4GB+ RAM), Dalvik's limitations became apparent, leading to ART.

1.3.11 JNI (Java Native Interface) – Bridging Worlds
JNI (Java Native Interface) is a programming framework that allows Java/Kotlin code running in the Android Runtime (ART) to call and be called by native applications and libraries written in C/C++. It's the bridge that connects the Java world with the native world, enabling high-performance operations and hardware access.
🔗 How JNI Works (Simple Explanation)
```

│   │                                                                             │   │
│   │   public class MainActivity {                                               │   │
│   │       // Load native library                                                │   │
│   │       static {                                                              │   │
│   │           System.loadLibrary("native-lib");                                 │   │
│   │       }                                                                     │   │
│   │                                                                             │   │
│   │       // Declare native method (no body - implemented in C)                 │   │
│   │       public native String stringFromJNI();                                 │   │
│   │                                                                             │   │
│   │       public void onClick() {                                               │   │
│   │           // Call native method                                             │   │
│   │           String result = stringFromJNI();                                  │   │
│   │           textView.setText(result);                                         │   │
│   │       }                                                                     │   │
│   │   }                                                                         │   │
│   │                                                                             │   │

│   │                                                                             │   │
│   │   • Converts Java types to C types (String ↔ char*)                         │   │
│   │   • Manages references (global/local)                                       │   │
│   │   • Handles exception propagation                                           │   │
│   │   • Provides access to JVM internals
