📋 Why Use JNI?
⚡ Performance: C/C++ code runs 10-100x faster than Java for number crunching
🔧 Hardware Access: Direct access to hardware (camera, sensors, GPU)
📦 Legacy Code: Reuse existing C/C++ libraries
🔐 Security: Native code is harder to reverse engineer
🎮 Gaming: Game engines (Unity, Unreal) use C++ for performance
⚠ JNI Security Risks (Critical!)
Buffer Overflows: No bounds checking in C/C++
Use-After-Free: Accessing freed memory
JNI Type Confusion: Incorrect casting across boundary
Memory Leaks: Forgetting to delete global references
Exception Bypass: Unchecked exceptions crash app
📊 JNI Data Type Mapping (Java ↔ C/C++)
| Java Type | JNI Type | C/C++ Type | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| int | jint | int32_t | int number = 42; |

| String | jstring | const char* | char* str = env->GetStringUTFChars(jstr); |
| Object[] | jobjectArray | jobjectArray | env->GetObjectArrayElement(array, 0); |
| byte[] | jbyteArray | jbyte* | jbyte* data = env->GetByteArrayElements(bytes); |

```
// 1. Calling Java method from C++
JNIEXPORT void JNICALL Java_com_example_Native_callJavaMethod(JNIEnv* env, jobject thiz) {
    jclass cls = (*env)->GetObjectClass(env, thiz);
    jmethodID mid = (*env)->GetMethodID(env, cls, "onNativeCallback", "(Ljava/lang/String;)V");
    jstring result = (*env)->NewStringUTF(env, "Callback result");
    (*env)->CallVoidMethod(env, thiz, mid, result);
}

// 2. Accessing Java field from C++
JNIEXPORT void JNICALL Java_com_example_Native_accessField(JNIEnv* env, jobject thiz) {
    jclass cls = (*env)->GetObjectClass(env, thiz);
    jfieldID fid = (*env)->GetFieldID(env, cls, "counter", "I");
    jint counter = (*env)->GetIntField(env, thiz, fid);
    counter++;
    (*env)->SetIntField(env, thiz, fid, counter);
}

// 3. Creating Java object from C++
JNIEXPORT jobject JNICALL Java_com_example_Native_createObject(JNIEnv* env, jobject thiz) {
    jclass cls = (*env)->FindClass(env, "com/example/Person");
    jmethodID cid = (*env)->GetMethodID(env, cls, "<init>", "(Ljava/lang/String;I)V");
    jstring name = (*env)->NewStringUTF(env, "John");
    jobject person = (*env)->NewObject(env, cls, cid, name, 25);
    return person;
}

// 4. Error handling in JNI
JNIEXPORT void JNICALL Java_com_example_Native_riskyOperation(JNIEnv* env, jobject thiz) {
    // Check for exceptions after JNI calls
    if ((*env)->ExceptionCheck(env)) {
        (*env)->ExceptionDescribe(env);
        (*env)->ExceptionClear(env);
        return;
    }
}

1.3.12 Garbage Collection in ART
Garbage Collection (GC) is automatic memory management in ART. It identifies and frees memory that is no longer used by the application, preventing memory leaks and out-of-memory errors. Think of it as an automatic housekeeper that cleans up unused objects so you don't have to.

🚨 Common Memory Leak Patterns
```
// 1. Static reference to Activity (BIG LEAK!)
public class LeakyClass {
    public static Activity sActivity = mainActivity;  // NEVER DO THIS!
}

// 2. Inner class holding reference to outer class
public class MainActivity extends Activity {
    private static Runnable sRunnable = new Runnable() {  // Leak!
        @Override public void run() { /* holds reference to Activity */ }
    };
}

// 3. Anonymous class in AsyncTask
new AsyncTask<Void, Void, Void>() {
    @Override protected Void doInBackground(Void... params) {
        // This holds reference to Activity until task completes
        return null;
    }
}.execute();

// FIX: Use WeakReference
public class SafeActivity extends Activity {
    private static class SafeRunnable implements Runnable {
        private WeakReference<SafeActivity> activityRef;
        SafeRunnable(SafeActivity activity) {
            activityRef = new WeakReference<>(activity);
        }
        @Override public void run() {
            SafeActivity activity = activityRef.get();
            if (activity != null) {
                // Access activity safely
            }
        }
    }
}
```

🖼 Bitmap Optimization Example
```
// BAD: Loading full 4000x3000 image (48MB!)
BitmapFactory.decodeFile("/sdcard/photo.jpg");

// GOOD: Load scaled version based on screen size
public static Bitmap decodeSampledBitmapFromFile(String path, int reqWidth, int reqHeight) {
    final BitmapFactory.Options options = new BitmapFactory.Options();
    options.inJustDecodeBounds = true;  // Just read dimensions
    BitmapFactory.decodeFile(path, options);
    
    // Calculate sample size
    options.inSampleSize = calculateInSampleSize(options, reqWidth, reqHeight);
    
    // Load actual bitmap
    options.inJustDecodeBounds = false;
    return BitmapFactory.decodeFile(path, options);
}

private static int calculateInSampleSize(BitmapFactory.Options options, int reqWidth, int reqHeight) {
    final int height = options.outHeight;
    final int width = options.outWidth;
    int inSampleSize = 1;
    
    if (height > reqHeight || width > reqWidth) {
        final int halfHeight = height / 2;
        final int halfWidth = width / 2;
        while ((halfHeight / inSampleSize) >= reqHeight 
                && (halfWidth / inSampleSize) >= reqWidth) {
            inSampleSize *= 2;
        }
    }
    return inSampleSize;
}
```

🛠 Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL)
1.4.1 Introduction to HAL
The Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL) is a critical component in Android architecture that defines standard interfaces for hardware vendors to implement. It acts as a boundary between the Android framework and the underlying hardware drivers, allowing the operating system to work across diverse devices without modification. Think of HAL as a "universal translator" that lets Android communicate with any camera, sensor, or audio chip, regardless of the manufacturer.
📌 What is HAL? (Simple Explanation)
Imagine you have a universal remote control that works with any TV brand - Sony, Samsung, LG, etc. The remote doesn't need to know the specific details of each TV; it just uses standard buttons (Power, Volume, Channel). That's exactly what HAL does for Android!
Without HAL: Android would need custom code for EVERY device (millions of combinations!)
With HAL: Android uses standard interfaces, vendors implement the hardware-specific details
Result: Your phone works whether it has Qualcomm, MediaTek, or Samsung chip!
🎯 HAL Core Functions
Hardware Abstraction: Hides vendor-specific implementation details
Standardized APIs: Provides consistent interfaces for all hardware types
Process Isolation: Each HAL runs in its own process (Android 8.0+)
Updateable: HALs can be updated via Mainline (Android 10+)
Cross-Vendor Compatibility: Same Android version works on any device
⚠ HAL Security Importance
Attack Surface: HAL vulnerabilities are common (30%+ of security patches)
Privilege Escalation: Compromised HAL can lead to kernel access
Privacy Risks: Camera/Audio HAL bugs can leak sensitive data
Isolation Benefits: Binderized HALs contain exploits to single process
SELinux Protection: Each HAL has its own security context
📜 Evolution of HAL in Android
| Android Version | HAL Type | Key Change | Security Impact |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Android 1.0 - 7.1 | Passthrough HAL | HAL loaded directly into framework process | ❌ HAL crash = framework crash |
| Android 8.0 - 9.0 | Binderized HAL (Treble) | Each HAL runs in isolated process via hwbinder | ✅ HAL vulnerability contained to its process |
| Android 10 - 12 | SP-HAL + AIDL Migration | Performance HALs in framework, AIDL replaces HIDL | ✅ Balanced performance & security |
| Android 13+ | Stable AIDL HALs | Stable interfaces, Mainline updateable | ✅ Faster security patches via Play Store |

🔧 HAL Interface Languages: HIDL vs AIDL
HIDL (Android 8.0-10)
Purpose: Designed specifically for binderized HALs
Communication: Uses hwbinder (separate from normal binder)
Backward Compatible: Works with older HALs
Performance: Good, but more overhead than AIDL
```
// HIDL interface example
package android.hardware.camera@2.0;

interface ICameraDevice {
    getResourceCost() generates (CameraResourceCost cost);
    open(ICameraDeviceCallback callback) 
        generates (CameraDeviceStatus status);
};
```
AIDL (Android 10+ HALs)
Purpose: Unified IPC for framework and HAL
Communication: Uses binder (same as framework services)
Performance: Better than HIDL (lower overhead)
Updateable: Can be updated via Mainline modules
```
// AIDL HAL interface (Android 10+)
package android.hardware.camera;

interface ICameraDevice {
    CameraResourceCost getResourceCost();
    CameraDeviceStatus open(
        ICameraDeviceCallback callback);
};
```
🔄 Passthrough HAL vs Binderized HAL
| Feature | Passthrough HAL (Legacy) | Binderized HAL (Modern) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Process Location | Loaded into framework process | Runs in separate isolated process |
| Communication | Direct function calls (very fast) | IPC via hwbinder/AIDL (slightly slower) |
| Security | ❌ Low - HAL crash kills framework | ✅ High - HAL crash isolated |
| Memory Access | Shared memory with framework | Separate memory space |
| Update Mechanism | Requires full OTA | Can be updated via Mainline |
| Android Version | Android 7.1 and below | Android 8.0 and above |
✅ Key Takeaways - Introduction to HAL
✓ HAL is the universal translator between Android framework and hardware
✓ Modern Android (8.0+) uses binderized HALs for better security isolation
✓ Project Treble separated HALs from framework, enabling faster updates
✓ HALs are moving from HIDL to AIDL for better performance and updateability
✓ VTS (Vendor Test Suite) ensures HAL compatibility across devices
✓ SELinux provides per-HAL domains (e.g., hal_camera_default) for fine-grained security

⚡ Low-Latency Audio (For Music Apps)
What is Low-Latency Audio?
Low-latency audio reduces the delay between when an audio sample is generated and when it's heard. This is crucial for:
🎸 Music creation apps (guitar tuners, synthesizers)
🎮 Gaming (real-time sound effects)
🎤 Karaoke apps (real-time voice monitoring)
📞 VoIP calls (echo cancellation)
Latency Targets: Standard Android: ~50ms, Professional audio: ~10-20ms, Hardware support needed!
✅ Audio HAL Best Practices for Developers
✓ Use OpenSL ES or AAudio for low-latency audio
✓ Request RECORD_AUDIO permission for microphone access
✓ Handle audio focus properly (duck or pause when other apps play)
✓ Use MediaPlayer for simple playback, AudioTrack for streaming
✓ Test on multiple devices - audio latency varies dramatically
✓ Always release audio resources in onPause()/onStop()
✓ Use AudioAttributes.Builder to specify use case (music, voice, alarm)

🔋 Sensor Batching (Power Efficiency)
What is Sensor Batching?
Instead of waking the CPU for every sensor event, sensor batching stores events in hardware FIFO and delivers them in batches.
Without Batching: 100 events = 100 wake-ups (high battery drain)
With Batching: 100 events = 1 wake-up (1% of battery usage!)
Use Cases: Step counting, fitness tracking, location monitoring
✅ Sensor HAL Best Practices
✓ Request minimum sensor delay appropriate for your use case (don't abuse!)
✓ Use SensorEvent timestamp instead of System.currentTimeMillis()
✓ Unregister sensors in onPause()/onStop() to save battery
✓ Use Batch Sensor for power-efficient background monitoring
✓ Check sensor wake-up vs non-wake-up capability
✓ Handle sensor availability gracefully (not all devices have all sensors)
✓ Use SensorManager.getDynamicSensorList() for pluggable sensors (Android 9+)
✓ Test on multiple devices - sensor quality varies dramatically!

🚨 Example: Driver Buffer Overflow Vulnerability
```
// VULNERABLE DRIVER CODE (simplified)
static long camera_ioctl(struct file *file, unsigned int cmd, unsigned long arg) {
    char user_buffer[256];
    char kernel_buffer[256];
    
    // Copy data from userspace (attacker controls size!)
    if (copy_from_user(user_buffer, (void __user *)arg, 1024)) {
        return -EFAULT;
    }
    
    // VULNERABILITY: No bounds check before copying!
    strcpy(kernel_buffer, user_buffer);  // BOOM! Buffer overflow
    
    // Attacker can overwrite kernel memory → privilege escalation!
    return 0;
}

// SAFE CODE - With bounds checking
static long camera_ioctl_safe(...) {
    char user_buffer[256];
    char kernel_buffer[256];
    
    // Proper bounds check
    if (copy_from_user(user_buffer, (void __user *)arg, sizeof(user_buffer))) {
        return -EFAULT;
    }
    
    // Use safe strncpy with size limit
    strncpy(kernel_buffer, user_buffer, sizeof(kernel_buffer) - 1);
    kernel_buffer[sizeof(kernel_buffer) - 1] = '\0';
    
    return 0;
}
```

1.5.1 Linux Kernel Overview
The Linux kernel is the foundation of the Android operating system. It is responsible for all core system functions: process management, memory management, power management, network stack, device drivers, and security. Android uses a modified version of the Linux kernel with additional features like Binder IPC, Low Memory Killer (LMK), and wakelocks.

📌 What is the Linux Kernel? (Simple Explanation)
Think of the kernel as the "conductor" of an orchestra:
Without conductor: Instruments play randomly (chaos)
With conductor: Instruments play together in harmony (smooth operation)
The kernel: Manages CPU (which app runs), Memory (where data is stored), Devices (camera, WiFi), and Security (who can access what)
⚠ Why Kernel Security Matters
Kernel has complete access to everything on device
Kernel vulnerability = full device compromise
Android security patches 70% are kernel-related
Root exploits target kernel vulnerabilities
Kernel runs in most privileged mode (Ring 0)

1.5.2 Process Management
Process management is responsible for creating, scheduling, and terminating processes. The kernel's process scheduler allocates CPU time to processes, ensuring fair distribution and real-time responsiveness. Android uses the Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) with modifications for mobile workloads and the Low Memory Killer (LMK) for process termination.

🧬 Zygote - The Mother of All Android Apps
What is Zygote?
Zygote is a special system process started during Android boot. It preloads core libraries and framework classes, then forks new app processes when needed. This dramatically speeds up app launch time.
Preloaded classes: 2000+ common framework classes
Preloaded resources: Drawables, themes, strings
Copy-on-Write (COW): Apps share read-only memory pages
Result: App launch time reduced by 70%!
```
# Check Zygote process

# Output: root      12345  1      ... zygote64 (main Zygote)
#         root      12346  12345  ... zygote (secondary for 32-bit)

# View Zygote preloaded classes

# Watch Zygote forking in real-time

Android implements several memory management features including virtual memory, paging, Low Memory Killer (LMK), ashmem (Anonymous Shared Memory), and ION allocator to optimize performance on resource-constrained mobile devices.

🚨 Common Memory Vulnerabilities
Buffer Overflow: Writing beyond buffer bounds
Use-After-Free: Accessing freed memory
Double Free: Freeing memory twice
Memory Leak: Not freeing allocated memory
Out-of-Bounds Read: Reading outside buffer
Integer Overflow: Overflow in size calculation
⚡ Low Memory Killer (LMK) - Deep Dive
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    LOW MEMORY KILLER (LMK) WORKFLOW                                 │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                                     │
│  1. Memory pressure detected (free memory < threshold)                           │
│         │                                                                           │
│         ▼                                                                           │
│  2. LMK calculates oom_score_adj for each process                                   │
│     based on:                                                                       │
│     • Process type (foreground, visible, service, cached)                           │
│     • Memory usage (RSS, PSS)                                                       │
│     • Process age (older processes might be kept)                                   │
│         │                                                                           │
│         ▼                                                                           │
│  3. LMK selects process with highest oom_score_adj                                  │
│     (lowest priority)                                                               │
│         │                                                                           │
│         ▼                                                                           │
│  4. LMK sends SIGKILL to selected process                                           │
│         │                                                                           │
│         ▼                                                                           │
│  5. Process terminated, memory freed                                                │
│         │                                                                           │
│         ▼                                                                           │
│  6. Memory pressure relieved - device stays responsive!                             │
│                                                                                     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

1.5.6 Binder IPC Driver
Binder is Android's primary Inter-Process Communication (IPC) mechanism. It allows one process to call methods in another process as if they were local (Remote Procedure Call). The Binder driver in the kernel manages communication channels, passing caller UID/PID with each transaction for security.
🔄 Binder IPC Architecture
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         BINDER IPC ARCHITECTURE                                     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                                     │
│   CLIENT PROCESS                         SERVER PROCESS                             │
│   ┌─────────────────────────┐            ┌─────────────────────────┐                │
│   │  Java/Kotlin App        │            │  System Server           │               │
│   │                         │            │  (Activity Manager,      │               │
│   │  • Calls method on      │            │   Window Manager, etc.)  │               │
│   │    proxy object         │            │                         │                │
│   │  • Data marshalled      │            │  • Receives transaction  │               │
│   │    into Parcel          │            │  • Unmarshalls Parcel    │               │
│   │                         │            │  • Executes method       │               │
│   └───────────┬─────────────┘            └───────────┬─────────────┘                │
│               │                                      │                              │
│               │ Binder Proxy (Client)                │ Binder Stub (Server)         │
│               │ (Transact)                           │ (onTransact)                 │
│               │                                      │                              │
│               └──────────────────┬───────────────────┘                              │
│                                  │                                                  │
│                                  │ Binder Driver (Kernel)                           │
│                                  │ /dev/binder                                      │
│                                  │                                                  │
│                                  │ • Manages transactions                           │
│                                  │ • Passes caller UID/PID                          │
│                                  │ • Enforces permissions                           │
│                                  │ • Manages shared memory (Parcel)                 │
│                                  │                                                  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Binder Transaction Flow:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    BINDER TRANSACTION FLOW                                          │
├───────────
```
```
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                                     │
│   1. Client creates Parcel with marshalled data                                     │
│          │                                                                          │
│          ▼                                                                          │
│   2. Client calls transact() on Binder proxy                                        │
│          │                                                                          │
│          ▼                                                                          │
│   3. Binder driver receives BC_TRANSACTION command                                  │
│      • Records caller UID/PID                                                       │
│      • Copies data to kernel buffer                                                 │
│      • Creates transaction record                                                   │
│          │                                                                          │
│          ▼                                                                          │
│   4. Binder driver sends BR_TRANSACTION to server                                   │
│          │                                                                          │
│          ▼                                                                          │
│   5. Server's onTransact() called                                                   │
│      • Unmarshalls Parcel                                                           │
│      • Executes actual method                                                       │
│      • Creates reply Parcel                                                         │
│          │                                                                          │
│          ▼                                                                          │
│   6. Binder driver sends reply to client                                            │
│          │                                                                          │
│          ▼                                                                          │
│   7. Client receives reply and continues execution                                  │
│                                                                                     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
📋 Binder Features
High Performance: One copy data transfer (shared memory)
Security: Kernel passes caller UID/PID with each transaction
Reference Counting: Automatic object lifecycle management
Synchronous/Asynchronous: Both call types supported
Death Recipients: Detect when remote process dies
Thread Pool: Server can handle multiple clients concurrently
🚨 Binder Security Risks
🔓 Permission Bypass: Malicious client calling protected services
💥 Transaction Flooding: DoS via excessive binder transactions
📊 Data Leakage: Sensitive data in Parcel
🔐 UID/PID Spoofing: Impersonating another process
💾 Memory Exhaustion: Large transactions consuming kernel memory

1.5.7 Security & SELinux
SELinux (Security-Enhanced Linux) provides Mandatory Access Control (MAC) beyond traditional Unix DAC (Discretionary Access Control). It enforces security policies that define exactly what each process can access, even if it's running as root. Android has run SELinux in enforcing mode since Android 5.0, making it much harder for exploits to compromise the system.
🔒 DAC vs MAC - What's the Difference?
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         DAC vs MAC COMPARISON                                       │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                                     │
│   DAC (Discretionary Access Control) - Traditional Unix/Linux                       │
│   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│   │                                                                             │   │
│   │   "I'm root, so I can access ANYTHING!"                                     │   │
│   │                                                                             │   │
│   │   • Access based solely on user ID (UID)                                    │   │
│   │   • If you're root, you have ALL permissions                                │   │
│   │   • One compromised process = entire system compromised                     │   │
│   │   • Example: App with root can read /data/data/any-app/database             │   │
│   │                                                                             │   │
│   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                                     │
│   MAC (Mandatory Access Control) - SELinux                                          │
│   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│   │                                                                             │   │
│   │   "I'm root, but I can ONLY access what policy allows!"                     │   │
│   │                                                                             │   │
│   │   • Access based on security context (domain)                               │   │
│   │   • Root is not all-powerful - policies restrict even root                  │   │
│   │   • Each process has least privilege                                        │   │
│   │   • Example: Camera HAL domain (hal_camera_default) can ONLY access camera  │   │
│   │                                                                             │   │
│   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                                     │
│   REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE:                                                               │
│   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│   │  Without SELinux:   
```
```
                                                        │   │
│   │  ┌──────────────┐                                                           │   │
│   │  │  Camera App  │ ──► (root exploit) ──► 📁 Read all files!                 │   │
│   │  └──────────────┘                                                           │   │
│   │                                                                             │   │
│   │  With SELinux (Enforcing):                                                  │   │
│   │  ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────────┐                                  │   │
│   │  │  Camera App  │ ──► │ Camera HAL domain│ ──► Permission denied!           │   │
│   │  └──────────────┘     │ (hal_camera)     │      (Can't access files)        │   │
│   │                       └──────────────────┘                                  │   │
│   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                                     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

📋 SELinux Security Contexts
| Context Component | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| User | SELinux user (not Linux user) | u (unconfined user) |
| Role | Process role | r (object_r for files, r for processes) |
| Type/Domain | Most important - defines permissions | system_app, untrusted_app, hal_camera_default |
| MLS Level擦了Multi-Level Security (sensitivity) | s0 (single level), s0-s15:c0.c1023 |  |
🔑 Common Android SELinux Domains
| Domain | Processes | Privileges |
| --- | --- | --- |
| init擦了init process擦了Full system initialization |  |  |
| system_app擦了System apps擦了High privileges, system UID |  |  |
| untrusted_app擦了Third-party apps擦了Limited, sandboxed |  |  |
|  | platform_app擦了Platform-signed apps擦了Medium-high privileges |  |
| hal_camera_default擦了Camera HAL擦了Camera hardware only |  |  |
| hal_audio_default擦了Audio HAL擦了Audio hardware only |  |  |
📊 SELinux Modes
| Mode | Description | Security Level | When Used |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Enforcing | Policies are enforced, violations denied | ✅ Highest | Production devices (default since Android 5.0) |
| Permissive | Policies are logged but NOT enforced | ⚠ Medium (debugging only) | Engineering builds, debugging |
| Disabled | SELinux completely off | ❌ None (very dangerous!) | Only custom kernels, never in production |
📝 SELinux Policy Example
```
# Example SELinux policy (from system_app.te)
# Allow system_app to read/write shared preferences
allow system_app app_data_file:file { read write open };

# Allow system_app to use Binder IPC
binder_call(system_app, system_server);

# Allow system_app to access network
allow system_app self:tcp_socket create_stream_socket;
allow system_app self:udp_socket create_socket;

# Allow system_app to send notifications
allow system_app notification_service:service_manager find;

# Neverallow rules (what's forbidden!)
neverallow { domain -untrusted_app } proc_security:file write;
neverallow { domain -appdomain } self:capability sys_admin;
```
```
# Check SELinux status
adb shell getenforce
# Output: Enforcing

# Get SELinux mode (Enforcing/Permissive)
adb shell getprop ro.boot.selinux

# View process security contexts
adb shell ps -Z

# View file security contexts
adb shell ls -Z /system/bin/

# Check SELinux denials (AVC logs)
adb shell logcat | grep "avc:"

# View all SELinux denials
adb shell dmesg | grep -i "avc"

# Temporarily set to permissive (requires root)
adb shell setenforce 0

# Back to enforcing
adb shell setenforce 1

# Check policy for specific domain
adb shell sesearch -A -s hal_camera_default /sys/fs/selinux/policy

# List all domains
adb shell seinfo -u

# Check if process has certain permission
adb shell dmesg | grep "avc: denied" | grep "com.example.app"
```
✅ SELinux Security Best Practices
✓ Keep SELinux in Enforcing mode on production devices
✓ Never disable SELinux - it's your last line of defense!
✓ Use least privilege - give processes only needed permissions
✓ Monitor AVC denials to find over-permissive policies
✓ Write neverallow rules to prevent dangerous operations
✓ Use type transitions for file creation in specific contexts
✓ Test with permissive mode first , then enforce
✓ Keep sepolicy up to date with Android security updates

🔐 dm-verity (Verified Boot)
What is dm-verity?
dm-verity (Device Mapper Verity) provides block-level integrity verification for system partitions. It creates a hash tree of the entire partition and verifies every block when read. If any block is modified (even by root), verification fails.
Purpose: Prevents persistent rootkits and system modification
Implementation: kernel module (dm-verity)
Android feature: Verified Boot since Android 4.4
Result: Device won't boot if system partition is tampered

Kernel modules (loadable kernel modules - LKMs) are pieces of code that can be loaded and unloaded into the kernel at runtime. They extend kernel functionality without rebooting. Android uses modules for hardware drivers, file systems, and security features. However, modules are also a common attack vector for rootkits.

Rootkits: Malicious modules hide processes, files, network connections
Privilege Escalation: Vulnerable modules give root access
Persistence: Modules survive reboots if loaded from init scripts
Kernel Hooking: Modules can intercept syscalls, modify kernel behavior
Module Loading Abuse: Insmod/rmmod without proper verification

adb shell getprop ro.hardware.keystore

# List security features
adb shell dumpsys security
```
✅ Security Best Practices Summary
✓ Keep SELinux enforcing - never disable it!
✓ Install security updates as soon as available
✓ Only install apps from Google Play Store
✓ Review app permissions before installing
✓ Enable Find My Device for remote wipe/lock
✓ Use strong lock screen (PIN/password, not pattern)
✓ Encrypt the device (already default on modern Android)
✓ Keep bootloader locked for production devices
✓ Use biometric authentication with fallback to PIN
✓ Be aware of phishing attacks (fake login screens)
1.5.13 Interrupt Handling
Interrupts are signals sent by hardware devices to the CPU to indicate that an event needs immediate attention. The kernel handles interrupts by pausing current work, saving context, executing interrupt handler (ISR), then resuming original work. Without interrupts, the CPU would have to constantly poll devices (wasting power).
⚡ Interrupt Handling Flow
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         INTERRUPT HANDLING FLOW                                     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                                     │
│   HARDWARE (Touch Screen)                                                           │
│   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│   │  User touches screen → Touch controller triggers interrupt                  │   │
│   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                      │                                              │
│                                      │ IRQ (Interrupt Request)                      │
│                                      ▼                                              │
│   CPU (Executing normal code)                                                       │
│   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│   │  • Completes current instruction                                            │   │
│   │  • Saves context (registers, PC)                                            │   │
│   │  • Disables interrupts (briefly)                                            │   │
│   │  • Jumps to interrupt vector table entry                                    │   │
│   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                      │                                              │
│                                      ▼                                              │
│   TOP HALF (Hardware ISR - Fast, minimal)                                           │
│   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│   │  • Acknowledges interrupt to device                                         │   │
│   │  • Saves minimal state                                                      │   │
│   │  • Schedules bottom half (tasklet/workqueue)                                │   │
│   │  • Restores interrupts                                                      │   │
│   │  • Returns from interrupt                                                   │   │
│   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                      │                      
```
```
                        │
│                                      ▼                                              │
│   CPU Resumes Normal Code                                                           │
│   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│   │  • Continues previously running process                                     │   │
│   │  • Interrupts are re-enabled                                                │   │
│   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                      │                                              │
│                                      │ (Scheduled)                                  │
│                                      ▼                                              │
│   BOTTOM HALF (SoftIRQ/Tasklet - Deferred processing)                               │
│   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│   │  • Reads touch data from device                                             │   │
│   │  • Processes touch coordinates                                              │   │
│   │  • Informs input subsystem                                                  │   │
│   │  • Wakes waiting processes                                                  │   │
│   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                      │                                              │
│                                      ▼                                              │
│   USER SPACE                                                                        │
│   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│   │  App receives touch event via getevent() or input subsystem                 │   │
│   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                                     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
📋 Interrupt Types
| Type | Description | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hardware IRQ擦了Device-generated (touch, timer, network)擦了Touch interrupt, network packet |  |  |
|  | Software Interrupt擦了Software-generated (system calls, exceptions)擦了int 0x80 syscall |  |
| Exception擦了Error conditions (page fault, divide by zero)擦了Segmentation fault |  |  |
| NMI (Non-Maskable)擦了Critical, cannot be disabled擦了Hardware watchdog, memory errors |  |  |
📊 Interrupt Statistics (/proc/interrupts)
```
# View interrupt statistics
adb shell cat /proc/interrupts

# Example output:
#            CPU0       CPU1       CPU2       CPU3
#   1:          0          0          0          0  GIC-0  37  timer
#  32:          0          0          0          0  GICv3 134  arch_timer
#  45:          0          0          0          0  GICv3 117  gpio
# 123:     123456          0          0          0  GICv3  45  wlan
# 125:      12345          0          0          0  GICv3  76  touch
```
```
# View interrupt statistics
adb shell cat /proc/interrupts

# View softirq statistics
adb shell cat /proc/softirqs

# Monitor interrupts in real-time
adb shell watch -n 1 cat /proc/interrupts

# Check interrupt affinity (which CPU handles which IRQ)
adb shell cat /proc/irq/*/smp_affinity

# View device IRQ mapping
adb shell cat /proc/irq/*/name

# Check interrupt latency
adb shell perf record -e irq:irq_handler_entry -a

# Monitor IRQ storm (excessive interrupts)
adb shell dmesg | grep -i "irq.*storm"

# Check for unhandled interrupts
adb shell dmesg | grep -i "unhandled"

# View IRQ balance
adb shell cat /proc/irq/*/smp_affinity_list

# Test interrupt handling (requires root)
adb shell echo 1 > /proc/irq/[IRQ_NUMBER]/debug
```
⚠ Interrupt Security Risks
⚡ IRQ Storm: Malicious device driver flooding interrupts (DoS)
🔓 Interrupt Hijacking: Replacing interrupt handler with malicious code
💾 Interrupt Stack Overflow: Kernel memory corruption
🕐 Timing Attacks: Measuring interrupt latency to extract secrets
1.5.14 CPU Scheduling
CPU scheduling determines which process runs on the CPU and for how long. Android uses the Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) with mobile optimizations. The scheduler balances responsiveness (foreground apps), fairness, and power efficiency (background tasks run less frequently).
⚙ Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS)
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    COMPLETELY FAIR SCHEDULER (CFS)                                  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                                     │
│   HOW CFS WORKS:                                                                    │
│   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│   │                                                                             │   │
│   │   Each process gets a "virtual runtime" (vruntime)                          │   │
│   │   • vruntime increases while process runs                                   │   │
│   │   • Higher vruntime = less likely to run (to be fair)                       │   │
│   │   • Scheduler always picks process with smallest vruntime                   │   │
│   │                                                                             │   │
│   │   SCHEDULER DECISION:                                                       │   │
│   │   "Pick the process that has run the least!"                                │   │
│   │                                                                             │   │
│   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                                     │
│   RUN QUEUE (Sorted by vruntime - always pick leftmost)                             │
│   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│   │                                                                             │   │
│   │   [Process A] ← [Process B] ← [Process C] ← [Process D] ← [Process E]       │   │
│   │    vruntime=100   vruntime=150   vruntime=200   vruntime=250   vruntime=300 │   │
│   │                                                                             │   │
│   │   CPU runs → Process A (vruntime increases)                                 │   │
│   │   After quantum: Reinsert Process A at end (with updated vruntime)          │   │
│   │                                                                             │   │
│   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                                     │
│   ANDROID SCHEDULER PRIORITIES:                                                     │
│   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│   │  Priority Level  │
```
```
  OOM Score  │  Examples                                  │   │
│   │  ────────────────┼─────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────│   │
│   │  Highest (RT)    │      0      │  Real-time (audio, video)                  │   │
│   │  Very High       │      0-100  │  Foreground app, user interaction          │   │
│   │  High            │    100-300  │  Visible app (not interacting)             │   │
│   │  Normal          │    300-600  │  Background service, music player          │   │
│   │  Low             │    600-900  │  Backup operation                          │   │
│   │  Very Low        │   900-1200  │  Home screen, launcher                     │   │
│   │  Lowest (Idle)   │  1200-2100  │  Cached app (empty)                        │   │
│   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                                     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
📋 Scheduling Policies
| Policy | Description | Use Case |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | SCHED_NORMAL (CFS)擦了Default for most processes擦了User apps, services |  |
| SCHED_BATCH擦了CPU-intensive, batch processing擦了Background tasks |  |  |
| SCHED_IDLE擦了Only runs when CPU idle擦了Very low priority tasks |  |  |
| SCHED_FIFO擦了Real-time, runs until blocked擦了Audio, video decoding |  |  |
| SCHED_RR擦了Real-time, round-robin擦了Time-critical tasks |  |  |
⚡ Android Scheduling Optimizations
EAS (Energy-Aware Scheduling): Balances performance vs power
HMP (Heterogeneous Multi-Processing): big.LITTLE CPU cores
CPU Boost: Temporarily increase frequency on touch
SCHED_LOAD_BALANCE: Distribute tasks across cores
CGroup Integration: Resource limits per process group
```
# Check process priorities and nice values
adb shell ps -o pid,pri,ni,cmd

# View scheduler statistics
adb shell cat /proc/schedstat

# Get process scheduling policy
adb shell chrt -p PID

# Change process priority (requires root)
adb shell renice -n -20 -p PID

# Set real-time priority (requires root)
adb shell chrt -f -p 99 PID

# View CPU frequency scaling
adb shell cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cpufreq/scaling_cur_freq

# Check CPU governor
adb shell cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cpufreq/scaling_governor

# View CPU load average
adb shell cat /proc/loadavg

# Monitor CPU usage per process
adb shell top -n 1 -b -o %CPU,NAME

# Check scheduler debug info
adb shell cat /sys/kernel/debug/sched/features

# View CPU affinity
adb shell taskset -p PID
```
✅ CPU Scheduling Best Practices
✓ Avoid busy loops - use sleep/wait instead
✓ Use AsyncTask, Coroutines, RxJava for background work
✓ Don't run CPU-intensive tasks on UI thread
✓ Use JobScheduler for deferrable background tasks
✓ Set thread priorities appropriately ( THREAD_PRIORITY_BACKGROUND )
✓ Respect doze mode - avoid waking device unnecessarily
✓ Test on big.LITTLE devices to ensure proper core assignment
✓ Monitor CPU usage during development (Android Studio Profiler)
1.5.15 Kernel Logging & Debugging
The kernel provides several logging and debugging interfaces: dmesg (kernel ring buffer), ftrace (function tracing), kprobes (dynamic instrumentation), perf (performance counters), and debugfs (debug filesystem). These tools are essential for kernel development, debugging driver issues, and security research.
📋 Kernel Logging Interfaces
| Interface | Purpose | Access |
| --- | --- | --- |
| dmesg擦了Kernel ring buffer (log messages) | User (restricted) |  |
| logcat -b kernel擦了Android kernel logs | User |  |
| ftrace擦了Function tracing, latency tracking擦了Root only |  |  |
| kprobes擦了Dynamic instrumentation擦了Root only |  |  |
|  | perf擦了Performance monitoring擦了Root only |  |
| debugfs擦了Debug filesystem擦了Root only |  |  |
⚠ Debugging Security Risks
🔓 kprobes/ftrace: Can read kernel memory (privilege escalation)
📊 debugfs: Exposes sensitive kernel information
💾 dmesg: May leak kernel addresses (ASLR bypass)
⚡ perf events: Side-channel attacks via performance counters
🔐 Kernel module debugging: Debug info helps attackers
🛠 Practical Kernel Debugging Commands
```
# View kernel log (dmesg)
adb shell dmesg
adb shell dmesg | tail -100  # Last 100 lines
adb shell dmesg -w           # Follow (like tail -f)

# Clear kernel log buffer
adb shell dmesg -c

# View kernel log with timestamps
adb shell dmesg -T

# Android kernel log via logcat
adb shell logcat -b kernel

# Filter kernel log by priority
adb shell dmesg -l err      # Error only
adb shell dmesg -l warn      # Warning only
adb shell dmesg -l info      # Info only

# Search kernel log for specific text
adb shell dmesg | grep -i "error\|fail\|panic"

# Enable dynamic debug for specific driver
adb shell echo "file drivers/gpu/drm/* +p" > /sys/kernel/debug/dynamic_debug/control

# Trace kernel function calls (ftrace)
adb shell echo function > /sys/kernel/debug/tracing/current_tracer
adb shell echo 1 > /sys/kernel/debug/tracing/tracing_on
adb shell cat /sys/kernel/debug/tracing/trace

# Trace specific function
adb shell echo "binder_ioctl" > /sys/kernel/debug/tracing/set_ftrace_filter

# View trace after operation
adb shell cat /sys/kernel/debug/tracing/trace

# Check kernel config (if available)
adb shell zcat /proc/config.gz | grep DEBUG

# View kernel symbols (kallsyms)
adb shell cat /proc/kallsyms | head -20

# Get kernel version and build info
adb shell cat /proc/version

# Check kernel command line
adb shell cat /proc/cmdline

# Monitor kernel messages in real-time
adb shell dmesg -w | while read line; do echo "$(date): $line"; done

# Save kernel log for analysis
adb shell dmesg > kernel_log.txt

# Check for kernel panics
adb shell dmesg | grep -i "panic"

# View last kernel panic (pstore)
adb shell ls -la /sys/fs/pstore/
adb shell cat /sys/fs/pstore/console-ramoops

# Check kernel soft lockups
adb shell dmesg | grep -i "soft lockup"

# View memory allocation failures
adb shell dmesg | grep -i "allocation failed"

# Check OOM kills
adb shell dmesg | grep -i "Out of memory"

# Monitor interrupt statistics
adb shell cat /proc/interrupts

# Check kernel slab allocations
adb shell cat /proc/slabinfo | head -20

# View kernel module memory usage
adb shell lsmod | while read line; do echo "$line"; done

# Enable kernel profiling
adb shell perf record -a -g sleep 10
adb shell perf report

# Check kernel security features
adb shell cat /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space  # ASLR
adb shell cat /proc/sys/kernel/kptr_restrict        # kptr restriction
```
📊 ftrace - Kernel Function Tracing
```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                FTRACE EXAMPLE OUTPUT                                         │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                                              │
│  # tracer: function                                                                          │
│  #                                                                                           │
│  #            TASK-PID        CPU#      TIMESTAMP        FUNCTION                            │
│  #               |  |          |            |               |                                │
│  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  │
│                                                                                              │
│  system_server-1234   [001]   12345.678:   binder_ioctl          ← binder_ioctl              │
│  system_server-1234   [001]   12345.679:   binder_ioctl_return   ← binder_ioctl              │

│  kworker/u16:2-567    [002]   12345.680:   try_to_wake_up       ← wake_up_process            │

One payment / Lifetime updates Get Motion+ Get Motion+ Advertise here AnimatePresence makes exit animations easy. By wrapping one or more motion components with AnimatePresence , we gain access to the exit animation prop. ``` {show && } ``` Copy code Copy code View source Open in Cursor Tutorial Hide Exit animation Open example Tap to unmute Your browser can't play this video. Learn more Video guide Open video Usage Import ``` import { AnimatePresence } from "motion/react" ``` Copy code Copy code Exit animations AnimatePresence works by detecting when its direct children are removed from the React tree. This can be due to a component mounting/remounting: ``` {show && } ``` Copy code Copy code Its key changing: ``` ``` Copy code Copy code Or when children in a list are added/removed: ``` {items.map(item => ( ))} ``` Copy code Copy code Any motion components within the exiting component will fire animations defined on their exit props before the component is removed from the DOM. ``` function Slide({ img, description }) { return ( {description} ) } ``` Copy code Copy code Like initial and animate , exit can be defined either as an object of values, or as a variant label. ``` const modalVariants = { visible: { opacity: 1, transition: { when: "beforeChildren" } }, hidden: { opacity: 0, transition: { when: "afterChildren" } } } function Modal({ children }) { return ( {children} ) } ``` Copy code Copy code NOTE Direct children must each have a unique key prop so AnimatePresence can track their presence in the tree. Changing key Changing a key prop makes React create an entirely new component. So by changing the key of a single child of AnimatePresence , we can easily make components like slideshows. ``` export const Slideshow = ({ image }) => ( ) ``` Copy code Copy code Access presence state Any child of AnimatePresence can access presence state with the useIsPresence hook. ``` import { useIsPresent } from "motion/react" function Component() { const isPresent = useIsPresent() return isPresent ? "Here!" : "Exiting..." } ``` Copy code Copy code This allows you to change content or styles when a component is no longer rendered. Access presence data When a component has been removed from the React tree, its props can no longer be updated. We can use AnimatePresence 's custom prop to pass new data down through the tree, even into exiting components. ``` ``` Copy code Copy code Then later we can extract that using usePresenceData . ``` import { AnimatePresence, usePresenceData } from "motion/react" function Slide() { const isPresent = useIsPresent() const direction = usePresenceData() return ( {isPresent ? "Here!" : "Exiting " + direction} ) } ``` Copy code Copy code View source Open in Cursor usePresenceData Open example Manual usage It's also possible to manually tell AnimatePresence when a component is safe to remove with the usePresence hook. This returns both isPresent state and a callback, safeToRemove , that should be called when you're ready to remove the component from the DOM (for instance after a manual animation or other timeout). ``` import { usePresence } from "motion/react" function Component() { const [isPresent, safeToRemove] = usePresence() useEffect(() => { // Remove from DOM 1000ms after being removed from React !isPresent && setTimeout(safeToRemove, 1000) }, [isPresent]) return
} ``` Copy code Copy code Propagate exit animations By default, AnimatePresence controls the exit animations on all of its children, until another AnimatePresence component is rendered. ``` {show ? ( {/* * When `show` becomes `false`, exit animations * on these children will not fire. */} {children} ) : null} ``` Copy code Copy code By setting an AnimatePresence component's propagate prop to true , when it's removed from another AnimatePresence it will fire all of its children's exit animations. ``` {show ? ( {/* * When `show` becomes `false`, exit animations * on these children **will** fire. */} {children} ) : null} ``` Copy code Copy code S A B C D F Find & fix animation performance issues with your agent. MotionScore for Agents grades animations in your source code S to F and hands your agent specific fixes before you ship. Part of the Motion+ AI Kit. Get the AI Kit 450+ production-ready examples. JavaScript, React, and Vue. Copy and paste straight into your project, adapt with AI, or pipe the whole set into your agent with the Examples MCP. See all examples Part of Motion+. One-time fee, lifetime access. Props initial By passing initial={false} , AnimatePresence will disable any initial animations on children that are present when the component is first rendered. ``` ``` Copy code Copy code custom When a component is removed, there's no longer a chance to update its props (because it's no longer in the React tree). Therefore we can't update its exit animation with the same render that removed the component. By passing a value through AnimatePresence 's custom prop, we can use dynamic variants to change the exit animation. ``` const variants = { hidden: (direction) => ({ opacity: 0, x: direction === 1 ? -300 : 300 }), visible: { opacity: 1, x: 0 } } export const Slideshow = ({ image, direction }) => ( ) ``` Copy code Copy code This data can be accessed by children via usePresenceData . mode Default: "sync" Decides how AnimatePresence handles entering and exiting children. View source Open in Cursor Tutorial sync wait popLayout Switch AnimatePresence modes Open example sync In "sync" mode, elements animate in and out as soon as they're added/removed. This is the most basic (and default) mode - AnimatePresence takes no opinion on sequencing animations or layout. Therefore, if element layouts conflict (as in the above example), you can either implement your own solution (using position: absolute or similar), or try one of the other two mode options. wait In "wait" mode, the entering element will wait until the exiting child has animated out, before it animates in. This is great for sequential animations, presenting users with one piece of information or one UI element at a time. WARNING wait mode only supports one child at a time. NOTE Try setting ease: "easeIn" (or similar) on the exit animation, and ease: "easeOut" on the enter animation for an overall easeInOut easing effect. popLayout Exiting elements will be "popped" out of the page layout, allowing surrounding elements to immediately reflow. Pairs especially well with the layout prop, so elements can animate to their new layout. ``` {items.map(item => ( )} ``` Copy code Copy code For a more detailed comparison, check out the full AnimatePresence modes tutorial. WARNING When using popLayout mode, any immediate child of AnimatePresence that's a custom component must be wrapped in React's forwardRef function, forwarding the provided ref to the DOM node you wish to pop out of the layout. onExitComplete Fires when all exiting nodes have completed animating out. propagate Default: false If set to true , exit animations on children will also trigger when this AnimatePresence exits from a parent AnimatePresence . ``` {show ? ( {/* This exit prop will now fire when show is false */} ) : null} ``` Copy code Copy code root Root element for injecting popLayout styles. Defaults to document.head but can be set to another ShadowRoot , for use within shadow DOM. Troubleshooting Exit animations aren't working Ensure all immediate children get a unique key prop that remains the same for that component every render. For instance, providing index as a key is bad because if the items reorder then the index will not be matched to the item : ``` {items.map((item, index) => ( ))} ``` Copy code Copy code It's preferred to pass something that's unique to that item, for instance an ID: ``` {items.map((item) => ( ))} ``` Copy code Copy code Also make sure AnimatePresence is outside of the code that unmounts the element. If AnimatePresence itself unmounts, then it can't control exit animations! For example, this will not work: ``` isVisible && ( ) ``` Copy code Copy code Instead, the conditional should be at the root of AnimatePresence : ``` {isVisible && } ``` Copy code Copy code Layout animations not working with mode="sync" When mixing exit and layout animations, it might be necessary to wrap the group in LayoutGroup to ensure that components outside of AnimatePresence know when to perform a layout animation. ``` {items.map(item => ( ))} ``` Copy code Copy code Layout animations not working with mode="popLayout" When any HTML element has an active transform it temporarily becomes the offset parent of its children. This can cause children with position: "absolute" not to appear where you expect. mode="popLayout" works by using position: "absolute" . So to ensure consistent and expected positioning during a layout animation, ensure that the animating parent has a position other than "static" . ``` {items.map(item => ( ))} ``` Copy code Copy code Stay in the loop.
