Fitts's Law and Touch Target Sizing That Holds Up on Mobile
Jun 06,2026 
Fitts's Law still works on mobile in its core claim, that bigger and closer targets are faster to hit, but the desktop habits built on top of it invert the moment a finger replaces a cursor. The clearest example is the corner. On a desktop the corner is the cheapest pixel on the screen to hit, and on a phone the most expensive, which is why the tiny close button placed there draws so many missed, repeated taps. Getting touch sizing right starts with knowing where those old instincts flip.
Fitts's Law Predictions and the Model's Original Scope
Paul Fitts published the law in 1954 after a tapping task that sounds quaint now. People moved a stylus back and forth between two metal plates as fast as they could, while landing inside the plate on at least 95% of taps. That accuracy constraint turns the result into a speed-accuracy tradeoff instead of a raw speed measure, which is what makes the law useful for design.
The model says movement time equals a + b * log2(2D / W), where D is the distance to the target and W is its width along the line of motion, with a and b fitted for a device and user. The log2(2D/W) term is the index of difficulty, counted in bits, treating the hand as a channel with limited capacity. Targets that are bigger and closer are faster to acquire, smaller and farther ones are slower and produce more errors, and the relationship is logarithmic, so doubling the distance does not double the time.
The law was validated heavily for the mouse, and it predicts mouse pointing almost perfectly, because a cursor is a single pixel with no occlusion. Moving the same rules to touch needs care.
The Breakdown of the Model on Touchscreens
A fingertip covers the target as it lands, so the user cannot see the precise point of contact, and the contact itself is an area, which standard Fitts treats as a point, so it under-predicts errors on small touch targets. A 2013 correction known as FFitts Law showed plain Fitts is insufficient for small-target acquisition with a fingertip. Its fix added a second source of spread, tied to the absolute precision of the finger, which has a floor no matter how slowly a person moves.
Below a certain size, slowing down stops helping, because the source of the imprecision is the finger's contact patch and no longer the aim. A mouse button has no such limit, while a touch button has one that no amount of careful aiming removes.
Work from the MIT Touch Lab put the average adult index fingertip near 8 to 10mm wide, the finger pad at 10 to 14mm, and the thumb contact area near 25mm. Several common minimums are smaller than the pad that lands on them. A 44-point Apple target is about 7mm, so the part of the finger doing the tapping is wider than the thing tapped, which is why a practical floor near 10mm keeps coming back.
The Minimum-Size Numbers and Which to Trust
Platform Minimums Compared
The platform guidelines do not agree, and the spread is wider than most assume. Apple's Human Interface Guidelines have called for a 44 by 44 point minimum since the 2007 iPhone guidance, and the number has held through current iOS. Points are not pixels, so at high density a 44-point control is many more device pixels than 44. Material Design asks for a larger 48 by 48 dp target plus at least 8dp of space between targets, around 9mm of physical screen, and Windows guidance is a notch lower near 7.5mm. The gap between the smallest and largest of these is real, and copying one platform's number onto another screen is a common way to ship something too small.
The WCAG Numbers and the Legal Floor
A 24-pixel close control can pass an accessibility audit and still take a user three taps to hit. That outcome is built into the standards, which add a second pair of numbers that often gets confused with the platform minimums. WCAG 2.5.5, the enhanced criterion from 2018, asks for 44 by 44 CSS pixels, but is at Level AAA, which almost no legislation enforces. WCAG 2.5.8, added in 2023, asks for 24 by 24 CSS pixels at Level AA, the level that shows up under accessibility law. So the comfortable number is not enforced by law, and the enforceable one is about 6.4mm, smaller than the finger pad. Practitioners treat 24 pixels as a floor to exceed, since a control built to the bare minimum is compliant and frustrating at once.
The Usability Floor from Error-Rate Research
The number worth designing toward comes from error-rate studies. A 2006 study of one-handed thumb use, later given a best historical paper award, found that targets around 9.2 to 9.6mm kept error rates low, while anything under 7mm pushed errors up steeply. Usability guidance rounds this into the rule that interactive elements should be at least 1cm by 1cm, roughly the size at which mis-taps drop off.
The Diminishing Returns of Bigger Targets
Past about 1cm, accuracy gains flatten, and button-size studies put the efficient ceiling near 20mm, where the largest of 20, 25, and 30mm buttons mostly wastes screen space.
There is a stranger failure at the top end. When a target gets too large, people stop perceiving it as a discrete control, and a giant tap zone registers as a banner rather than a button. So the reflex that bigger is always safer fails past a threshold, because it trades a hit-accuracy problem for a perception problem. The work is finding the band where a target is easy to hit and still obviously a control.
The Corner Inversion and the Thumb Zone
On a desktop, screen edges behave as if they were infinitely deep. The cursor stops at the edge, so an edge target has effectively unlimited width along the approach, and a person can fling the mouse at it at full speed without overshooting. The four corners are better still, two infinite edges meeting at a point, so the macOS menu bar is on the top edge and the Windows Start button is in a corner.
None of that survives the move to touch. A finger does not stop at the screen edge the way a cursor does, so there is no overshoot protection, and bezels and gesture zones interfere. Worse, the top corners are the hardest region for a one-handed thumb to reach. The easiest spot to hit on a desktop is the hardest on a touchscreen, and the only thing close to a good edge on a phone is the bottom, which is inside the natural arc of the thumb. Tab bars and bottom navigation succeed there because a top-corner control is outside the thumb's reach.
The Thumb Zone and Its Walk-Back
The thumb zone maps how easily a thumb reaches each part of a phone held in one hand, easy at the bottom and on the side opposite the thumb, hard at the far top corners. A field study of 1,333 observations found about 49% of people held the phone one-handed and roughly 75% used a thumb. That data became the reach heat map most designers met first, where only about a third of the screen counts as effortless.
The catch is that Steven Hoober, whose field study built the original map, later argued against treating it as fixed. Working from millions of captured touches, he found that people constantly change their grip rather than locking into one, and that they prefer to touch the center of the screen, where they tap fastest, and will move content there if a design lets them. The current reading favors designing for the center and making important controls repositionable. A designer who cites only the older map will get corrected.
The Misapplications Worth Fixing
A few patterns repeat often enough to name. The top-corner hamburger menu borrows a desktop habit and parks the entry point to navigation in the hardest spot for a thumb, then often opens a panel whose items are also up top. The tiny close X on a modal or ad combines the worst reach region with a target too small to hit cleanly, beside the content you least want to trigger, and few combinations produce more rage tapping. Treating the 24-pixel WCAG minimum as a usability target rather than a legal floor ships controls that pass review and annoy everyone. Target reworked its app in 2019 to enlarge the Search and Scan buttons to roughly 0.8 by 0.8 inches, explicitly to make it workable one-handed, and reported less frustration after.
Spacing as the Underrated Half of the Problem
Size has dominated the touch-target conversation for so long that spacing, the other requirement, gets treated as polish when it is a separate constraint. Material Design names 8dp between targets as a separate minimum, and a 48dp target with zero gap around it still fails in practice. WCAG 2.5.8 makes the trade explicit by letting a sub-24-pixel target pass if a 24-pixel circle centered on it does not overlap a neighbor, which formalizes the idea that small is fine when isolated.
The sharpest argument for spacing comes from people with hand tremors. For them, the danger is hitting a button by accident while scrolling, so they rest a finger in the gap between list items, trusting that the gap is dead space. Back-to-back targets with no gap remove that resting spot and turn a scroll into a run of accidental taps. Spacing is an accessibility feature that protects the users packed, undersized controls hurt most.
Fitts gives the design a floor and a map of bad regions, and stops there. The guidelines settle the minimum, the corner inversion marks where not to put things, and the thumb-zone research says to expect grip to change, but none of them name which control fails for which real grip on which device. A 44-point button your thumb hits without thinking can fall outside the arc of a smaller hand on a larger phone, and your own device is the worst place to learn that, since it reports only your own hand. Reviewing the layout in Evelance against personas with different thumb sizes and grips shows early which controls a one-handed user cannot reach, while the design is still easy to change. The sizes worth checking against are physical ones, a finger pad of 10 to 14mm meeting a 44-point control of about 7mm, with at least 8dp of space between targets, the gap that gives an unsteady finger somewhere safe to rest.
Frequently Asked Questions
What is the formula for Fitts's law?
Movement time equals a + b * log2(2D / W), where D is the distance to the target, W is the target width along the axis of motion, and a and b are constants fitted for the device and user. The log2(2D/W) term is the index of difficulty, measured in bits. The relationship is logarithmic, so doubling the distance does not double the movement time.
What is the index of difficulty in Fitts's law?
The index of difficulty is the log2(2D/W) portion of the formula, a single number in bits that captures how hard a target is to acquire based on its distance and width. A higher index means a harder and slower acquisition. It lets dissimilar targets be compared on one scale of difficulty rather than by raw size or distance alone.
Does Fitts's law apply to touchscreens?
Partly. It still captures that bigger and closer targets are easier to hit, but it under-predicts errors on small finger targets because of occlusion and the finger's contact area. The 2013 FFitts correction adds a fixed-precision term that models finger touch accurately, accounting for the floor below which moving slower no longer improves accuracy.
What is the minimum touch target size?
There is no single answer. WCAG 2.5.8 at Level AA sets a 24 by 24 pixel legal minimum, Apple recommends 44 by 44 points, WCAG 2.5.5 at Level AAA recommends 44 by 44 pixels, and Material Design recommends 48 by 48 dp. Usability research points to about 1cm by 1cm as a practical floor for low error rates.
How big is the average fingertip for touch design?
MIT Touch Lab research found the average adult fingertip is about 8 to 10mm wide, the finger pad 10 to 14mm, and the thumb contact area around 25mm. Several common minimum target sizes are smaller than the finger pad that lands on them, which is the physical reason occlusion and mis-taps happen on small controls.
What is the difference between Apple and Android touch target guidelines?
Apple's Human Interface Guidelines specify a 44 by 44 point minimum. Google's Material Design specifies a larger 48 by 48 dp minimum plus at least 8dp of spacing between targets. Material is the more generous of the two, and its separate spacing requirement means a target can meet the size rule and still fail if it has no gap around it.
What is the thumb zone in mobile design?
The thumb zone is the area of a phone screen a person can comfortably reach with their thumb while holding the device one-handed. It is easiest at the bottom and on the side opposite the thumb, and hardest at the far top corners. Later research complicates it, since people change grip often rather than holding the phone one way the whole time.
Is bigger always better for touch targets?
No. Accuracy improves with size only up to about 1cm, after which the gains flatten. Oversize targets waste screen space and can stop registering as discrete, clickable buttons, so a giant tap zone may be mistaken for a banner or background instead. There is a usable sweet spot rather than a rule that bigger is always safer.
How much space should there be between touch targets?
Material Design recommends at least 8dp of spacing between targets, and WCAG 2.5.8 lets smaller targets pass if a 24-pixel circle around each one does not overlap a neighbor. Spacing is a separate requirement from size. Adequate gaps prevent accidental activation, which matters most for people scrolling past tightly packed controls.
Why do screen corners matter in Fitts's law?
On desktop, screen edges and corners act as effectively infinite targets because the cursor stops at them, so they are easy to hit at full speed. This is why the macOS menu bar is on the top edge and the Windows Start button is in a corner. The advantage does not transfer to touch, since a finger does not stop at the edge.
Where should the navigation menu go on mobile?
Toward the bottom of the screen, inside the natural arc of the thumb. Placing the hamburger or primary navigation in a top corner forces a regrip and puts it in the hardest region for a one-handed thumb, which is a common Fitts's Law misapplication on mobile. Bottom navigation and tab bars solve this because they are where the thumb already rests.
What is the difference between Fitts's law and Hick's law?
Fitts's Law concerns the physical motor cost of reaching a target, based on its size and distance. Hick's Law concerns the cognitive cost of choosing among options, where decision time grows with the number of choices. Fitts governs the reach toward a target, while Hick governs the decision a person makes first. The two get cited together because both shape the same tap, though one measures movement and the other choice.

Fitts's law
Fitts's law is a model of human movement which predicts that the time to reach a target depends on the distance to it and its size. In interface design it means important actions should be large and close to where the pointer or thumb already is.
UX Audit starten
Die Kernideen
The main points of Fitts's law:
Larger targets are faster and easier to hit
Closer targets are faster to reach than distant ones
Screen edges and corners act as large targets for a mouse
Touch interfaces need generous minimum target sizes
So wenden Sie es auf Ihr Produkt an
Size primary actions generously, place them near the content they act on, and keep touch targets at platform minimums: 44 by 44 points on Apple platforms and 48 by 48 dp on Android. Keep destructive actions away from frequent ones.
Überprüfen Sie Ihre Designs mit Fleck
Das UX Audit von Fleck prüft einen Screen oder eine Live-URL auf Probleme bei Usability, Accessibility und visueller Hierarchie und liefert konkrete Korrekturen, die Sie direkt im Projekt anwenden können.
Häufige Fehler
Small icon-only buttons as the primary action
Placing a confirm button far from the field the user just completed
Putting delete right next to save
Häufig gestellte Fragen
What is the minimum touch target size?
Apple's Human Interface Guidelines recommend at least 44 by 44 points and Material Design recommends at least 48 by 48 dp.

Design Generalist
Four Design Philosophies Shaping Modern UI
March 12, 2026
The Swiss grid you use, the breathing room you leave, the warmth you feel, and the system you architect all descend from four distinct design philosophies - each born from specific cultural soil and each offering irreplaceable tools for building modern applications. Swiss design gives you the grid and typographic clarity that makes dense productivity tools scannable. Japanese design gives you ma - the meaningful void that transforms cluttered interfaces into calm ones. Scandinavian design gives you democratic warmth that makes complex tools feel approachable. German design gives you the systematic, modular thinking that is design systems. Understanding the deep "why" behind each tradition transforms you from someone applying aesthetic patterns to someone making principled design decisions. What follows is a comprehensive guide through each tradition's philosophical roots, core principles, and specific applications to building modern UI - from productivity tools to marketing sites to component libraries.
Swiss International Typographic Style: the grid as moral imperative
From Swiss neutrality to your 8px spacing token
The Swiss Style didn't emerge from aesthetic preference - it emerged from a country that needed to communicate across four national languages (German, French, Italian, Romansh) without ambiguity. Post-WWII Switzerland, neutral and untouched by the devastation surrounding it, produced designers who believed visual communication could rebuild rational, peaceful civilization. The grid was not a layout tool - it was an ethical stance against propaganda, subjectivity, and visual noise.
Ernst Keller began teaching at the Zurich Kunstgewerbeschule in 1918 with a philosophy that would seed everything: "The solution to the design problem should emerge from its content." Wikipedia His students became the movement's founders. The style synthesized Russian Constructivism's geometric abstraction, De Stijl's primary-color grids, Aesthetics Wiki Big Human Jan Tschichold's Die neue Typographie (1928), and the Bauhaus diaspora that fled Nazi Germany into Swiss schools. Wikipedia
Josef Muller-Brockmann (1914-1996) codified the grid as organizing principle. Wikipedia His Grid Systems in Graphic Design (1961) remains canonical. Tapflare He insisted on Akzidenz-Grotesk over its successors, used all-lowercase for "total objectivity," Williamipark and when asked about his best work, replied: "The white reverse sides of my posters." Stuartmcmaw Emil Ruder at the Basel School Blogger published Typographie: A Manual of Design (1967) and declared: "Typography has one plain duty before it and that is to convey information in writing." Blogger TypeRoom Adrian Frutiger designed Univers (1957) Inkbot Design - 21 systematically organized weights marketed with a chart inspired by the periodic table Wikipedia - and later Frutiger for Charles de Gaulle Airport signage. His insight that "the eye does not read letters, but the space between them" Inkbot Design directly shapes how we think about letter-spacing in CSS today.
Neue Grafik, the journal co-founded by Muller-Brockmann in 1958, published 18 issues through 1965 and became the programmatic platform that spread Swiss principles internationally. Lars Muller Publishers Massimo Vignelli then carried the style into corporate America, designing the New York City Subway signage, Baytas American Airlines identity, and establishing Helvetica as the default corporate typeface Creative Bloq by 1970. Design Repository
The core principles that translate directly to code
Swiss design rests on mathematical grids as organizing principle, sans-serif typography with hierarchy achieved only through size and weight, Medium flush-left ragged-right alignment, asymmetric layouts balanced through grid discipline, Wikipedia and white space as active design element Wikipedia - not emptiness but deliberate negative space governed by mathematical ratios. Wikipedia Color is limited: black, white, grays, plus one strong accent. Every element must serve communication; decoration is eliminated. Wikipedia Zeka Design
The modern 8px grid system is the direct digital heir to Muller-Brockmann's modular grid. Both Apple and Google recommend it because most screen resolutions divide evenly by 8, UI UX News it scales cleanly across devices, and it creates the "mathematical precision in spacing" that Swiss designers demanded with rulers and now lives in your --space- tokens.
Where Swiss thinking lives in modern products
Linear is the quintessential Swiss-inspired digital product - so influential that "Linear design" now describes the entire minimalist SaaS aesthetic. Co-founder Karri Saarinen's approach uses Medium an 8px spacing scale, opacity-based color systems (black and white at various transparencies for light/dark mode support), and hierarchy through typography weight rather than decoration. Linear doesn't actually use a traditional layout grid but maintains modular components, each designed for specific content formats LogRocket - a subtlety that separates mature Swiss-inspired design from naive grid worship.
Notion's block-based system is a digital manifestation of Swiss grids - everything is grid-aligned. Envato Figma uses Inter (designed by Rasmus Andersson, first designer at Spotify). Stripe's marketing site, Vercel, and GitHub all draw heavily from Swiss principles. The font Inter itself - a free neo-grotesque sans-serif optimized for screen readability Tetrisly - was accessed 414 billion times on Google Fonts in the 12 months ending May 2025, making it the Wikipedia dominant Swiss-lineage typeface of the digital era.
Swiss design excels at data-dense UIs (dashboards, tables, project management), scalability across screen sizes and themes, internationalization (neutral design accommodates multiple languages), and longevity (timelessness is built in). Its limitation is real: stripped of personality, every product risks looking identical. Wolfgang Weingart's rebellion at the Basel School asked the question that still haunts Swiss-inspired SaaS: "What's the use of being legible, when nothing inspires you to take notice of it?" Tapflare
Japanese design: emptiness as the most generous gift to users
From Zen gardens to empty states
Japanese design is inseparable from three spiritual currents: Shinto (reverence for nature and sensitivity to energy between persons and environment), Zen Buddhism (all things are "either evolving from or dissolving into nothingness" - and this nothingness is a space of potentiality), and the tea ceremony ( chanoyu), which embodies deliberate pauses that create rhythm inviting serenity. Ikko Tanaka himself likened the designer's role to that of a tea host - a mediator between private interests and public audiences. Wikipedia
The concepts that matter most for building interfaces:
Ma (間) is not "white space." The character combines "gate" (門) and "sun" (日) - light beaming through a doorway's empty space. Wikipedia globis Ma is "an emptiness full of possibilities, like a promise yet to be fulfilled." Wikipedia Bri's Blog It extends beyond visual into sonic (silence between notes), temporal (pauses in ceremony), and social (deliberate pauses in bowing). JAPAN HOUSE Los Angeles In Japanese, ma-nuke (simpleton) literally means "someone missing ma" Kyoto Journal - revealing how central the concept is to competent functioning.
Wabi-sabi (侘寂) celebrates three realities: "nothing lasts, nothing is finished, nothing is perfect." globis Diva-portal Critically different from Western minimalism: where Western minimalism celebrates the machine and precision (cold, abstract, universal), wabi-sabi celebrates the natural and handmade (warm, authentic, unique). Silphium Design Kintsugi - repairing broken pottery with gold - captures this perfectly: Wikipedia breakage signals renewal, not failure. Globis EU Japandistore
Kanso (簡素) means simplicity through omission of the non-essential. KimuraKami Presentation Zen Fukinsei (不均整) means asymmetric balance J-Life International - the Zen circle (Enso) is deliberately drawn incomplete because leaving something unfinished invites the beholder to participate. polyglottando Shibui describes objects that "appear simple overall but include subtle details, such as textures, that balance simplicity with complexity" - ensuring you never tire of them. Wikipedia
Japan's geography shaped everything: an island nation with limited space put a premium on spatial economy (tatami rooms serve for sitting, sleeping, and gathering; sliding shoji doors blur indoor/outdoor boundaries). ArchitectureCourses.org Four distinct seasons embedded themselves in a color vocabulary with specific palettes for each - spring's sakura pink, autumn's akane red, App Growth Summit winter's mouse-gray ( nezumi-iro) sophistication.
Kenya Hara and the philosophy of emptiness
Kenya Hara, art director of MUJI since 2001 Wikipedia and author of Designing Design and White, Lars Muller Publishers provides the bridge between Japanese philosophy and modern product thinking. His central insight: MUJI embodies "emptiness" not "minimalism." Shakespeare & Company Lars Muller Publishers Emptiness is a vessel waiting to be filled by the user; Wikipedia minimalism is an endpoint. "Giving users the freedom to use our products however they wish is what I mean by emptiness." Globis EU globis This directly translates to UI: an empty dashboard isn't failure - it's potential.
Naoto Fukasawa's "Without Thought" philosophy seeks design that dissolves into behavior - products so natural they're used unconsciously. Design+Encyclopedia Wikipedia His MUJI wall-mounted CD player (pull-cord inspired by kitchen ventilator fans) sits in MoMA's permanent collection. Octobercomms With Jasper Morrison, he developed "Super Normal" Lars Muller Publishers - objects of "satisfying modesty" Fast Company where the brand name ±0 literally means plus-minus zero, "just right."
Tadao Ando, the self-taught Pritzker Prize architect, The Curative Company captures the design aspiration: "If you give people nothingness, they can ponder what can be achieved from that nothingness." His Church of Light - a cross cut into a concrete wall, illuminated entirely by natural light - is architecture as ma. JAPAN HOUSE Los Angeles
The critical nuance: minimalism and maximalism are both Japanese
The Western fixation on Japanese minimalism is incomplete. Photographer Kyoichi Tsuzuki dismissed it as "some Japanophile's dream" - actual Japanese domestic life is often crammed with things. Aeon Rakuten, Yahoo! Japan, Medium and Cookpad are dense, text-heavy, information-rich. MUJI and Uniqlo are minimalist globis because they target global audiences. Medium As researcher Matt Alt observed, "the subtractive and additive are deeply entwined in Japan, locked in a cultural conversation since time immemorial." Aeon The sophisticated lesson: minimalism and maximalism are contextually deployed tools, not absolute values. Every choice is "rooted in function, emotion, and cultural code." Medium
Applying Ma to your productivity tools and marketing sites
For dense productivity tools, Ma doesn't mean universal spaciousness - it means strategic breathing room. Dense data areas need concentrated Ma (focused padding) to prevent cognitive overload while maintaining information density where needed. The Shinkansen dashboard is clean; the content areas can be dense. Ma creates the frame; content fills the frame.
For marketing sites, Ma plus Fukinsei (asymmetry) creates calm authority: generous whitespace, off-center headlines, organic content flow. Instead of two equal 50% columns, try 65% and 35% - this imbalance is more natural and visually engaging. Silphium Design
For design systems, Japanese color philosophy offers a complete alternative palette. The traditional 和色 (wairo) system at nipponcolors.com catalogs 250+ nature-derived colors with digital codes. Art Learnings Key characteristics: subdued saturation, heightened brightness, and natural warmth - never stark or synthetic. Art Learnings A Japanese-inspired token system might use --washi-white: #F7F5F0 (warm like handmade paper), --sumi-ink: #2C2C2C (never pure black), and --nezumi: #9EA1A3 (the sophisticated mouse-gray family that originated in the Edo period as an alternative to "hai," gray associated with fires and war). Art Learnings
The Jo-ha-kyu temporal principle (begin slowly, accelerate, end swiftly) directly shapes animation: micro-interactions should ease in gently, move with purpose, and resolve quickly - natural rhythm rather than mechanical timing.
German Bauhaus and industrial design: the system is the design
From Peter Behrens's AEG to your component library
The German tradition begins in 1907 with the Deutscher Werkbund and Peter Behrens, who created the world's first comprehensive corporate identity for AEG - designing everything from the logotype to products to factory buildings to workers' housing. Wikipedia Behrens embraced machine production while maintaining craft quality, a philosophical stance that runs through all subsequent German design. His office trained three future titans: Walter Gropius, Mies van der Rohe, and Le Corbusier.
Gropius founded the Bauhaus on April 1, 1919, Envato in Weimar, ART Envato with a vision of Gesamtkunstwerk - the total work of art ART unifying all disciplines. The Metropolitan Museum of Art The school operated under three directors across three cities in just 14 years: Wikipedia Gropius in Weimar (1919-1925) pivoted from Arts & Crafts to industrial production with the motto "Art and Technology - A New Unity"; History in the Margins Hannes Meyer in Dessau (1928-1930) pushed toward functionalism and social responsibility; Mies van der Rohe in Berlin (1930-1933) emphasized architecture before the Nazis forced closure. The Metropolitan Museum of Art
Herbert Bayer created the Universal typeface (1925) - a lowercase-only geometric sans-serif based on pure geometric forms, declaring the abolition of uppercase as unnecessary waste. Josef Albers published Interaction of Color (1963), Louisapenfold proving that "color is the most relative medium in art" Louisapenfold - no color exists in isolation, and every color changes based on surrounding colors. This principle is fundamental to building color systems that work across light/dark modes and component contexts. Laszlo Moholy-Nagy declared: "Typography must be communication in its most intense form." Wikipedia
The forced Bauhaus closure scattered masters worldwide: Gropius to Harvard, Mies to IIT Chicago, Moholy-Nagy to found the New Bauhaus in Chicago, the Alberses to Black Mountain College Google Arts & Culture and then Yale. The White City of Tel Aviv contains over 4,000 Bauhaus buildings - a UNESCO World Heritage Site. MasterClass
The Ulm School: where design became systems thinking
The Hochschule fur Gestaltung (HfG) Ulm, founded in 1953 by Inge Aicher-Scholl, Otl Aicher, and Max Bill, Wikipedia was born from moral imperative PRINT Magazine - named in memory of Hans and Sophie Scholl, White Rose resistance members executed by the Nazis. The founders believed "good design can lead to a better life" Norse Projects and sought to rebuild German society morally through design education.
After Max Bill (former Bauhaus student) resigned as rector in 1957, Tomas Maldonado and Aicher radicalized the approach: they integrated sociology, psychology, semiotics, and cybernetics into design education, creating the "Ulm Model" - design as systematic problem-solving, not individual expression. Ulm's achievements were staggering: the Braun SK4 radio-phonograph ("Snow White's Coffin," Norse Projects 1956) with Hans Gugelot and Dieter Rams; Otl Aicher's Lufthansa visual identity (1962) using strict modular grids and Univers; Hartdesignselection and Aicher's 1972 Munich Olympics pictograms that established international wayfinding standards still in use today. Hartdesignselection The term "corporate identity" was coined in the 1950s Artsy for the type of comprehensive visual standards systems that Ulm pioneered. Despite only 15 years of operation before closing in 1968, Artsy HfG Ulm remains the most influential design school after the Bauhaus Artsy - and it anticipated the modern concept of a design system where diverse outputs all adhere to unified rules.
Dieter Rams and the ten principles that became Apple's DNA
Dieter Rams (born 1932) joined Braun in 1955, became head of design from 1961 to 1995, and oversaw more than 500 products. Onlyonceshop His motto - "Weniger, aber besser" (Less, but better) Shutterstock - captures the entire German design tradition. In the late 1970s, growing concerned by "an impenetrable confusion of forms, colours and noises," he formulated his ten principles of good design. Vitsoe
The principles that matter most for UI engineering: "Good design makes a product understandable" - it clarifies structure; at best, it is self-explanatory. "Good design is unobtrusive" - products are tools, not decorative objects; their design should be neutral and restrained to leave room for the user's self-expression. "Good design is thorough down to the last detail" - nothing must be arbitrary or left to chance; care and accuracy show respect toward the user. "Good design is as little design as possible" - concentrate on the essential aspects; back to purity, back to simplicity. Heurio
The Rams -> Apple pipeline is direct and documented. Jonathan Ive called Rams's work "a profound influence": Medium the Braun T3 pocket radio (1958) begat the iPod; CNN the ET66 calculator begat iOS Calculator; rams foundation the entire Braun white/silver aesthetic begat Apple's product ecosystem. Ive stated: "Dieter Rams in so many ways articulated the framework for the profession that was inspirational and responsible." rams foundation Rams, for his part, called Apple "one of the few companies that take design seriously." Hammer Agency Design Museum
Applying German systematic thinking to design systems
The evolution is linear and traceable: Bauhaus taught design as a system of interrelated elements -> Ulm formalized "systems design" -> Braun created a product family sharing visual DNA -> Aicher's Lufthansa manual pioneered comprehensive brand systems -> modern design systems are direct descendants. SAP's Fiori design system embodies this with five principles that echo Rams: role-based (useful), adaptive (systematic), simple (as little design as possible), coherent (modular), and delightful (aesthetic).
For your component library, Rams's principles translate precisely:
Every component must solve a real user task - remove components that exist "just in case" (Principle 2: useful). Components should be self-explanatory; at best, no tooltip needed (Principle 4: understandable). UI is a tool - design neutral, restrained components that recede to let user content shine (Principle 5: unobtrusive). Every pixel, every state - hover, focus, disabled, error, loading - must be designed; nothing left to chance (Principle 8: thorough). If an element doesn't serve the user, remove it (Principle 10: as little design as possible).
German design excels at dense productivity tools (systematic components handle information-rich interfaces), design systems (the tradition is systems thinking - reproducible, modular, standardized), and scalability (mathematical grids and modular components scale by nature). Its limitation: the emphasis on rationality and system can lack emotional warmth - Rams's work "rarely feels inhuman" thanks to warm wood and tactile knobs, The Awl but in digital translation, that warmth often gets lost.
Scandinavian design: simplicity that refuses to be cold
Democratic design from the People's Home to Spotify
Scandinavian design's ideological foundation was laid in 1919 when Gregor Paulsson published "Vackrare Vardagsvara" ("More Beautiful Things for Everyday Use") Rug & Kilim - the revolutionary premise that aesthetic quality should be available to ordinary people, not just the elite. The 1930 Stockholm Exhibition was the breakthrough moment: The Modern Dane ~4 million visitors experienced functionalist apartments with modern furniture. Rug & Kilim Alvar Aalto, reporting for the Finnish press, wrote: "The exhibition speaks out for joyful and spontaneous everyday life." Wikipedia But critics found the architecture "too crisp and cold to consider living with permanently" Wikipedia - sparking the evolution toward warm functionalism that distinguishes Scandinavian design from Bauhaus severity.
The movement was deeply intertwined with Nordic social democracy. Prime Minister Per Albin Hansson's concept of Folkhemmet ("The People's Home") drove architects and reformers to collaborate on housing that embodied egalitarian values. Wikipedia The Law of Jante (Janteloven), introduced in Aksel Sandemose's 1933 novel, distilled Nordic collective values into one idea: be humble; no one is above anyone else. UX Design In design culture, this produces less rockstar-driven attitudes, greater cross-collaboration, and egalitarian work structures. Medium
Lagom (Swedish: "just the right amount") summarizes the entire philosophy Aesthetics Wiki - not too much, not too little. Communication Generation The Modern Dane Hygge (Danish: "a cozy, contented mood") finds joy in simple things. Aesthetics Wiki The Modern Dane As Meik Wiking of Copenhagen's Happiness Research Institute puts it: "What freedom is to Americans, hygge is to Danes." prescientuk Friluftsliv (Norwegian: "open-air living") transfers to interiors through greenery, wooden accents, and organic textiles. ZME Science
Geography shaped everything: long dark winters drove the need for warmth, light, and brightness - white walls, large windows, multiple light sources. Poul Henningsen's Scandinavia Standard PH Lamp (1926, still iconic) Wikipedia was designed specifically to spread light widely without visible glare. Scandinavia Standard Harsh climate demanded that products simply work. Vast forested landscapes made wood the natural material of choice Wikipedia - oak, ash, birch, pine in their light, natural state.
Alvar Aalto's humanist critique that still applies to your UI
Alvar Aalto (1898-1976) Wikipedia wrote the philosophical cornerstone in his 1940 essay "The Humanizing of Architecture": rationalization in early modernism "has not gone deep enough" - it addressed only technical aspects, not psychological and humanitarian needs. His insistence that "form must have a content, and that content must be linked with nature and the human soul" Bookey directly applies to building tools today. Scandinavian functionalism evolved to also meet the emotional needs of people Smashing Magazine - and this is its enduring distinction from Swiss or German approaches.
Arne Jacobsen's Egg Chair (1958), Wikipedia Hans Wegner's Wishbone Chair (1949), and IKEA's Democratic Design Manifesto (1995) Museo Nacional Thyssen-Bornemisza - formally defining five dimensions of Form, Function, Quality, Sustainability, and Low Price IKEA - all carry this thread. When IKEA says "our mission is the almost impossible idea to combine beautiful form with good function, long-lasting quality, produced in a sustainable value chain with a low price," Museo Nacional Thyssen-Bornemisza they're articulating the Scandinavian design challenge that maps directly to building design systems: can you create something that is beautiful, functional, accessible, sustainable, and scalable all at once?
Spotify as living Scandinavian design system
Spotify (Swedish, founded 2006) Pomeroll offers the most instructive case study. Their three design principles - Relevant ("the right info at the right time"), Human ("Spotify is rooted in technology but it's all about people"), and Unified ("everything we design looks and feels reassuringly Spotify") Spotify Design - are Scandinavian values encoded as design operations.
Their design system Encore evolved from a centralized model (GLUE) that became a bottleneck into a federated family of design systems matching Spotify's culture of "aligned autonomy." Spotify Design Btng Their typography journey reveals a broader trend: from Gotham -> Proxima Nova -> Circular (2015, geometric, clean) FontsArena -> Spotify Mix (2024, more expressive and human). Fonts In Use Rasmus Wangelin, Spotify's Global Head of Brand Design, explained the shift: "People want to connect to humanity a bit more and are pivoting away from things that feel too perfect, because they tend to feel a bit sterile and kind of impersonal." itsnicethat This is the Scandinavian correction applied to their own system - precision that went too far toward Swiss coldness, pulled back toward warmth.
Sweden's design heritage is remarkable for a nation of ~10 million: Spotify, Klarna, Skype, Minecraft, IKEA, H&M, Volvo, Ericsson - and Rasmus Andersson, the Swedish designer who created Inter (the de facto Swiss-digital typeface) while at Figma. The fact that the world's most-used Swiss-style screen font was designed by a Swede captures the cross-pollination perfectly.
Building warmth into dense tools
For productivity tools, Scandinavian design offers a critical intervention: making complex tools feel approachable without sacrificing power. Use warm neutral backgrounds (off-whites around #FAFAF8 , not stark white), rounded corners and soft shadows (organic forms that feel human), generous line-heights for breathing room, and typography that balances precision with personality. The Scandinavian approach to data density: clarity through restraint, but not at the expense of power - every element must serve a purpose but feel approachable.
For design systems, encode accessibility as a first-class dimension - not retrofitted but foundational. This connects directly to democratic design: if your components don't work for everyone, they fail the Scandinavian test. Color contrast ratios become design constraints, not afterthoughts. Focus states are visible but not jarring. Screen reader support is built into the component API.
Scandinavian design excels at onboarding (warm, inviting, anxiety-reducing), trust (clean, honest design critical for fintech and health tech), and long-term engagement (designs that don't fatigue). Its limitation: it can trend toward generic - the ubiquity of "Scandi-style" means it can feel like undifferentiated "Airbnb minimalism" without distinctive character.
Where traditions collide, overlap, and synthesize
The hidden connections between all four
These traditions are not isolated islands - they share deep structural connections. Max Bill studied at the Bauhaus, PRINT Magazine became "the single most decisive influence on Swiss graphic design," Blogger then co-founded the Ulm School. Blogger PRINT Magazine He is literally the living bridge between German and Swiss design. Emil Ruder, the Swiss typography master, TypeRoom was "fond of asymmetry, a concept he found in Japanese texts on Zen philosophy and tea drinking" Blogger - Swiss rationalism absorbing Japanese spatial thinking.
The Japanese-Bauhaus connection runs deeper than commonly known. Johannes Itten's Bauhaus preparatory course drew on Japanese ink painting and Buddhist philosophy. Something Curated Japanese students attended the Bauhaus in the late 1920s, and Pen ペン Renshichiro Kawakita opened the "Japanese Bauhaus" in Tokyo in 1931. Something Curated Photographer Yasuhiro Ishimoto, trained at Chicago's New Bauhaus, discovered that Japan's Katsura Imperial Villa and Bauhaus modernism were "markedly similar" - photographing the Villa revealed it as "a series of rectangular forms a la Mondrian," Mastermind showing that modernism mirrors the visual cues of Japanese ma.
The Japandi movement Muji Renovation (emerging ~early 2010s) formally fuses Japanese wabi-sabi with Scandinavian hygge: Japanese Taste MUJI both traditions value nature connection, craftsmanship, material honesty, and functional restraint. Paradigm Press Japandi Supply House MUJI and IKEA are frequently compared Envato - "the IKEA of the East" - though their philosophical roots diverge (Japanese emptiness vs. Swedish democratic accessibility).
All four traditions are branches of the modernist tree: rejecting ornament, embracing function, seeking universal communication. Robern The difference is temperament - German rationalism, Swiss objectivity, Japanese spirituality, Scandinavian humanism - applied to a shared project.
The productive tensions that sharpen your design decisions
The most valuable insight is understanding where traditions disagree, because these tensions force design decisions:
Swiss rigidity vs. Japanese organic flow. Swiss design uses mathematically constructed grids as backbone. Justinmind Japanese design embraces asymmetry rooted in nature and organic rhythms. Presentation Zen The resolution: use the Swiss grid as structural foundation but apply Ma within it - let elements breathe more than feels "efficient." The "wasted" space actually reduces cognitive load.
German systematic precision vs. Scandinavian human warmth. Rams pursued "neutral" products that "won't become out of style." Explore Everyday Scandinavian design explicitly centers comfort and coziness. Apple's evolution shows this tension in action - Hartmut Esslinger (German designer hired by Apple) coined "form follows emotion" to counterbalance cold rationalism. Smithsonian Magazine The resolution: systematize with German rigor (design tokens, mathematical scales) but choose warm values (natural color palettes, generous line heights, readable sizes).
Cold rationalism (Swiss/German) vs. warmth (Scandinavian/Japanese). This is the central tension in modern design. Swiss/German can produce what critics called "a cold, emotionally sterile grid style." Blogger Scandinavian/Japanese generate warmth through natural materials, organic imperfection, and human-centered comfort. The Modern Dane The resolution: use Swiss/German for structure, Scandinavian/Japanese for surface treatment and spatial philosophy.
Apple as paradigm of multi-tradition synthesis
Apple is the most instructive case of blending traditions. German (via Rams): Steve Jobs and Jony Ive explicitly drew from Rams' ten principles Palos Publishing - the iPod echoed the Braun T3, the calculator mirrored the ET44. MIDMODMOOD Weekly Cult of Mac Japanese Zen: Jobs was a Zen Buddhist practitioner who said "I have always found Buddhism - Japanese Zen Buddhism in particular - to be aesthetically sublime." Maya Lin observed that "he embraced minimalism, which came from his Zen devotion to simplicity, but he avoided allowing that to make his products cold." Smithsonian Magazine Swiss typography: Jobs' calligraphy class at Reed College led to the Mac's typography revolution; Apple's marketing uses Swiss-style grids and clean sans-serif type. Envato Scandinavian warmth: Esslinger injected "a bit of rebellion and natural sex appeal" to counterbalance cold rationalism. Smithsonian Magazine
A framework for choosing which tradition to apply
Rather than adopting one tradition wholesale, the most effective approach is contextual deployment - recognizing which tradition's strengths match each design challenge:
For data-dense productivity tools (dashboards, dev tools, project management), lead with Swiss grid systems and typographic hierarchy supported by German systematic rigor. Muller-Brockmann's grids ensure scannability; Rams's "thorough down to the last detail" ensures every state is designed. Linear proves this combination works.
For marketing and landing pages, lead with Scandinavian warmth (emotional connection, trust-building) supported by Japanese Ma (generous whitespace creating calm authority). Emotional warmth drives conversion; breathing room creates the perception of confidence and quality.
For design systems and component libraries, lead with German Bauhaus systematic thinking supported by Swiss typographic consistency. Systems need modular, repeatable, scale-invariant components. Vignelli's Unigrid system for US National Parks - where the same grid structure adapts to brochures of any size - is the model. Pixartprinting
For consumer apps and onboarding flows, lead with Scandinavian democratic design (accessibility, human warmth) supported by Japanese craft and subtle detail. Fukasawa's "Without Thought" - interfaces that dissolve into behavior Wikipedia - is the aspiration.
Building the hybrid design system
The most powerful design system draws from all four traditions in layers:
Structure layer (Swiss + German): Mathematical grid systems on an 8px base unit. Cieden Systematic type scales with limited typefaces - Inter or one well-chosen sans-serif plus one monospace. Modular, composable components following Bauhaus industrial thinking. Strict alignment and visual hierarchy from Swiss objectivity.
Space layer (Japanese): Intentional, generous whitespace that creates breathing room - Kenya Hara's "emptiness as potential." Lars Muller Publishers Asymmetric balance within the grid, influenced by Ruder's Zen-inspired typography. Content density that varies purposefully - dense where needed, spacious where breathing serves comprehension.
Warmth layer (Scandinavian): Color palettes rooted in nature - warm neutrals, soft grays, muted accent tones rather than synthetic primaries. Accessibility as first-class concern (WCAG compliance as design constraint, not afterthought). Microcopy in a friendly, human voice. Subtle texture and materiality for tactile quality.
Precision layer (German): Every element justifies its existence through Rams's filter. Systematic token-based design where spacing, typography, and color all derive from mathematical systems. Durability and timelessness over trends. Ruthless functional testing before aesthetic polish.
Conclusion: the "Super Normal" aspiration
The deepest insight from studying all four traditions is Naoto Fukasawa and Jasper Morrison's "Super Normal" concept - design that is so good it disappears. Their 2006 exhibition included works by Jacobsen (Scandinavian), Rams (German), Bill (Swiss), and Noguchi (Japanese-American), literally curating across all four traditions to identify objects of "satisfying modesty." Morrison wrote: "The design world has drifted away from normality... Super Normal is a bridge between the two worlds."
Applied to your productivity tools, marketing sites, and design systems, this means the interface should feel inevitable, not designed. Users accomplish tasks without noticing the design - they only feel its absence of friction. Swiss grids give you the invisible skeleton. Japanese Ma gives you the breathing room that prevents cognitive overload. Scandinavian warmth ensures complex tools feel approachable rather than hostile. German systematic thinking ensures your components compose reliably at scale.
The designer who understands these four traditions doesn't pick one - they deploy each contextually, knowing that a data table needs Swiss clarity, an empty state needs Japanese emptiness-as-potential, an onboarding flow needs Scandinavian warmth, and the underlying system architecture needs German rigor. Kenya Hara's most useful insight for any design engineer: "Emptiness is itself a possibility of being filled." Your job is not to fill every pixel - it's to create the conditions where users' work becomes the most important thing on screen.

Compare Motion (formerly Framer Motion) and GSAP across bundle size, performance, and licensing. Copy page Copy page Presented by + On this page Adoption Licensing Performance Features Conclusion On this page Adoption Adoption Licensing Performance Features Conclusion The professional animation toolkit. One payment / Lifetime updates Get Motion+ Get Motion+ Advertise here When deciding which JavaScript animation library to trust for your project, two libraries often get mentioned because of their feature set and popularity: Motion (formerly Framer Motion) and GSAP (formerly GreenSock). Both can create stunning animations, but they have fundamental differences. This guide compares Motion and GSAP on adoption, licensing, performance, and features (complete with full comparison table), to help you decide which is right for your project. Adoption Before delving into the libraries themselves, it's helpful to see what other developers are choosing. For modern applications, npm is a great measure of a library's adoption and momentum. Here, the numbers are clear: Motion is growing exponentially, making it the most-used and fastest-growing animation library in the ecosystem. It even just passed 16 million downloads per month. Licensing Motion is fully independent and MIT open source. It's financially supported by a mix of incredible industry-leading sponsors like Framer, Figma, Sanity, Tailwind CSS and LottieFiles, as well as sales from Motion+. GSAP, by contrast, is closed source and owned and funded by Webflow. While it can be used for free in many projects, its license contains a critical restriction: You're prohibited from using GSAP in any tool that competes with Webflow. Furthermore, its license states that Webflow can terminate it at its discretion. With Motion, you have a guarantee of freedom. That MIT license is irrevocable. You will never be forced to remove and replace your animation library because of a business decision made by another company. This provides the stability and peace of mind that professional development teams require. Motion's independence and self-sufficiency also means we work with a broad base of users and companies, creating a library that works for the whole web, rather than the interests of a single company. Performance Performance is more than just smooth animations. It's about providing a flawless 120fps, faster start-up times, and minimal bundle sizes. This is where Motion's modern architecture provides an advantage. Hardware accelerated animations You might already know that for best animation performance you should stick to animating opacity , transform , filter and clipPath , because these styles can be rendered entirely on the GPU. But when animating with Motion, these values can enjoy an extra performance boost using "hardware accelerated" animations. This means the animations themselves also run entirely the GPU - separate from the JavaScript running on your CPU. This means if your website or app is performing heavy work, animations remain smooth. To illustrate, in the following example the ball on the left is animated with Motion, and the ball on the right by a traditional animation library. Press the "Block JavaScript" button to block JS execution for two seconds: In the majority of browsers, the left ball will continue animating at 60/120fps, even as the website becomes unresponsive. Traditional animation libraries like GSAP will pause and stutter where Motion remains perfectly smooth. What's more, Motion can even perform hardware accelerated scroll animations. Because browsers render all scroll on the GPU, JS-based scroll animations are always slightly out-of-sync. Not so with Motion. ``` const animation = animate(element, { opacity: [0, 1] }) scroll(animation) ``` Copy code Copy code Start-up time Two animate any two values, they have to be mixable. Think, two numbers, or two colors. But what if we want to perform an animation where we don't even know the initial value? Or we do - but it's a value like height: auto , or a color defined in a CSS variable like var(—my-color) ? To make these values mixable, the library first needs to measure them. But measuring something that's just been rendered forces a layout or style calculation. These are slow. To solve this, Motion introduced deferred keyframe resolution. This ensures we batch all measurements into a single operation, drastically reducing style and layout calculations. In benchmarks, Motion is 2.5x faster than GSAP at animating from unknown values, and 6x faster at animating between different value types. This is great for user experience, and also great for performance scores like Interaction to Next Paint (INP). Bundle size Motion is built with a modern, modular architecture. If your bundler supports tree-shaking (like Vite, Rollup or Webpack), you only ever include the code you actually use. GSAP's older architecture, by contrast, means that importing any part of the library includes all of it. This, combined with Motion's focus on leveraging native browser APIs, results in a significantly smaller footprint. | Library | Size | | --- | --- | | animate() (mini) | 2.6kb | | animate() (full) | 18kb | | GSAP | 23kb | A smaller bundle means a faster site load and a better user experience, especially on mobile devices. With Motion, you can deliver stunning animations with a minimal performance cost. S A B C D F Find & fix animation performance issues with your agent. MotionScore for Agents grades animations in your source code S to F and hands your agent specific fixes before you ship. Part of the Motion+ AI Kit. Get the AI Kit Features Of course, performance means little if a library can't deliver the features you need. While there is plenty of overlap, both libraries have unique strengths. React & Vue APIs Motion provides a first-class, declarative API that is a natural extension of React and Vue. Animations are defined directly in your components via props, keeping your code clean, readable and easy to maintain. ``` ``` Copy code Copy code GSAP, by contrast, uses an imperative model. While it has a useGSAP hook to help integrate into React's lifecycles, it still requires using refs. Mixing its imperative API into React's declarative components leads to more verbose and error-prone code. ``` const container = useRef() useGSAP(() => { gsap.to(".box", { x: 100 }) }, { scope: container }) return (
); ``` Copy code Copy code Furthermore, Motion for React and Vue features an industry-leading layout animation engine, which goes far beyond the FLIP animations in GSAP. Timelines & sequencing GSAP is famous for its powerful timeline function, which uses an imperative, chain-based API to build complex animation sequences. It's mature, and an industry standard for good reason. ``` const tl = gsap.timeline() tl.to("h1", { opacity: 1 }) tl.to("p", { y: 0 }, "-=0.5") ``` Copy code Copy code Motion provides a modern, declarative alternative. Instead of chain-based commands, animate() accepts a simple JavaScript array, making it easy to read, modify and dynamically generate animation sequences. ``` animate([ ["h1", { opacity: 1 }], ["p", { y: 0 }, { at: "-0.5" }] ]) ``` Copy code Copy code This timeline can animate anything the animate() function can, mixing HTML elements, SVG elements, motion values, and even 3D objects from libraries like Three.js - all within the same sequence. As mentioned earlier, it's also 5kb lighter. The benefit to GSAP's timeline API is that it's mutable. Once playback has begun, individual tracks can be added and removed to the overarching sequence, an ability that Motion doesn't yet offer. Motion is an animation library that's easy to start and fun to master.
Its unique hybrid engine combines the performance of the browser with the limitless potential of a JavaScript engine. This means you can animate anything, like:
HTML/CSS
SVG (like path drawing animations)
WebGL (3D graphics)
The best part? It's also tiny, with a mini HTML/SVG version of the animate() function that's just 2.3kb!
By the end of this quick guide, you'll have installed Motion and made your first animation.
Tap to unmute
Your browser can't play this video.
Learn more 
Video guide Open video
Install
You can install Motion in two ways:
A package manager like npm or Yarn ( most popular)
HTML script tag
Package manager
Motion can be installed via the "motion" package.
```
npm install motion
```
Copy code Copy code
Then imported in your JavaScript:
```
import { animate, scroll } from "motion"
```
Copy code Copy code
script tag
It's possible to import Motion directly using a script tag. This is perfect if you're working with a basic HTML page, or using a no-code tool like Webflow.
Import using the modern import syntax:
```
<script type="module">
  import { animate, scroll } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/motion@latest/+esm"
</script>
```
Copy code Copy code
Or you can add Motion as a global variable using the legacy include:
```
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/motion@latest/dist/motion.js"></script>
<script>
  const { animate, scroll } = Motion
</script>
```
Copy code Copy code
NOTE
It's best practise to replace "latest" in these URLs with a specific version, like 11.11.13 . You can find the latest version in the site footer.
Create an animation
The "Hello world!" of any animation library is a simple transform animation.
Let's start by importing the animate function.
```
import { animate } from "motion"
```
Copy code Copy code animate can animate one or more elements. You can either use a CSS selector (like ".my-class" ) or provide the elements directly:
```
// CSS selector
animate(".box", { rotate: 360 })

// Elements
const boxes = document.querySelectorAll(".box")

animate(boxes, { rotate: 360 })
```
Copy code Copy code
You can see here we're setting rotate to 360 . This will rotate the element 360 degrees:
View source Open in Cursor Tutorial
Rotate Open example
What can be animated?
Motion lets you animate anything:
CSS properties (like opacity , transform and filter )
SVG attributes and paths
Independent transforms ( x , rotateY etc)
JavaScript objects (containing strings/colors/numbers)
With Motion, you don't have to worry about achieving the best performance available. When a value can be hardware accelerated, like opacity , filter or transform , it will be. animate isn't limited to HTML. It can animate single values or any kind of object. For example, the rotation of a Three.js object:
```
animate(
  cube.rotation,
  { y: rad(360), z: rad(360) },
  { duration: 10, repeat: Infinity, ease: "linear" }
)
```
Copy code Copy code
View source Open in Cursor Tutorial
Three.js Open example
Customising animations
View source Open in Cursor Tutorial
Basic animation Open example
Motion comes with smart defaults, so your animations should look and feel great out of the box. But you can further tweak options like:
Duration (how long the animation lasts)
Delay (how long it waits before starting)
Easing (how it speeds up and slows down)
Repeat (how it repeats, how many times, etc)
```
animate(
  element,
  { scale: [0.4, 1] },
  { ease: "circInOut", duration: 1.2 }
);
```
Copy code Copy code
Motion also has amazing spring animations for natural, kinetic animations:
```
animate(
  element,
  { rotate: 90 },
  { type: "spring", stiffness: 300 }
);
```
Copy code Copy code
View source Open in Cursor Tutorial
Spring Open example
Stagger animations
When animating multiple elements, it can feel more natural or lively to offset the animations of each. This is called staggering.
Motion provides a stagger function that can be used to dynamically set delay :
```
import { animate, stagger } from "motion"

animate(
  "li",
  { y: 0, opacity: 1 },
  { delay: stagger(0.1) }
)
```
Copy code Copy code
View source Open in Cursor Tutorial
Stagger Open example
Development tools
The Motion AI Kit provides visual editing and AI tools to enhance your animation development workflow, like inline bezier editing, CSS spring generation and more. Those two need Motion+.
The kit's /motion skill and its installer are free and open source (MIT): run npx motion-ai to install them, or read the source on GitHub.
One click install for Cursor
Documentation search is free. No token, account or configuration is required. Motion+ unlocks CSS spring generation, MotionScore performance audits, plus example and Motion UI source in the editor.
Add Motion for Cursor
Using Claude Code, Codex or another agent? See the AI Kit install guide.
What's next?
You've just learned the basics of Motion and created a simple animation. But there's so much more to discover, like:
Keyframes and sequences: Create more complex animations
Controls: Pause, resume or change animations
Scroll-linked animations: Link values to scroll position
Scroll-triggered animations: Trigger animations when elements enter the viewport
Or you can dive straight into our examples, which include copy & paste source code to add straight to your project.

You may also want to constrain its height to not exceed the viewport. We expose several CSS custom properties such as --radix-hover-card-trigger-width and --radix-hover-card-content-available-height to support this. Use them to constrain the content dimensions. ``` // index.jsx import { HoverCard } from "radix-ui"; import "./styles.css"; export default () => ( … … ); ``` ``` /* styles.css */ .HoverCardContent { width: var(--radix-hover-card-trigger-width); max-height: var(--radix-hover-card-content-available-height); } ``` Origin-aware animations We expose a CSS custom property --radix-hover-card-content-transform-origin . Use it to animate the content from its computed origin based on side , sideOffset , align , alignOffset and any collisions. ``` // index.jsx import { HoverCard } from "radix-ui"; import "./styles.css"; export default () => ( … … ); ``` ``` /* styles.css */ .HoverCardContent { transform-origin: var(--radix-hover-card-content-transform-origin); animation: scaleIn 0.5s ease-out; } @keyframes scaleIn { from { opacity: 0; transform: scale(0); } to { opacity: 1; transform: scale(1); } } ``` Collision-aware animations We expose data-side and data-align attributes. Their values will change at runtime to reflect collisions. Use them to create collision and direction-aware animations. ``` // index.jsx import { HoverCard } from "radix-ui"; import "./styles.css"; export default () => ( … … ); ``` ``` /* styles.css */ .HoverCardContent { animation-duration: 0.6s; animation-timing-function: cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1); } .HoverCardContent[data-side="top"] { animation-name: slideUp; } .HoverCardContent[data-side="bottom"] { animation-name: slideDown; } @keyframes slideUp { from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(10px); } to { opacity: 1; transform: translateY(0); } } @keyframes slideDown { from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(-10px); } to { opacity: 1; transform: translateY(0); } } ``` Accessibility The hover card is intended for sighted users only, the content will be inaccessible to keyboard users. Preface
The term Information Architecture (IA) was coined by a brick-and-mortar architect Richard Wurman in the early 1970s as a profession of “gathering, organizing, and presenting information.” The World Wide Web accelerated the information explosion and created the real needs for the profession to help more people find and manage useful information online. Similarly, User Experience (UX), a term first used by Don Norman at Apple Computer in the 1990s, grew exponentially along with the web. Our revised third edition positions IA and UX design are two sides of the same humancentered design (HCD) coin. IA is associated with taxonomy, metadata, thesaurus, and other “information findability” related tasks that often happen behind the scenes, along with labeling and defining channels for information access. UX design is responsible for the vision and design solutions that people interact with and experience. The authors believe that the continuous evolution of the information spaces supported by the web, cloud, and Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies makes it possible to deliver ever more sophisticated interactions and user activities. The increasing importance of large language models (LLMs) and Generative AI (GenAI) have had profound impacts on work, play, and society at large. UX and AI converge in human-centered AI (HCAI), with the responsibility to make AI work for people. This requires a team effort including data scientists, machine learning engineers, developers, product owners, graphic designers, user researchers, and many more. Convergence calls for higher level of seamless collaboration among all the disciplines, but it does not eliminate the need for dedicated IA and UX work. Instead, this work spreads from traditional web design to digital devices, apps, medical devices, automobiles, and many other places. IAs and UX designers are part of the team determining the business and UX strategy, based on user needs and business goals, and making sure the strategy gets carried out.

Preface
Drawing on the authors' extensive experience as practitioners, HCI researchers, and IA instructors, this book outlines a balanced view of the UX discipline by connecting practitioner's real-world experience and IA/UX practices to human information behavioral theories, design principles, and guidelines. In addition to demonstrating conventional IA deliverables, techniques, and tools, this book emphasizes that IA is about the design and integration of information spaces (both digital and physical) beyond the Web. This expansion requires new skillsets like Design Thinking and Systems Thinking, to analyze and design highly interconnected systems that exponentially increase the benefits to the people in them.
Uses of the Book This book is a result of our teaching of a graduate-level course on Information Architecture at Drexel University for many years. The content has been constantly updated to incorporate the latest developments in the field—including GenAI and Systems Thinking for this third edition. The objective of the course was to introduce fundamental IA/UX concepts, theories, processes, and techniques in the context of human-centered design, to graduate students majored in Information Sciences and Information Systems. As the book was originally written as lecture notes, we believe it is most suitable to be used as textbook for similar courses in other schools. The key features of the book include concise discussions structured around each topic and the balanced coverage of theoretical and practical issues. As Drexel's courses are quarter courses typically include 10 lecture weeks, we have conveniently structured the book into ten chapters, one for each week. The content for each week can be easily expanded when used for a semester course. User experience practitioners should also find this book useful and inspiring as a starting point in their exploration of this exciting field. We hope this book can help bridge the gap between the community of practice and academia.
Structure of the Book The book covers the following topics: • Information Architecture and UX Design: Definition and Evolution: Chapter 1 discusses the definition of Information Architecture and UX in the context of integrated information spaces, its impact on the way people interact with information, and relationships to other disciplines. Chapter 2 takes a historical perspective to examine the evolution of the web and beyond, and identifies new challenges and opportunities for UX in the context of a generative generation marked by rapid development of GenAI.
Preface
vii
•
Human-Centered Design methods and principles: Chapter 3 introduces the HumanCentered Design methodology, which is the prerequisite for conducting any IA/UX practices. As the core of the book, Chaps. 4–7 are dedicated to the IA key concepts and foundations including information organization and navigation, human information behavior, and the corresponding design implications, as well as interaction design patterns, principles, and best practices. These chapters incorporate the latest developments in the field like AI for user research, and reflect the current state of knowledge for usability researchers and user experience design professionals. • Design Thinking and Systems Thinking: This new Chap. 8 compares Design Thinking and Systems Thinking, two important approaches for integrating information spaces. We share the zoom-in/zoom-out approach, examining systems from a high level in Systems Thinking to find leverage points where and intervention may have a substantial impact, and the more detailed approach in Design Thinking to craft human-centered solutions that are also viable for the business. • IA in Practice: In Chap. 9, the design and development team is discussed. Frameworks like Agile development and Lean UX are related to the ideas presented in previous chapters. The growing importance of team culture is also shared. • The Future of Information Architecture: Chapter 10 identifies IA trends and future directions, including global and increasing AI considerations. We urge practitioners to work together to continue to promote and grow the discipline to help improve people's lives through design. The chapter ends with a revisit of the IA definition used throughout the book. Washington, DC, USA Philadelphia, PA, USA Ambler, PA, USA

Information Architecture and UX Design: Definitions and Scope
Information architecture (IA) and User Experience Design (UX) is an exciting area of study that is growing in importance in academics, industry, as well as in everyday life. As we all interact with technology—websites, search engines, mobile apps, or smart home devices, why do we have good experience with some of them but not others? Who creates and designs these things that make our life pleasant (or miserable)? How to structure information in a usable way so that we can all find it when we need it? Clearly, it is valuable to study the “space” between human cognitive abilities, information content, and the context of use. Enter Information Architecture and User Experience Design, an interdisciplinary field that is rooted in psychology, ergonomics, user interface design, system design, information organization, information access, and information use. IA and UX design are critical in many aspects of our world today. While our primary focus will be on web and mobile applications, the principles we discuss are applicable to any digital information space, including medical devices, home automation systems, and more. We consider the terms IA and UX designer mostly interchangeable and will use them throughout the book. IA is typically used when working with the information content and structure, while UX designer is used when discussing the user interface and interaction. In the following chapters, we will explore the growing demand for exceptional design in our society. Our goal is to provide you with the knowledge and skills needed to become capable of creating user-friendly and useful digital experiences.

1 Information Architecture and UX Design: Definitions and Scope
1.1
Definitions of Information Architecture
Information architecture is a field of study, a field of practice, and a discipline that changes as the use of technologies evolves. Like many other evolving disciplines, there exist many definitions of information architecture. Let's start with a look at a few examples of the definitions first. One cannot talk about information architecture without mentioning Richard Saul Wurman, who coined the term “Information Architecture” or, at least, brought it to wide attention in the 1970s. Wurman was trained as an architect and skilled at graphical design, but “making information understandable” has been “the singular passion of his life.” He sees the problems of gathering, organizing, and presenting information as closely analogous to the problems an architect faces in designing a building that will serve the needs of its occupants. His definition of information architects emphasizes the organization and presentation of information (Wurman, 1996): (1) the individual who organizes the patterns inherent in data, making the complex clear. (2) a person who creates the structure or map of information which allows others to find their personal paths to knowledge. (3) the emerging 21st century professional occupation addressing the needs of the age focused upon clarity, human understanding, and the science of the organization of information.
While Wurman insightfully bridged information with architecture, Morville et al. (2015) brought information architecture to the mainstream with their popular “polar bear” book on information architecture. In the fourth edition (with Jorge Arango as an additional author), the authors took a multi-perspective approach to define information architecture: 1. The structural design of shared information environments 2. The synthesis of organization, labeling, search, and navigation systems within digital, physical, and cross-channel ecosystems 3. The art and science of shaping information products and experience to support usability and findability, and understanding 4. An emerging discipline and community of practice focused on bringing principles of design and architecture to the digital landscape (p. 24). This definition provides a focus on structure, cross-channel systems, findability and usability, and finally the spirit of IA—bringing principles of design (art) and architecture (science) to the digital landscape. Resmini and Rosati (2011) similarly emphasize in their definition that, as the pervasive information environment evolves, “information architecture was moving into uncharted territories becoming a boundary practice whose contributions were crucial where complexity, unfamiliarity, and information overload
